***Applying SLAP***
* When you notice a function mixing levels, extract the low-level details into well-named helper functions whose names **express the next level of detail**.
* The top-level function becomes a readable summary — almost a table of contents — of the work.
* This is the **Composed Method** pattern (Kent Beck, _Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns_, 1996): build functions from calls to other methods at the same conceptual level.

***Relation to Clean Code***
Robert C. Martin formalised SLAP as one of the function-design rules in _Clean Code_ (2008), alongside "Functions should be small", "Do one thing", and "Use descriptive names". SLAP is the organising principle that makes "small functions" readable rather than just fragmented.

***Key Proponents***: Kent Beck (_Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns_, 1996 — "Composed Method"), Robert C. Martin (_Clean Code_, 2008).

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Refactoring a long function that "does too much" — SLAP tells you **how** to split it, not just that you should
* Code review: a natural smell-detector for functions that mix orchestration with mechanics
* Teaching junior developers a concrete, checkable rule that produces readable code
* Designing a new algorithm top-down: write the high-level steps as calls to not-yet-existing helpers, then fill them in
* Reconstructing the intent of legacy code — lift the orchestration out and the design becomes visible

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Cohesion Criteria - SLAP produces functional cohesion by keeping a function focused on one conceptual step
* KISS Principle - SLAP is one concrete technique for keeping functions simple
* SOLID SRP - SRP applies at the class level what SLAP applies at the function level
* Clean Architecture - Layered abstraction at the architectural scale mirrors SLAP at the code scale

### SOLID-Dependency Inversion Principle

***Full Name***: SOLID Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

[discrete]
## **Intent**:
High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:
* High-level business logic directly instantiates infrastructure classes
* Changing a database or framework requires modifying business logic
* Unit testing requires running actual external services

[discrete]
## **Prompt Example**:
"Refactore diese Klasse nach dem SOLID-Dependency Inversion Principle, sodass die Abhängigkeiten über Interfaces injiziert werden."

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:
* SOLID Principles (Umbrella)
* Hexagonal Architecture - Architectural application of DIP

### SOLID-Interface Segregation Principle

***Full Name***: SOLID Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

[discrete]
## **Intent**:
Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. Prefer many specific interfaces over one general-purpose interface.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:
* Classes implement interface methods they don't need (empty or throwing)
* Changes to an interface affect clients that don't use the changed methods
* Fat interfaces with many methods serving different client groups

[discrete]
## **Prompt Example**:
"Refactore dieses Interface nach dem SOLID-Interface Segregation Principle in kleinere, clientspezifische Interfaces."

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:
* SOLID Principles (Umbrella)

### SOLID-Liskov Substitution Principle

***Full Name***: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

[discrete]
## **Intent**:
Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program. Derived classes must honor the contracts of their base classes.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:
* Subclass overrides break expected behavior of the base class
* instanceof/type checks appear in client code
* Inheritance hierarchies violate "is-a" relationships

[discrete]
## **Prompt Example**:
"Überprüfe diese Vererbungshierarchie auf Verletzungen des SOLID-Liskov Substitution Principle."

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:
* SOLID Principles (Umbrella)

### SOLID-Open/Closed Principle

***Full Name***: SOLID Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

[discrete]
## **Intent**:
Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. Add new behavior by adding new code, not changing existing code.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:
* Adding new features requires modifying existing working code
* Frequent changes to a module break other parts of the system
* You need a plugin or strategy-based extension mechanism

[discrete]
## **Prompt Example**:
"Refactore diesen Code nach dem SOLID-Open/Closed Principle, sodass neue Varianten ohne Änderung des bestehenden Codes hinzugefügt werden können."

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:
* SOLID Principles (Umbrella)
* GoF-Strategy Pattern - Common OCP implementation

### SOLID Principles

***Full Name***: SOLID Object-Oriented Design Principles

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)***: Each class should have one responsibility

***Open/Closed Principle (OCP)***: Entities should be open for extension, closed for modification

***Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)***: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types

***Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)***: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use

***Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)***: Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations

***Key Proponent***: Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob")

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing maintainable and scalable object-oriented systems
* Refactoring legacy code to improve structure
* Building systems where flexibility and testability are important
* Teaching or enforcing good software design practices

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Dan North, https://dannorth.net/cupid-for-joyful-coding/["CUPID — for joyful coding"] (2022; preceded by his 2017 talk "Why Every Single Element of SOLID is Wrong") — the principles are too vague to guide decisions ("responsibility" is undefined) and optimise for a style of OO design that mainstream practice has moved past; he proposes the CUPID properties as an alternative
* John Ousterhout, https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/book.php["A Philosophy of Software Design"] (2018) — SRP-driven decomposition produces many shallow classes whose interfaces add more complexity than their implementations hide; he argues for fewer, deeper modules
* The principles rest on anecdote and authority rather than empirical evidence — a recurring point in the debate around both critiques

### SOLID-Single Responsibility Principle

***Full Name***: SOLID Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

[discrete]
## **Intent**:
A class should have only one reason to change. Each module or class should be responsible for a single part of the software's functionality.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:
* A class has multiple unrelated responsibilities
* Changes to one feature require modifying unrelated code
* Unit testing requires complex setup due to tangled concerns

[discrete]
## **Prompt Example**:
"Refactore diese Klasse nach dem SOLID-Single Responsibility Principle. Trenne die Verantwortlichkeiten in separate Klassen."

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:
* SOLID Principles (Umbrella)

### SSOT (Single Source of Truth)

***Full Name***: Single Source of Truth

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Conceptual principle***: Focuses on establishing trust and authority for data

***Authoritative source***: One canonical, trusted location for each piece of data

***Data integrity***: All consumers reference the same trusted source

***Version control***: Single source ensures consistent versioning

***Derived data***: Other representations are derived from the single source

***Trust and reliability***: The source is the definitive version when conflicts arise

***System of record***: The primary data store for critical business information

***Organizational practice***: Applied at the architecture and business process level

[discrete]
## **Key Application Areas**:

* Version control systems (Git as SSOT for code)
* Database design and data warehousing
* Documentation and knowledge management
* Configuration management
* Master data management (MDM)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing data architecture for enterprise systems
* Establishing documentation standards and knowledge bases
* Building data pipelines and ETL processes
* Implementing microservices with clear data ownership
* Creating audit trails and ensuring compliance
* Resolving conflicts between multiple data sources

***Difference from SPOT***: SSOT emphasizes the authoritative, trusted nature of a data source and is used at the architecture/organizational level, while SPOT focuses on the implementation pattern

***Related Concepts***: DRY, SPOT, Event sourcing, Data lakes, Master data management

### Tufte Style

***Full Name***: Tufte Style -- the information-design principles of Edward R. Tufte

***Also known as***: Tufte's principles of information design. In tooling the eponym is already a style token: `theme_tufte` in R's ggthemes, https://edwardtufte.github.io/tufte-css/[Tufte CSS], the https://ctan.org/pkg/tufte-latex[tufte-latex] document classes, `matplotlib-tufte`.

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **Data-ink ratio.** Of all the ink on the page, the share that encodes data should be as large as it usefully can be. Gridlines, frames, fills, shadows and 3-D effects encode no data; at best they help the eye find its way. They are therefore the first candidates for removal, not automatic deletions: a gridline that lets the eye read a value off the chart is doing work, and muting it usually beats deleting it.
* **Chartjunk.** The name for decoration that competes with the evidence -- moiré patterns, ornamental icons, gratuitous colour. Naming it as a defect is what makes it removable.
* **Graphical integrity, measured by the lie factor.** The size of the effect shown should equal the size of the effect in the data. A distorted axis or a scaled-area icon is a quantitative error, not a matter of taste.
* **Small multiples.** Repeat one compact panel across subsets on identical axes. The comparison then happens in the eye rather than in the reader's memory.
* **Sparklines.** A word-sized graphic set inside the sentence it belongs to, so the number and its history occupy the same line.
* **Direct labelling instead of legends.** Put the name on the line. A legend forces the reader to hold a colour in memory and look it up again for every mark.
* **Density is the point, not emptiness.** This is the distinction that decides whether the term was understood: remove what carries no information, then spend the reclaimed space on more information. A Tufte-style page usually contains **more** than the one it replaces.
* **Words, numbers and images belong together.** Caption, annotation and graphic sit in one place rather than in three. The sidenote layout that carries Tufte's name is this principle applied to running text.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing a dashboard or a status report, especially where the default is large KPI tiles, gauges and traffic lights
* Reviewing a chart before it goes into documentation, a slide deck or a paper
* Anywhere a graphic has to survive being printed in black and white, or read at a glance
* When a report has grown to several pages because each number was given its own panel

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Reading it as minimalism.** A minimalist chart contains little; a Tufte-style chart often contains a great deal and merely wastes no ink. Stripping detail to look clean inverts the principle.
* **Treating it as a visual skin.** It is a set of decisions about evidence -- what is compared, at what scale, against what baseline -- not a palette and a font.
* **Taking the data-ink ratio for a law.** It is a heuristic, and experiment has put some of its premises in question. See _Criticism_.
* **Confusing the two things the name covers.** "Tufte style" names both the chart principles and the sidenote page layout of Tufte CSS and tufte-latex. They share an author and a motive, but a request for one does not deliver the other; say which you mean.

## **Criticism**:

* **The data-ink position was tested empirically, and it did not survive intact.** Bateman, Mandryk, Gutwin, Genest, McDine and Brooks put embellished charts against plain ones in https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/communication/Bateman2010.pdf["Useful Junk?"] (CHI 2010) and report: "people's accuracy in describing the embellished charts was no worse than for plain charts, and their recall after a two-to-three-week gap was significantly better. Although we are cautious about recommending that all charts be produced in this style, our results question some of the premises of the minimalist approach to chart design." Decoration that aids memory is not junk by Tufte's own criterion of usefulness.
* **Readers do not want the minimum either.** Inbar, Tractinsky and Meyer, https://cris.bgu.ac.il/en/publications/minimalism-in-information-visualization-attitudes-towards-maximiz/["Minimalism in information visualization"] (ECCE 2007): "The results indicate a clear preference of non-minimalist bar-graphs, suggesting low acceptance of minimalist design principles such as high data-ink ratio." This measures preference, not comprehension -- a weaker claim than Bateman's, and worth keeping separate.
* **The debate is live, not settled, and it has defenders on Tufte's side.** Stephen Few, writing from the same minimalist position, takes Bateman's conclusion apart in https://www.perceptualedge.com/articles/visual_business_intelligence/the_chartjunk_debate.pdf["The Chartjunk Debate"] (Perceptual Edge, 2011), objecting to the claim that "many examples exist of embellished charts that seem to be successful" with a flat "Many examples?" Harvard's own summary of Borkin et al.'s https://seas.harvard.edu/news/what-makes-data-visualization-memorable[memorability study] frames the field the same way: researchers teaming up "to settle a debate over 'chart junk'" that "still rages among visualization experts".
* **The Challenger analysis is contested by one of the engineers in it.** Wade Robison, **Roger Boisjoly**, David Hoeker and Stefan Young published "Representation and misrepresentation: Tufte and the Morton Thiokol engineers on the Challenger" in _Science and Engineering Ethics_ 8(1), January 2002, 59-81 -- and Boisjoly was one of the Thiokol engineers who argued against the launch. The paper "examines the role of the Morton Thiokol engineers in the decisions surrounding the launch of the Challenger, particularly with reference to an analysis of this event by Edward Tufte", and concludes "that the engineers thus did what they were ethically as well as professionally obligated to do" -- against Tufte's reading that a better graphic would have prevented the launch decision.
* **Don Norman attacks the PowerPoint essay, and the attack lands on the method.** In https://jnd.org/in-defense-of-powerpoint/["In Defense of PowerPoint"], responding to Tufte's _The Cognitive Style of PowerPoint_, Norman writes: "Just because Tufte, in hindsight (when he already knows the answers), can look back and show they were wrong, and then point to discrepancies in their presentation, does not mean the fault lies in the presentation, nor in the tool used to present it." He adds that on the slide in question, "the slide should have had less information on it -- Tufte wants more information."
* **Keep the three targets apart.** Bateman, Inbar and Borkin test the **principles**; Robison and colleagues dispute the **Challenger analysis**; Norman argues with the **PowerPoint essay** and the Columbia slide reading inside it. None of them is a rebuttal of the others, and the Columbia shuttle is not the Challenger.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The four books, as the publisher lists them.** https://www.edwardtufte.com/books/[Graphics Press] gives _The Visual Display of Quantitative Information_ as "1983 / 2nd Edition 2001" -- the same book under two years, and the second edition is the one in print. Then _Envisioning Information_ (1990), _Visual Explanations_ (1996, widely miscited as 1997) and _Beautiful Evidence_ (2006). A fifth, _Seeing with Fresh Eyes_, followed in 2020, so "his four books" is no longer accurate.
* **The name is baked into tooling, which is why it holds as an anchor.** `theme_tufte` in R's https://jrnold.github.io/ggthemes/reference/theme_tufte.html[ggthemes] cites the data-ink chapter by name: "No border, no axis lines, no grids." https://edwardtufte.github.io/tufte-css/[Tufte CSS] and the https://ctan.org/pkg/tufte-latex[tufte-latex] classes carry the sidenote layout; https://pypi.org/project/matplotlib-tufte/[matplotlib-tufte] carries the chart rules into Python. A term that ships as an installable default is one a model has seen in code as well as in prose.
* **The typographic branch is stable to the point of dormancy.** CTAN lists tufte-latex at 3.5.2 with its most recent announcement in 2015. That is not decay -- the layout was finished -- but it means the second meaning of the name lives on in copies rather than in active development.
* **There is no German-language critical tier to cite.** A search on 2026-08-25 across six German query forms returned method descriptions, university slides and translations of English originals; the German Wikipedia article has no Kritik section. What criticism exists from German-speaking practitioners is published in English -- the https://www.datawrapper.de/blog/bookclub-tufte-review/[Datawrapper book club], run from Berlin, is the clearest case. This is a language-frame result, not an absence of opinion: see the [prior-test register](#/prior-tests) for the terms searched.

### Unix Philosophy

***Also known as***: Software Tools philosophy, Unix design philosophy

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Do one thing well***: "Make each program do one thing well. To do a new job, build afresh rather than complicate old programs by adding new features." (Doug McIlroy, Bell System Technical Journal, 1978)

***Compose small tools***: Expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program; small sharp tools combine into larger workflows via pipes

***Text streams as universal interface***: "Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface" — plain text is the lingua franca that lets independent tools interoperate

***Build prototypes early***: Don't hesitate to throw away the clumsy parts and rebuild them; favour fast prototyping over over-design

***Worse is better***: Richard P. Gabriel's observation that simple, available implementations spread faster than elegant, complete ones — a descriptive lens on why the Unix style won

***Rule of Modularity***: Build a program out of simple parts connected by clean, well-defined interfaces (Eric S. Raymond)

***Rule of Composition***: Design programs to be connected to other programs; keep formats parseable so tools chain together (Eric S. Raymond)

***Rule of Silence***: "When a program has nothing surprising to say, it should say nothing" — quiet success keeps output usable as another program's input (Eric S. Raymond)

***Key Proponents***: Doug McIlroy (Bell System Technical Journal, 1978), Eric S. Raymond ("The Art of Unix Programming", 2003, with 17 design rules)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing CLI tools, scripts, and pipelines meant to compose with others
* Deciding whether to extend an existing program or build a separate, focused one
* Arguing for plain-text, line-oriented data formats over opaque binary blobs
* Reviewing a tool that is accumulating flags and feature creep
* Prompting an LLM to produce small, single-purpose, composable Unix-style programs

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Separation of Concerns
* DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)
* KISS Principle
* Code Smells

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Rob Pike and Brian Kernighan, "Program Design in the UNIX Environment" / "cat -v Considered Harmful" (1984) — argue that Unix itself drifted from the philosophy, with utilities like `cat` accreting flags (`-n`, `-s`, `-b`, `-v`) that violate "do one thing well"; summarized at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_philosophy[Unix philosophy (Wikipedia)]
* Simson Garfinkel, Daniel Weise, Steven Strassmann (eds.), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_UNIX-HATERS_Handbook[The UNIX-HATERS Handbook] (1994) — a compilation of the UNIX-HATERS mailing list attacking the "worse is better" design culture as a source of obscure flags, cryptic errors, and lost work
* Richard P. Gabriel, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worse_is_better["The Rise of Worse is Better"] (1989, published 1991) — frames the philosophy descriptively rather than as a virtue: simple-but-incomplete designs (C, Unix) outcompeted more correct, elegant ones (Lisp machines), implying the style spreads for market reasons, not because it is right

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The philosophy remains the conceptual core of CLI tooling, shells, and pipelines, but sits in tension with modern monolithic GUI/IDE and all-in-one platform tooling, where integration and discoverability are valued over composition of small text-stream tools
* Eric S. Raymond's https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_philosophy[17 rules] (2003) are the most cited modern codification; training-data priors most plausibly serve the McIlroy summary and Raymond's rules, while the Pike/Kernighan critique of Unix's own drift is the documented counter-current

### YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)

***Full Name***: You Aren't Gonna Need It

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Don't build for hypothetical futures***: Only implement functionality when it is actually needed, not when you foresee it might be needed

***Speculative generality***: Anti-pattern of building abstractions for imagined future requirements that may never materialize

***Incremental design***: Let design emerge through actual needs; evolve architecture as requirements become concrete

***Cost of carry***: Unused code adds maintenance burden, increases complexity, and creates cognitive load for the entire team

***Delete dead code***: Aggressively remove code that no longer serves a current purpose

***Extreme Programming origin***: Core XP practice alongside TDD, refactoring, and continuous integration

***Reversibility***: Prefer simple, changeable decisions over premature commitments to complex solutions

***Key Proponents***: Ron Jeffries (coined the phrase), Kent Beck ("Extreme Programming Explained", 1999)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Fighting over-engineering and premature abstraction
* Agile projects with iterative delivery and evolving requirements
* Refactoring legacy systems burdened with unused features
* When tempted to add "just in case" functionality or configurability

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* DRY - Eliminates duplication of existing knowledge (complementary but distinct)
* SPOT - Single Point of Truth, related simplicity principle
* TDD, Chicago School - YAGNI is a core principle of classicist TDD
* KISS Principle - Keep systems as simple as possible (complementary simplicity principle)

---

## Development Workflow

### 50/72 Rule

***Full Name***: 50/72 Rule for Git Commit Messages

***Also known as***: Git Commit Message Convention, Seven Rules of Git Commits

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***50-character subject line***: Keep the subject line to roughly 50 characters — a soft limit that focuses the author on stating the change concisely. GitHub truncates at 72 characters; `git log --oneline` truncates earlier. Aim for 50; treat 72 as the hard ceiling.

***Imperative mood***: Write the subject in the imperative: "Fix bug" not "Fixed bug" or "Fixes bug." This mirrors the convention Git itself follows — `git merge` generates "Merge branch…", `git revert` generates "Revert…".

***Blank line separator***: Separate the subject from the body with a blank line. Git tools — `rebase`, `format-patch`, `log --oneline` — rely on this separator to distinguish the summary from the explanation. Running them together confuses these tools.

***72-character body wrap***: Wrap the commit body at 72 characters. With Git's 4-space indentation, a 72-character line fits within an 80-column terminal. The same limit makes the message usable as an email patch via `git format-patch`.

***Body explains why, not how***: The code diff already shows what changed. The commit body explains the reasoning — context, decision, tradeoffs. How the code works belongs in source comments; why this change exists belongs in the commit.

***Key Proponents***: Tim Pope (https://tbaggery.com/2008/04/19/a-note-about-git-commit-messages.html["A Note About Git Commit Messages", tbaggery.com, 2008] — popularized the rule); Chris Beams (https://cbea.ms/git-commit/["How to Write a Git Commit Message", cbea.ms] — codified it as the "Seven Rules")

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Writing commit messages in any Git repository
* Configuring `commit.template` or linting with `commitlint` or a `.gitmessage` hook
* Code review: checking whether a commit message gives reviewers and future `git bisect` users enough context
* Instructing an LLM to generate a commit message — naming "50/72 Rule" activates the full convention without repeating each constraint

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Plain English (Strunk & White) — the same economy-of-words discipline applied to prose
* BLUF — state the conclusion (subject line) first; supporting detail follows in the body
* Inverted Pyramid Style — most important information first, supporting context below

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* Chris Beams' https://cbea.ms/git-commit/["How to Write a Git Commit Message"] is the most widely linked elaboration of Tim Pope's original post; it adds capitalization, no trailing period, and the "explain why vs. how" distinction as formal rules
* Conventional Commits adds a `type(scope):` prefix that competes directly with the 50-character budget; https://blog.thirstybear.co.uk/2025/05/git-commit-messages-why-keep-50.html[Thirstybear (2025)] argues that this metadata belongs in commit trailers rather than the subject line, and defends the 50-character limit on typographic grounds — citing Swiss designer Emil Ruder's 50–60 characters per line as the readability optimum

### Andon

***Full Name***: Andon (行灯), Japanese for "paper lantern" — the signal system of the Toyota Production System

***Also known as***: andon cord, andon board, andon light, stop-the-line authority, the visible half of jidoka

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Two Halves, One Word***: Andon names both the **display** — a board or lamp above the line showing the status of every station — and the **trigger**, the cord or button an operator pulls when something is wrong. Wikipedia's definition covers the display side: "a system which notifies managerial, maintenance, and other workers of a quality or process problem."

***The Radical Part Is the Authority, Not the Hardware***: Any operator may signal, and the signal is binding on everyone above them. That is an inversion of ordinary factory hierarchy, and it is the part that does not ship in the box. Mark Graban puts it flatly: "It's not the cord or a button that matters… It's the process and the management system that matters."

***Three Colours, One Sentence Each***: Jane Slaughter's description of the board: "A green light indicates there are no problems; a yellow light shows that the operator is having trouble keeping up and needs help; and a red light means there is a problem which requires stopping the line."

***It Is a Call for Help Before It Is a Stop***: Graban corrects the popular version: a pull "sounds an alarm and turns on a yellow light", the line keeps moving to the next **fixed position**, and a team leader gets a window of "maybe 5 to 30 seconds" to respond. If they succeed, "the line never stops at all." Stopping at a fixed position — between work cycles, not mid-task — is deliberate, so an interrupted job does not compound the defect.

***A Rising Pull Count Is a Good Sign***: Early in an andon rollout, more pulls mean more problems **surfacing**, not more problems existing. Graban's comparison is the standard evidence: Toyota's Georgetown plant recorded roughly 2,000 pulls a week, a new Ford plant in Dearborn two — not because Ford had fewer problems, but because its workers did not trust the response. A count near zero is the alarming reading.

***The Visible Half of Jidoka***: Jidoka — automation with a human touch — means a process stops itself when it produces a defect. Andon is how a **human** exercises the same authority, and how the stop becomes visible to everyone at once.

***Software Analogues***: A red build that nobody may build on top of; blocking a deploy; halting a canary rollout on a failing metric; a pager that any engineer may fire without asking permission. In each case the mechanism is trivial and the authority is the whole design.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Establishing who may halt work — the naming makes the authority explicit rather than implicit
* Red-build discipline and stop-the-line rules around CI, the direct descendant of the idea (`red-green-tdd`)
* Canary and progressive rollouts, where an automatic or manual abort is the andon
* Diagnosing a quiet team: if nobody ever stops anything, ask whether the authority exists or only the button does
* Designing escalation paths where the responder, not the reporter, owns the problem once the signal is raised

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "One worker pulling the cord stops the whole factory" — Graban calls this the myth; buffers between sections absorb a local stop, and the line halts only at the next fixed position
* ❌ "Andon is a line-stop device" — it is first a call for help; most pulls are resolved before any stop
* ❌ "Install the cord and you have andon" — without a responder within seconds and a no-blame reaction, the cord is decoration
* ❌ "Many pulls means the process is bad" — early on it means the process is finally visible
* ✓ "Andon is jidoka performed by a person" — accurate, and the reason it belongs next to `kaizen` rather than to tooling

## **Criticism**:

* **Read from the other side of the line, the board is a pacing device.** Jane Slaughter, in her account of what Labor Notes called "management by stress", treats andon as the emblem of the whole system: "Management by stress is the most sophisticated version of team concept, even though it contradicts many traditional notions of good management." The objection is precise, and it is about tuning: "The ideal state is achieved when the plant is running with all stations just on the line between green and yellow." A system deliberately balanced at the edge of "cannot keep up" uses the operator's distress signal as its control input. https://www.multinationalmonitor.org/hyper/issues/1990/01/slaughter.html[Slaughter, "Management by Stress", _Multinational Monitor_, January/February 1990]. Slaughter is co-author, with Mike Parker, of _Choosing Sides: Unions and the Team Concept_.
* **The transplanted version failed on arrival.** The Toyota/Ford pull-count gap is usually told as a culture story, but it is also a criticism of the mechanism: copied without the management system, the cord produced silence. Graban: Ford's rare pulls reflected worker distrust of how management would respond, not a better process. https://www.leanblog.org/2026/06/andon-cord-stop-the-line-myth/[Graban, "No, One Toyota Worker Can't Stop the Whole Factory"] (29 June 2026).
* **The popular story is wrong in its details, and the details carry the design.** Graban's whole piece is a correction of the andon legend circulating in management writing and software conference talks — the instant total stop, the lone heroic worker. The fixed-position stop, the 5-to-30-second response window and the required proximity of capable help are what make the practice work, and they are exactly what the legend omits.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Toyota replaced the cords with buttons.** Starting at the Toyota City plant in 2013, overhead cords gave way to wireless, waist-high yellow buttons, rolled out gradually worldwide while some plants kept cords. The stated reasons are mundane: "reduce overhead clutter, improve safety by removing tools…that could snag on the cord" and "simplify line reconfiguration". https://www.leanblog.org/2014/08/toyota-andon-cord-buttons/[Graban, "Why Toyota is Eliminating the Andon Cord from its Factories"] (2 August 2014, updated 17 May 2026). The word "cord" in "andon cord" is therefore already historical at the source.
* **The term survives in software mostly as metaphor.** "Pull the andon cord" is common shorthand in DevOps and SRE writing for stopping a release. The prior most training data carries is this metaphorical sense plus the myth version; the fixed-position stop and the responder-within-seconds requirement are usually absent, which is precisely why naming the anchor is worth doing.

### BEM Methodology

***Full Name***: Block Element Modifier (BEM) (S)CSS Methodology

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Motivation***: Solve CSS specificity wars, naming conflicts, and stylesheet maintainability issues in large codebases

***Block***: Standalone component that is meaningful on its own (e.g., `menu`, `button`, `header`)

***Element***: Part of a block with no standalone meaning (e.g., `menu__item`, `button__icon`)

***Modifier***: Flag on blocks or elements that changes appearance or behavior (e.g., `button--disabled`, `menu__item--active`)

***Naming convention***: `block__element--modifier` structure

***Independence***: Blocks are self-contained and reusable

***No cascading***: Avoid deep CSS selectors, use flat structure

***Explicit relationships***: Clear parent-child relationships through naming

***Reusability***: Components can be moved anywhere in the project

***Mix***: Combining multiple BEM entities on a single DOM node

***File structure***: Often paired with component-based file organization

[discrete]
## **Naming Examples**:

* Block: `.search-form`
* Element: `.search-form__input`, `.search-form__button`
* Modifier: `.search-form--compact`, `.search-form__button--disabled`

***Key Proponents***: Yandex development team

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Large-scale web applications with many components
* Team projects requiring consistent (S)CSS naming conventions
* When (S)CSS maintainability and scalability are priorities
* Projects where developers need to quickly understand (S)CSS structure
* Component-based architectures (React, Vue, Angular)

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The definition at https://getbem.com/[getbem.com] and https://bem.info/en/methodology/[bem.info] is stable and still accurate — BEM itself is a finished methodology
* Mainstream practice has shifted: https://2024.stateofcss.com/en-US/tools/[State of CSS 2024] shows Tailwind CSS "far ahead of other, more traditional competitors", and the survey no longer even tracks naming methodologies as it did in https://2020.stateofcss.com/en-US/technologies/methodologies/[2020]; CSS Modules, CSS-in-JS, and native scoping/nesting/cascade layers solve by platform the global-namespace problem BEM solved by convention

### Boy Scout Rule

***Full Name***: The Boy Scout Rule

***Also known as***: Leave the campground cleaner than you found it, Check in cleaner than you checked out

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **Check the module in cleaner than you checked it out.** The unit of improvement is the visit, not the project. Every time a file is opened for some other reason, it leaves in slightly better shape than it arrived.
* **Scoped to what you already touched.** The cleanup rides along with work that was going to happen anyway. Code you did not need to open is out of scope -- that is the line between the rule and drive-by refactoring.
* **Small enough to need no permission.** Rename an unclear variable, extract a method, delete dead code, fix a stale comment. If it needs a ticket, it is no longer this rule.
* **Aimed at entropy, not at perfection.** The target is the slow decay of a codebase nobody is responsible for, not a standard of cleanliness. Slightly better, repeatedly, beats a rewrite that never comes.
* **Safe only under test.** The rule assumes a green test suite. Without one, "improvement" is an unverified change to code you opened for a different reason.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Fixing a bug in a file nobody has read in years
* Codebases with no dedicated refactoring budget, where improvement has to be smuggled into ordinary work
* As a shared team norm, so the cleanup is expected rather than defended in review
* Where code is generated or changed faster than humans critically review it, and decay would otherwise accumulate unobserved

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Reading it as a licence to refactor anything nearby.** The rule is bounded by what the task already touched. Unbounded, it produces pull requests whose reviewers cannot find the actual change.
* **Mixing structural and behavioural change in one commit.** The cleanup and the fix should be separable, so that a reviewer can read one without the other and a revert does not take both. Kent Beck's _Tidy First?_ makes that separation its central rule.
* **Confusing "cleaner" with "in my style".** Reformatting to personal preference adds diff noise and removes no decay.
* **Applying it without tests.** Then it is not tidying, it is an unreviewed change under a virtuous name.

## **Criticism**:

* **The cleanup and the fix arrive in the same diff.** Jason Swett states the two consequences plainly: "It will be harder for any pull request reviewer to tell what exactly changed between the old code and the new code", and "If a feature/bugfix and piece of refactoring are mixed into one piece of work, it's impossible to roll one back without rolling back the other." https://www.codewithjason.com/boy-scout-rule-insufficient/[Swett, "Why the Boy Scout Rule is insufficient"] (17 December 2018). He also names a class of change the rule cannot hold -- "park-level" problems that "need to be discussed among everyone and then applied as a distinct project".
* **It cannot reach the debt that matters most.** Philippe Bourgau: "the boy scout rule is local and does not address large scale design or architecture issues". And a second bound that is rarely stated: "programmers will be able to clean the code only as much as their skills allow them to". https://philippe.bourgau.net/when-the-boy-scout-rule-fails/[Bourgau, "When the Boy Scout Rule Fails"] (2 August 2016). The rule is limited both by scope and by whoever happens to open the file.
* **The review burden is real, and has a proposed remedy.** Marius Elvert writes that cleanup found along the way "'pollutes' your merge-/pull-requests, making it harder to review", and answers it with cleanup in its own commit, marked with a `BSR:` prefix so a reviewer can skip or read it separately -- an approach he restricts to small refactorings. https://schneide.blog/2022/01/13/the-boy-scout-rule-and-git-in-practice/[Elvert, Schneide Blog] (13 January 2022).
* **The judgement the rule depends on is the one it does not supply.** Every critic above converges on the same missing piece: what counts as "minor" cleanup. The rule states the obligation and leaves the boundary to the person holding the editor.
* **No citable German-language criticism surfaced** in a search for Pfadfinderregel and Pfadfinderprinzip -- the German results were advocacy. French, Spanish, Japanese and Chinese were not searched. This is an absence in our search, not in the discourse.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Martin credits the rule to the Boy Scouts, not to himself.** _Clean Code_ (Prentice Hall, 2008), chapter 1: "The Boy Scouts of America have a simple rule that we can apply to our profession. Leave the campground cleaner than you found it." https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=1235624&seqNum=6[Excerpt at InformIT]. His contribution is the transfer to code, which is what this anchor names -- the campground formulation itself is older and not his.
* **Still advocated, now with conditions attached.** The advocacy since 2022 keeps the rule and adds guards rather than dropping it: cleanup should be "local and limited", and "large refactoring still require a separate task with a separate time slot" -- https://dev.to/anton9/boy-scout-rule-and-its-limitations-5404[Anton, DEV Community] (23 February 2025).
* **The discourse moved to the separation discipline, not away from the rule.** Kent Beck's _Tidy First?_ (2023) made "structural and behavioral changes should be kept in separate PRs (or at least in separate commits)" the mainstream framing -- which is exactly the remedy the rule's critics ask for. Worth stating precisely: Beck does not name the Boy Scout Rule. He supplies the discipline; he is not on record as correcting it.
* **No retraction found.** Martin has publicly qualified several _Clean Code_ positions, and a second edition exists. We found no citable evidence that this rule is among the things he revised -- an absence in our check rather than a confirmed continuity.

### Chesterton's Fence

***Full Name***: Chesterton's Fence

***Also known as***: The fence-and-gate parable; "don't remove a fence until you know why it was put up"

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **The parable moves the burden of proof onto the remover.** G.K. Chesterton, _The Thing_ (1929), chapter "The Drift from Domesticity": "There exists in such a case a certain institution or law; let us say for the sake of simplicity, a fence or gate erected across a road. The more modern type of reformer goes gaily up to it and says, 'I don't see the use of this; let us clear it away.' To which the more intelligent type of reformer will do well to answer: 'If you don't see the use of it, I certainly won't let you clear it away. Go away and think. Then, when you can come back and tell me that you do see the use of it, I may allow you to destroy it.'" Not seeing a reason is a fact about the observer, not about the fence.
* **The unexplained artifact is evidence, not noise.** Chesterton's supporting argument is the half that travels best into engineering: "The gate or fence did not grow there. It was not set up by somnambulists who built it in their sleep." A hard-coded seven-second retry delay, a feature flag that has been on for two years, a defensive check nobody can justify -- each one is a cheap record of a failure that once happened to somebody.
* **It buys a delay, not a veto -- and Chesterton wrote the exit clause himself.** Two sentences later in the same essay: "If he knows how it arose, and what purposes it was supposed to serve, he may really be able to say that they were bad purposes, or that they have since become bad purposes, or that they are purposes which are no longer served." A good-faith, timeboxed investigation that turns up nothing earns the removal. Take it out reversibly -- behind a flag, in a revertible commit -- and watch the signal that would tell you the fence was load-bearing.
* **It looks backwards, where second-order thinking looks forwards.** `second-order-thinking` asks "and then what?" about a change you are about to make. Chesterton's Fence asks "and why is this here?" about something already standing. The two compose: recover the reason first, then trace what removing it sets in motion.
* **The dig is a method, not an attitude.** `git log` and `git blame` on the line, `git log -S` on the unexplained string, the ticket or pull request that introduced it, the incident it followed, the on-call runbook and the alert definitions, and the author if they are still reachable. Operational documentation usually explains a strange line of code faster than the code does.
* **The effort scales with the blast radius.** An unused CSS class and a retry delay in a payment flow do not deserve the same archaeology. Let what breaks if you are wrong set the timebox.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Inheriting or modernising a system whose oddities nobody on the current team can explain -- the case the principle was made for
* Any cleanup list that already contains the words "safe", "obviously unused" or "quick win"
* Reviewing a pull request whose diff is mostly deletions
* Deprecating an API, a config flag, a cron job or a database column that appears to have no callers
* Joining a team and meeting a process that looks pointless from the outside
* As a brake on a static analyser -- or an LLM -- that confidently reports dead code

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "Never change anything you don't understand" -- the principle demands an investigation, not permanent preservation. Chesterton explicitly allows destruction once the purpose is known and found wanting.
* ❌ "The fence stays until someone proves it useless" -- that turns the burden into an unfalsifiable one, because nobody can prove the absence of a reason. The test is a serious attempt to find the reason, bounded in time.
* ❌ "It is an argument for tradition" -- in Chesterton's essay it was one. Applied to a codebase it is an argument about evidence: the artifact is the only surviving witness to a failure whose ticket is long closed.
* ❌ "Understanding it means reading the code" -- the reason is rarely in the code. It is in the incident, the contract, the regulator's letter, the vendor who used to time out.
* ✓ "It is a stopping rule for confident deletion" -- fair, and that is what makes it usable rather than merely wise.

## **Criticism**:

* **Reformers usually do see the use of the fence.** Paul Currion reads the original essay against itself: "The problem is that, even in Chesterton's day, none of the reformers he so clearly disdained failed to see the use of the fence; it was simply that they disagreed with people like Chesterton that that use was worth preserving the fence for." He also calls the framing gatekeeping rather than argument -- Chesterton "doesn't just want to have a debate about the anti-domestic drift; he wants to decide who is allowed to have that debate based on whether they meet his philosophical criteria", so "Chesterton's fence is being erected to exclude somebody". https://currion.net/2020/09/20/tearing-down-chestertons-fence/[Currion, "Tearing down Chesterton's fence"] (20 September 2020).
* **Invoked as a conversation-stopper, it is toothless.** Kevin Corcoran's objection is that the people arguing for removal have typically done the archaeology already: "Public choice theory meets Chesterton's injunction to understand what led to these regulatory fences being created." Where that is so, "invoking Chesterton's Fence is likewise toothless -- the person doing so only shows they are a step behind in the discussion." https://www.econlib.org/misusing-chestertons-fence/[Corcoran, "Misusing Chesterton's Fence", Econlib] (15 December 2022).
* **The removal process is itself a fence.** Stuart Armstrong's one-sentence post turns the principle on itself as "Chesterton's meta-fence": "in our current system (democratic market economies with large governments) the common practice of taking down Chesterton fences is a process which seems well established and has a decent track record, and should not be unduly interfered with (unless you fully understand it)". https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/WxDpeBi6aQAMH4BGB/stub-the-problem-with-chesterton-s-fence[Armstrong, LessWrong] (5 January 2016). This is the cuts-both-ways form: caution about removal is a policy too, and it has costs nobody counts.
* **The principle cannot tell a wise fence from an unjust one.** Arnold Kling: "Conservatives use the shorthand 'Chesterton's Fence' to describe their position." His counter-example is segregation -- "Racial segregation was wrong. But it was like a fence that had been in place for a long time. Does that mean it should be left in place?" -- and his conclusion is a repair rather than a rejection: the argument "has to be more nuanced than just 'never tear down the fence'". https://arnoldkling.substack.com/p/the-trouble-with-chestertons-fence[Kling, "The Trouble with Chesterton's Fence"] (25 August 2023).
* **No named German-language critique was found.** A German search returned only approving restatements. French, Spanish, Japanese and Chinese were not searched. That is a gap in our search, not in the discourse.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The name is not Chesterton's.** The string "Chesterton's fence" does not occur anywhere in _The Thing_; the https://www.gkc.org.uk/gkc/books/The_Thing.txt[full text at gkc.org.uk] carries the parable in "The Drift from Domesticity" and never the label. Chesterton wrote the parable, someone else named it. Who, and when, we could not establish from a citable source, so no coinage is claimed here.
* **The compressed version that circulates is also not his.** https://fs.blog/chestertons-fence/[Farnam Street] states it as "Do not remove a fence until you know why it was put up in the first place" -- shorter, sharper and not a sentence in the essay. The same page carries the caveat the short form loses: "The point is not that the status quo is always right, that every fence should remain standing." The https://www.lesswrong.com/w/chesterton-s-fence[LessWrong wiki entry] is the other main route by which the label spread, and it collects the counter-arguments alongside it.
* **Software adopted it as a rule about legacy code, not about institutions.** Oskar Dudycz's https://event-driven.io/en/chesterton_fence_and_software_architecture/[essay on Chesterton's Fence and software architecture] (17 August 2022) is representative of the genre: the fence becomes the line of code whose purpose is lost, and the reform becomes a refactoring. This is a genuine shift of subject -- Chesterton was defending the household, not a retry delay -- and it is the sense in which the anchor is used today.
* **The drift is worth naming in one direction only.** Nothing in the software reading contradicts the original argument; it narrows it. Where Chesterton's critics attack the essay's politics, the engineering use inherits none of it, because a payment service has no opponents to exclude.
* **A prior test on 2026-09-30 measured what naming it changes.** On a legacy-modernisation scenario that did not imply the principle, no baseline named it unprompted. A weak-tier model without the anchor called removing always-on feature flags a "safe, high-confidence win"; with the anchor it inserted an "Understand the fence" phase and asked whether the flags were finished rollouts or kill switches for a known bad vendor path. A strong-tier baseline was already cautious, and what the anchor added there was method -- read the runbook and the alert definitions before the code -- plus an explicit rule for when removal is earned. See the [prior-test register](#/prior-tests).

### Conventional Commits

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* A specification for adding human and machine readable meaning to commit messages
* Determining a semantic version bump (based on the types of commits landed)
* Communicating the nature of changes to teammates, the public, and other stakeholders
***Schema***: <type>[!][(optional scope)]: <description> + optional body/footer

***Common Types***
* **feat:** - introduce new feature to the codebase (-> Semver Minor)
* **fix:** - patches a bug in your codebase (-> SemVer Patch)
* **docs:** - documentation improvements to the codebase
* **chore:** - codebase/repository housekeeping changes
* **style:** - formatting changes that do not affect the meaning of the code
* **refactor:** - implementation changes that do not affect the meaning of the code
* **!** - BREAKING CHANGE (-> SemVer Major)

* **BREAKING CHANGE:** introduces a breaking API change

***Key Proponents***: Benjamin E. Coe, James J. Womack, Steve Mao

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* everything-as-code paradigm targeted
* team-/community-communication
* repository quality improvements

### Definition of Done

***Also known as***: DoD, Done Criteria, Acceptance Criteria (team-level)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Shared agreement***: A formal, team-wide checklist of quality criteria that every increment must satisfy before it is declared "done"

***Increment quality gates***: Concrete, verifiable conditions — e.g., code reviewed, tests passing, documentation updated, no known defects

***Transparency***: Makes the meaning of "done" visible and unambiguous to all stakeholders, preventing hidden technical debt

***Sprint-level vs. product-level DoD***: Teams may maintain separate DoD lists for Sprint increments and for releasable product increments

***Continuous refinement***: The DoD evolves as the team matures; stricter gates are added over time

***Undone work***: Work that does not meet the DoD is not counted as complete; it returns to the Product Backlog

***Shared responsibility***: The entire Scrum team (Developers, Product Owner, Scrum Master) owns and respects the DoD

***Key Proponents***: Ken Schwaber & Jeff Sutherland ("The Scrum Guide", 2020); Mike Cohn ("Succeeding with Agile", 2009)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Establishing a consistent quality standard across a Scrum or agile team
* Onboarding new team members so they understand what "finished" means
* Reducing rework and late-cycle defects by agreeing on criteria upfront
* Aligning developers, QA, and product owners on release readiness

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* BDD (Behavior-Driven Development) - Given-When-Then scenarios that operationalize acceptance criteria
* User Story Mapping - Planning technique that identifies the scope Definition of Done must cover
* MoSCoW - Prioritization method used to decide which DoD items are must-haves

### Effective Go

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Formatting (gofmt)***: Code is auto-formatted; style debates are eliminated by tooling

***Package names***: Short, lowercase, no underscores; package name is part of the qualified identifier

***Named return values***: Return values can be named and used as documentation

***Defer***: Deferred function calls run in LIFO order when the surrounding function returns; used for cleanup (close, unlock)

***Goroutines***: Lightweight concurrently executing functions; "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating"

***Channels***: Typed conduits for goroutine communication; first-class synchronization primitive

***Interfaces***: Implicit satisfaction — a type implements an interface simply by implementing its methods; enables duck typing

***Error handling***: Errors are values; idiomatic pattern is `if err != nil` at each call site; no exceptions

***Blank identifier (_)***: Discard unwanted values from multi-value returns without compiler error

***Embedding***: Composition over inheritance; types can embed other types to gain their methods

***Key Proponent***: The Go Authors (https://go.dev/doc/effective_go)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Onboarding new Go developers to idiomatic Go style
* Code review discussions about Go conventions
* Establishing team-wide Go coding standards
* Explaining Go idioms that differ from other languages (e.g. error handling, interfaces)
* Prompting an LLM to produce idiomatic, production-quality Go code

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* Dated by its own admission — https://go.dev/doc/effective_go[the document] opens with: "This document was written for Go's release in 2009 and is not actively updated. While it remains a good guide for using the core language, it does not cover significant changes to the language (generics), ecosystem (modules), or libraries added since." The Go team has deliberately frozen it (https://go.dev/issue/28782[golang/go #28782], still open)
* It predates the entire modern toolchain era — modules (2018/19) and generics (Go 1.18, 2022) — so its guidance is **silent** on these topics rather than wrong about the core language
* Modern complements: the curated https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments[Go Code Review Comments] (self-described "supplement to Effective Go") and Google's maintained https://google.github.io/styleguide/go/[Go Style series] (Guide, Decisions, Best Practices)

### Effective Java

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Items format***: A catalog of ~90 short, self-contained "Items", each a concrete best-practice rule with rationale and trade-offs

***Object creation***: Static factory methods over constructors; the Builder pattern for many parameters; enforce singletons and non-instantiability deliberately

***The general object contracts***: Obey the `equals`/`hashCode`/`compareTo`/`clone` contracts; always override `hashCode` when overriding `equals`; consistently override `toString`

***Classes and interfaces***: Minimize accessibility and mutability (favour immutable classes); favour composition over inheritance; prefer interfaces to abstract classes; design and document for inheritance or prohibit it

***Generics***: Eliminate unchecked warnings; prefer lists to arrays and generic types/methods; use bounded wildcards by the PECS rule (Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super)

***Enums and annotations***: Use enums instead of `int` constants; use the `EnumMap`/`EnumSet`; prefer annotations to naming patterns; consistently use `@Override`

***Lambdas and streams***: Prefer lambdas to anonymous classes and method references to lambdas; use streams judiciously and favour side-effect-free functions (Java 8 features, added in the 3rd edition)

***Methods and exceptions***: Check parameters for validity; design method signatures carefully; use exceptions only for exceptional conditions; favour standard exceptions; document all thrown exceptions

***Resource and concurrency hygiene***: Prefer try-with-resources to `try`-`finally`; prefer executors and tasks to threads; favour concurrency utilities over `wait`/`notify`; document thread safety

***Key Proponent***: Joshua Bloch ("Effective Java", Addison-Wesley) — former Sun/Google engineer who led the design of the Java Collections Framework and other core APIs

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Onboarding Java developers to idiomatic, robust API and class design
* Code review discussions grounded in a shared, citable rule set ("Item 17: minimize mutability")
* Establishing team-wide Java coding standards and design conventions
* Explaining Java-specific contracts (`equals`/`hashCode`, generics, PECS) and their pitfalls
* Prompting an LLM to produce idiomatic, robust Java code

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Effective Go
* Builder Pattern
* SOLID Principles

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The 3rd edition (Addison-Wesley, https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/effective-java/P200000000138/9780134685991[published December 2017], commonly cited as 2018) is the current edition. It added items for Java 7-9 features — lambdas, streams, the `java.time` package, and try-with-resources
* Because it predates Java's six-month release cadence, some Item advice now has newer language alternatives: **records** (Java 16) replace much hand-written immutable-class and Builder boilerplate; **sealed classes** (Java 17) and **pattern matching for `switch`** (Java 21) supersede some inheritance and `instanceof` guidance; **virtual threads** (Java 21) change the "prefer executors to threads" calculus
* The book's design principles (favour immutability, composition over inheritance, the object contracts, PECS) remain valid; only the mechanics for some Items have shifted. A training-data prior keyed on "Effective Java" most plausibly reflects the 3rd edition and is therefore silent on records, sealed classes, and virtual threads

### Effective Python

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Items format***: A catalog of ~125 short, self-contained "Items", each a concrete best-practice rule with rationale and trade-offs (grouped into chapters)

***Pythonic thinking***: Follow PEP 8 style and the Zen of Python; prefer f-strings over `%` and `str.format`; know the difference between `bytes` and `str`; prefer helper functions to complex expressions

***Lists and dictionaries***: Prefer comprehensions to `map`/`filter`; use `enumerate` instead of `range`; use `zip` to iterate in parallel; use catch-all unpacking over indexing; avoid `else` blocks after `for`/`while`

***Functions***: Prefer raising exceptions to returning `None`; enforce clarity with keyword-only and positional-only arguments; return generators instead of building lists; never modify default argument values (use `None` and docstrings)

***Comprehensions and generators***: Use generator expressions for large comprehensions; compose generators with `yield from`; reach for `itertools` before hand-rolling iteration

***Classes and interfaces***: Compose classes rather than nesting dicts/tuples deeply; use `@classmethod` polymorphism; prefer public attributes and `@property` over getters/setters; use functions instead of classes for simple interfaces

***Metaclasses and attributes***: Use `@property` and descriptors for reusable attribute behaviour; prefer `__getattr__`/`__getattribute__` sparingly; validate subclasses with `__init_subclass__`

***Concurrency and parallelism***: Use threads for blocking I/O, not parallelism (the GIL); use `Queue` to coordinate pipelines; use coroutines and `asyncio` for many concurrent functions; use `concurrent.futures` and processes for true parallelism

***Robustness, testing, and collaboration***: Make programs robust and performant (new chapters in the 3rd edition); test with `unittest`/`Mock`; document with docstrings; isolate dependencies with virtual environments (`venv`)

***Key Proponent***: Brett Slatkin ("Effective Python", Addison-Wesley) — principal software engineer at Google and creator of the book's runnable example suite

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Onboarding Python developers to idiomatic, robust ("Pythonic") code
* Code review discussions grounded in a shared, citable rule set ("Item 30: consider generators instead of returning lists")
* Establishing team-wide Python coding standards and conventions
* Explaining Python-specific idioms and pitfalls (comprehensions, generators, the GIL, `@property`, keyword-only arguments)
* Prompting an LLM to produce idiomatic, production-quality Python code

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Effective Java
* Effective Go
* SOLID Principles

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The 3rd edition (Pearson Addison-Wesley, https://www.informit.com/store/effective-python-125-specific-ways-to-write-better-9780138172183[published 20 November 2024], ISBN 978-0-13-817218-3) is the current edition. It expands from the 2nd edition's 90 Items to 125 Items — https://effectivepython.com/[35 new Items] plus two new chapters on robustness and performance
* The 1st edition (2015) targeted Python 2 as well as 3; the 2nd edition (2019) was Python-3-only through ~3.8; the 3rd edition covers modern Python 3, including features such as the walrus operator, structural pattern matching, and updated typing and `asyncio` guidance
* The book's core advice (prefer comprehensions and generators, respect the GIL, compose classes, use `@property`) remains stable across editions; only specific Items track the language. A training-data prior keyed on "Effective Python" most plausibly reflects the 2nd edition (90 Items) and is therefore silent on the 35 Items added in the 3rd edition

### GitHub Flow

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* A lightweight, branch-based workflow where `main` is always deployable
* Feature branches are short-lived, created from `main` for every change
* Pull Requests are the central collaboration mechanism — used for code review, discussion, and CI validation before merging
* Merging to `main` triggers immediate deployment (continuous delivery)
* Branch naming reflects the work: issue number or short descriptive slug

***Workflow steps***
1. Create a branch from `main` (named after the issue or feature)
1. Commit changes with descriptive messages
1. Open a Pull Request early for visibility and feedback
1. Discuss, review, and iterate until the PR is approved
1. Merge to `main` — `main` is always in a deployable state
1. Deploy immediately after merge

***Key Proponent***: Scott Chacon ("GitHub Flow", 2011)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Teams practicing continuous delivery or continuous deployment
* Projects where `main` must always be production-ready
* Issue-driven or ticket-driven development workflows
* Agentic coding workflows where context brevity matters

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Conventional Commits
* Semantic Versioning (SemVer)

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The prior most plausibly reproduces Scott Chacon's https://scottchacon.com/2011/08/31/github-flow/[original 2011 formulation], where continuous deployment is the point — "anything in the master branch is deployable", and merged work is deployed immediately, often several times a day
* GitHub's https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow[current official description] has narrowed to a generic branch → PR → review → merge workflow with no deployment step at all — say which of the two you mean

### Kaizen

***Full Name***: Kaizen (改善) — kai, "change", plus zen, "for the better"; conventionally rendered "continuous improvement"

***Also known as***: continual improvement, gemba kaizen, daily kaizen; popularised in the West by Masaaki Imai (1930–2023), founder of the Kaizen Institute (1985)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Small, Continuous, By Everyone***: The unit is the small change made by the person doing the work, repeated without end. Imai's most-quoted formulation, as reported by Mark Graban: "Kaizen is everyone, everywhere, every day." The improvement is not delegated to a specialist function.

***Kaikaku Is the Deliberate Contrast***: **Kaikaku** (改革) is radical, discontinuous change — Jim Womack glosses it as "the Japanese word for revolution, in contrast with kaizen, which is incremental improvement". The pair is what keeps kaizen precise: without kaikaku as its opposite, "continuous improvement" drifts into meaning any change at all. Womack's own position is sequential: "lean transformation will always need to begin with evolution: kaizen and model lines…These create the basic stability", and only afterwards "we really do need to go fast".

***Standardise the Gain, Then Improve From the New Standard***: The second thing that keeps the term precise. An improvement that is not written into the standard is not kaizen; it is a good day. Art Smalley: "Permanent conditions change when the gains get built into standards and held by an operating system that runs daily", with "standardized work as the mechanism connecting daily management to daily improvement — not as a document in a binder". Standard and improvement alternate: the standard is the floor the next improvement starts from, never a freeze.

***A Habit, Not a Project***: Graban summarises Imai's position: "Not a project. Not an event. A daily practice, distributed across the entire organization, expected of everyone — not delegated to a kaizen office or a specialist team."

***It Needs Something to Look At***: Kaizen without `muda-mura-muri` has no diagnosis and without `genchi-genbutsu` no evidence. It is the habit; those supply what the habit examines.

***In Software***: The `boy-scout-rule` is kaizen scoped to a file. Retrospective actions that actually change the working agreement are kaizen; retrospective actions that produce a list are not, because nothing was standardised.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Framing improvement as an everyday obligation of the whole team rather than a quarterly initiative
* Distinguishing a small, reversible, local change from a redesign — say kaizen or say kaikaku, and the conversation separates
* Any improvement effort where the gain will evaporate unless the new way becomes the documented default
* As the daily counterpart to a project-shaped method such as `dmaic`, and as the cultural ground under `toyota-kata`

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "Kaizen means a week-long improvement workshop" — that is a kaizen event, a Western packaging, and the thing the criticism below targets
* ❌ "Kaizen is any improvement" — kaikaku exists precisely so that the word keeps meaning **incremental**
* ❌ "Kaizen is the opposite of standardisation" — it depends on it; without a standard there is nothing to improve from and no way to hold a gain
* ❌ "Kaizen is a Toyota tool" — it is a management philosophy that Imai generalised well beyond manufacturing
* ✓ "It is a habit that produces small, standardised changes made by the people doing the work" — accurate

## **Criticism**:

* **The event replaced the habit.** Art Smalley's critique is aimed squarely at the packaged form: "Kaizen events most commonly fail because organizations never make the transition from running improvement events to building an operating and management system that sustains results daily." And on the arithmetic of the format itself: "A one-week event cannot change permanent conditions on its own. At most it is a vehicle for local change and learning." His conclusion is the line the criticism turns on: "The event is not the system. The daily discipline is the system." https://artoflean.com/gemba-coach/why-does-kaizen-fail/[Smalley, "Why Does Kaizen Fail?", Art of Lean].
* **"Kamikaze kaizen".** Smalley reports that Jim Womack coined the term for such efforts — "intense bursts of activity with no lasting effect other than a fiery death". We verified this quotation only in Smalley's article, not in an original Womack publication; treat it as attributed via Smalley.
* **Imai himself was frustrated by how the West took it up.** In his foreword to _Healthcare Kaizen_, quoted by Graban: "I am profoundly frustrated with the slow pace at which Kaizen strategy has been embraced by the business community", and "Embracing Kaizen is a long-term journey. It is not a flavor of the month and requires the cultural change, commitment and self-discipline that needs to be sustained over many decades." https://www.leanblog.org/2023/06/in-memoriam-masaaki-imai-the-father-of-kaizen-1930%E2%81%A0-%E2%81%A02023/[Graban, "In Memoriam: Masaaki Imai"] (16 June 2023).
* **Continuous improvement without respect for people is the standard failure.** Bob Emiliani: Fake Lean is "the technical application of 'Continuous Improvement' tools and methods, invariably in a zero-sum fashion"; Real Lean requires both continuous improvement **and** respect for people. https://bobemiliani.substack.com/p/back-story-real-vs-fake-lean[Emiliani, "The Backstory: Real vs. Fake Lean"] (13 September 2013).

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The founding text is _Kaizen (Ky'zen), the Key to Japan's Competitive Success_** — Masaaki Imai, Random House Business Division, New York, 1986, 259 pages. The widely cited later edition is published by McGraw-Hill; the title is often given without the "(Ky'zen)" of the original.
* **The more influential book is the second one.** _Gemba Kaizen: A Commonsense, Low-Cost Approach to Management_ (McGraw-Hill, 1997) moved the emphasis to the actual place of work and won the Shingo Research Prize in 1999. Imai's last book was _Strategic KAIZEN_ (McGraw-Hill, 2021). He died on 12 June 2023, aged 92.
* **The trademarked form is a live complication.** The Kaizen Institute, which Imai founded in 1985, writes the term as KAIZEN™ in its own material. The word is simultaneously generic Japanese vocabulary, a management philosophy and a consultancy's brand — worth knowing when a source's capitalisation looks odd.
* **"Kaizen event" remains the dominant Western usage** despite the criticism above, and it is the sense a model is likeliest to reach for. Naming daily kaizen, or naming kaikaku as the contrast, is what steers it back.

### Keep a Changelog

***Full Name***: Keep a Changelog, the changelog convention published at keepachangelog.com

***Also known as***: the `CHANGELOG.md` convention, keepachangelog format, the Added/Changed/Fixed format

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***The Reader Is a Person***: The first guiding principle is the whole argument: "Changelogs are _for humans_, not machines." Everything else in the convention follows from choosing an audience.

***Six Change Types, No More***: Quoted exactly as the standard prints them -- `Added` for new features; `Changed` for changes in existing functionality; `Deprecated` for soon-to-be removed features; `Removed` for now removed features; `Fixed` for any bug fixes; `Security` in case of vulnerabilities. "Breaking Changes" is **not** one of them; a breaking change appears under `Changed` or `Removed`, and the break is signalled by the version number.

***The Remaining Guiding Principles***: "There should be an entry for every single version." "The same types of changes should be grouped." "Versions and sections should be linkable." "The latest version comes first." "The release date of each version is displayed." Adherence to Semantic Versioning should be mentioned.

`[Unreleased]` Sits at the Top:: Version 2.0.0 states the mechanics: "Keep an `Unreleased` section at the top to collect upcoming changes. It shows readers what to expect, and at release time you move its contents into a new version." It is the one section that makes the convention sustainable, because entries get written while the change is fresh.

***ISO Dates, Largest Unit First***: "Use the `YYYY-MM-DD` format. It orders from the largest unit to the smallest, avoids the confusion of regional date formats, and is an ISO standard." So: `## [1.2.0] - 2026-10-03`.

***The Convention Rejects Generated Changelogs, Explicitly***: Version 1.1.0 puts it bluntly: "Using commit log diffs as changelogs is a bad idea: they're full of noise." Version 2.0.0 restates the position as a division of labour -- "machines can draft, but humans curate" -- and keeps CI "in a supporting role" for "mechanical tasks: move the Unreleased section into a dated version at release time, check that the file is formatted correctly".

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Writing or restructuring a `CHANGELOG.md` for a library or product with external users
* Pairing with `semantic-versioning`, which the convention asks you to mention and which supplies the version numbers the sections are keyed on
* Settling the argument about what belongs in a release entry: notable user-visible change, yes; internal refactor and typo fix, no
* Reviewing a release process in which the changelog is a `git log` dump, and the question is whether anyone reads it
* Asking an LLM for release notes, where naming the convention is what produces the correct six categories rather than a plausible-looking set

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "`Breaking Changes` is one of the standard sections" -- it is not; the six types are fixed, and this is the single most common error
* ❌ "Keep a Changelog is a tool" -- it is a convention for a plain text file; the tools are other projects
* ❌ "The changelog is generated from the commit log" -- the convention says the opposite in both published versions
* ❌ "Every commit needs an entry" -- only notable changes do; the curation is the work
* ✓ "Machines can draft, humans curate" -- the standard's own formulation of where automation stops

## **Criticism**:

* **The opposing position is held openly by the Conventional Commits specification, in its own words.** Its stated benefits list opens with "Automatically generating CHANGELOGs." and "Automatically determining a semantic version bump (based on the types of commits landed)." That is the claim Keep a Changelog denies: that a structured commit history converts into a changelog without a person in the loop. https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/[Conventional Commits 1.0.0]. The tool ecosystem built on it -- semantic-release, release-please, Changesets, git-cliff -- is named on the Keep a Changelog 2.0.0 page itself: "A convention such as Conventional Commits, with tools such as semantic-release, release-please, Changesets, and git-cliff, reads structured commits to choose the next version and draft a changelog."
* **Keep a Changelog's answer, and the sentence the argument turns on.** "A commit and a changelog entry are written for different people, and one does not convert cleanly into the other." https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/[Keep a Changelog 2.0.0]. Whether that holds is an empirical question about your audience, not a settled one -- for an internal library whose only readers are the contributors, the two audiences coincide and the objection loses its force.
* **Two named critics argue the file does not belong in the repository at all.** Josh Triplett, in the Hacker News thread on Keep a Changelog, makes the version-control objection: "Projects that still insist on maintaining a changelog file in git end up constantly fighting git's conflict resolution, and they make rebase almost completely unusable. For an actual log of individual changes, that's what 'git log' is for." https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=9054627[Triplett] (16 February 2015). Jan Krutisch, co-founder of Depfu, grants the generated side more than the convention does -- "If you are willing to use (and enforce) a specific format for your commit messages, the results can be pretty decent" -- and names the cost of the manual route: "the further away you move the changelog writing from the actual code changes, the higher are the chances to either forget things or to actually get details wrong". https://depfu.com/blog/changelogs-to-write-or-to-generate[Krutisch, "Changelogs: To write or to generate?"] (2 October 2018). He is not a clean opponent: he closes with "If in doubt, use the simple, handwritten approach."
* **What was not found.** No named critic of the **format** itself -- the six change types, the `[Unreleased]` section, the ordering. Searched in English and German. The disagreement on record is about who writes the file and where it lives, not about how it is laid out.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Two published versions, and the site's front page does not point at the newer one.** Version 2.0.0 was published on 7 June 2026, but keepachangelog.com still links "Continue to Keep a Changelog" to `/en/1.1.0/`. Quote the format safely; quote a version number carefully. https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/[1.1.0] -- https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/[2.0.0]. Created and maintained by Olivier Lacan, designed by Tyler Fortune.
* **The format itself did not drift.** The six change types, the `[Unreleased]` section, `YYYY-MM-DD` dates and latest-version-first are identical in 1.1.0 and 2.0.0. What 2.0.0 adds is the explicit stance on automation.
* **The anchor buys correctness, not recall.** Two of four no-anchor baselines on `claude-haiku-4-5` named the convention unprompted -- and then listed the wrong sections; one produced "Breaking Changes, New Features, Fixed, Deprecated", which is not the standard's set. Naming the term produced all six canonical types plus `[Unreleased]`. This is a dense prior whose details are commonly misremembered, which is exactly where naming pays.

### Programming as Theory Building (Naur)

***Also known as***: Mental Model according to Naur

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:
