The tool ecosystem built on it -- semantic-release, release-please, Changesets, git-cliff -- is named on the Keep a Changelog 2.0.0 page itself: "A convention such as Conventional Commits, with tools such as semantic-release, release-please, Changesets, and git-cliff, reads structured commits to choose the next version and draft a changelog."
* **Keep a Changelog's answer, and the sentence the argument turns on.** "A commit and a changelog entry are written for different people, and one does not convert cleanly into the other." https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/[Keep a Changelog 2.0.0]. Whether that holds is an empirical question about your audience, not a settled one -- for an internal library whose only readers are the contributors, the two audiences coincide and the objection loses its force.
* **Two named critics argue the file does not belong in the repository at all.** Josh Triplett, in the Hacker News thread on Keep a Changelog, makes the version-control objection: "Projects that still insist on maintaining a changelog file in git end up constantly fighting git's conflict resolution, and they make rebase almost completely unusable. For an actual log of individual changes, that's what 'git log' is for." https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=9054627[Triplett] (16 February 2015). Jan Krutisch, co-founder of Depfu, grants the generated side more than the convention does -- "If you are willing to use (and enforce) a specific format for your commit messages, the results can be pretty decent" -- and names the cost of the manual route: "the further away you move the changelog writing from the actual code changes, the higher are the chances to either forget things or to actually get details wrong". https://depfu.com/blog/changelogs-to-write-or-to-generate[Krutisch, "Changelogs: To write or to generate?"] (2 October 2018). He is not a clean opponent: he closes with "If in doubt, use the simple, handwritten approach."
* **What was not found.** No named critic of the **format** itself -- the six change types, the `[Unreleased]` section, the ordering. Searched in English and German. The disagreement on record is about who writes the file and where it lives, not about how it is laid out.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Two published versions, and the site's front page does not point at the newer one.** Version 2.0.0 was published on 7 June 2026, but keepachangelog.com still links "Continue to Keep a Changelog" to `/en/1.1.0/`. Quote the format safely; quote a version number carefully. https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/[1.1.0] -- https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/[2.0.0]. Created and maintained by Olivier Lacan, designed by Tyler Fortune.
* **The format itself did not drift.** The six change types, the `[Unreleased]` section, `YYYY-MM-DD` dates and latest-version-first are identical in 1.1.0 and 2.0.0. What 2.0.0 adds is the explicit stance on automation.
* **The anchor buys correctness, not recall.** Two of four no-anchor baselines on `claude-haiku-4-5` named the convention unprompted -- and then listed the wrong sections; one produced "Breaking Changes, New Features, Fixed, Deprecated", which is not the standard's set. Naming the term produced all six canonical types plus `[Unreleased]`. This is a dense prior whose details are commonly misremembered, which is exactly where naming pays.

### Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100)

***Full Name***: ASD-STE100, Simplified Technical English

***Also known as***: STE; formerly AECMA Simplified English

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **A specification, not a style preference.** 53 writing rules in 9 sections, plus a dictionary of roughly 900 approved words and about 1,200 non-approved words with suggested alternatives.
* **One word, one meaning, one part of speech.** Each approved word is admitted in a single sense. "To follow" means to come after, never to obey.
* **Write for the reader who is not a native speaker**, and for the translator and the machine that come after them.
* **Procedures and descriptions are different text types** with different rules, rather than one undifferentiated notion of "clear writing".
* **Compliance is not fully checkable.** Boeing, whose checker has been in use since 1990, states plainly that "no language checker can guarantee full compliance with STE, because the goal of STE is clarity."

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Maintenance, operating and safety instructions, especially where readers are not native English speakers
* Documentation that will be translated, where source ambiguity multiplies across target languages
* Regulated or safety-critical contexts where a misread instruction has physical consequences

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Reading it as "write simply".** The specific content is the closed word list and the 53 rules; a general instruction to simplify is not STE and does not need the name.
* **Using the bare abbreviation.** "STE" is unambiguous in this field, but the qualified form is what the measurement covers -- see the [prior-test register](#/prior-tests) for which models were tested and with what result.
* **Assuming it is an ISO standard.** ASD describes the move "from specification to international standard" as its own ambition; no formal ISO status is documented.
* **Confusing it with Plain Language.** https://www.sis.se/en/produkter/standardization/information-sciences-publishing/writing-and-transliteration/iso-24495-12023/[ISO 24495-1:2023] is principle-based and audience-oriented; STE is rule- and wordlist-based. The ISO scope names controlled languages as a neighbouring field, not the same one.

## **Criticism**:

* **The efficacy evidence is thinner than the reputation, and its own authors say so.** Heather Holmback (Boeing) with Serena Shubert and Jan Spyridakis (University of Washington), who conducted the Boeing-funded evaluations, name the limits in https://mt-archive.net/90/CLAW-1996-Holmback.pdf["Issues in Conducting Empirical Evaluations of Controlled Languages"] (CLAW '96): there is "no compliance standard for SE", so "there is no universal agreement as to what counts as 'good,' 'typical' or even acceptable SE"; the measured benefit appeared only for the more complex of two procedures; and "we did not find any significant differences for time between the SE and non-SE documents". Translatability results were "less clear-cut", with no significant difference for Chinese.
* **The open question is whether the standard beats good writing at all.** The same paper asks "whether SE is any more beneficial than good quality, professional technical writing that does not conform to the SE standard". That question is still open, and our own measurement reproduced it: on a weak model the anchored rewrite was not distinguishable from an unanchored one. The entry therefore records Haiku as tested with no measurable effect, and Sonnet and Opus as tested and working. See the [prior-test register](#/prior-tests).
* **Adoption costs are real.** Karin Disborg's https://liu.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2%3A16816[2007 thesis at Linköping University] names the "extensive learning time" and reports, from her literature base, roughly 20 percent more writing time in a controlled language. The study is qualitative with a small sample and was commissioned by a documentation service provider; its readability results favoured STE.
* **Strict compliance can work against other goals.** TechScribe notes that following STE strictly harms findability in search engines, because synonyms are what readers actually search for, and cites Barry Rosenberg's argument that synonyms improve readability for non-technical verbs.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Actively maintained, and free.** https://www.asd-ste100.org/about_STE.html[ASD-STE100] is published by the AeroSpace and Defence Industries Association of Europe and maintained by the Simplified Technical English Maintenance Group. **Issue 9** appeared on 15 January 2025: no new rules, but 31 of the 53 rules reworded and 555 dictionary entries revised. The specification is https://www.asd-ste100.org/STE_faq.html[available free of charge], as PDF, on request.
* **Older than its name.** It began as AECMA Simplified English, first issued in 1986; the maintenance group was founded in 1983 and renamed STEMG in 2004 when AECMA became ASD. The official site dates the origin to the late 1970s, Wikipedia to the 1980s -- the starting point is not settled, the 1986 first issue is.
* **In use beyond aerospace.** ASD names land and sea vehicles, renewable energy and medical technology. Tooling exists (the Boeing Simplified English Checker, in use since 1990, and commercial alternatives), but ASD and the STEMG explicitly "do not endorse or certify any company, organization, or individual that sells tools claimed to be 'fully compliant'".
* **Detail beyond the counts is second-hand here.** The sentence-length limits usually quoted -- 20 words for procedures, 25 for descriptions -- and the restrictions on -ing forms come from secondary sources. The specification is distributed only on individual request, so we did not read the rule text itself.

---

## Knowledge Management

### ADDIE Model

***Also known as***: ADDIE, Instructional Systems Design (ISD)

***Full Name***: Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Analysis***: Clarify the instructional problem; identify needs, audience characteristics, learning goals, constraints, and the existing knowledge gap

***Design***: Define measurable learning objectives, assessment instruments, content structure, and media selection — the blueprint produced before any materials are built

***Development***: Build and assemble the actual learning materials (content, storyboards, media, technology) against the design blueprint; includes pilot testing

***Implementation***: Deliver the instruction — train facilitators, prepare learners, and run the program in its intended environment

***Evaluation***: Assess effectiveness through both formative (ongoing, each phase) and summative (final outcome) evaluation; frequently paired with Kirkpatrick's four levels

***Iterative, not strictly waterfall***: Though originally sequential, modern ADDIE is drawn as a cyclical, dynamic process where Evaluation feeds back into every phase

***Key Proponents***: Florida State University's Center for Educational Technology (~1975, for the US Army, later all US armed forces via the IPISD framework); Robert Maribe Branch ("Instructional Design: The ADDIE Approach", Springer, 2009) — a key modern codification. ADDIE is a generic label for the ISD process rather than a single-author model.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing structured training, courses, or learning materials from scratch
* Producing documentation or onboarding programs that require measurable learning outcomes
* Coaching or consulting engagements that build organizational capability
* Establishing a shared vocabulary for an instructional-design or e-learning team
* Prompting an LLM to scaffold a curriculum or training plan along defined phases

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Bloom's Taxonomy — frames the learning objectives set in the Design phase
* 4MAT — a learning-cycle model that complements ADDIE's structure
* Feynman Technique — a learning method usable within Development
* Double Diamond — a comparable diverge/converge process model from design

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Roundtable Learning, https://roundtablelearning.com/what-is-the-addie-model-less-than-100-words/["What is the ADDIE Model? Strengths & Weaknesses"] — criticizes ADDIE for its linear nature, overly-detailed approach, and the time required to create and implement it; defects surface only in late phases
* Michael Allen / Allen Interactions, https://elearningindustry.com/sam-successive-approximation-model-for-rapid-instructional-design["SAM: A Rapid Design And Development Model"] (eLearning Industry) — calls ADDIE "rigid and too linear," "slow to evaluate," and burdened by the "waterfall nature of execution"; proposes SAM (Successive Approximation Model), a rapid, iterative, agile alternative that always keeps something usable in front of learners
* Broader discourse pairs this with Agile / rapid-prototyping instructional design as the modern answer to ADDIE's front-loaded sequencing

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* Still the most widely taught ISD framework, but increasingly presented as iterative rather than strict waterfall; Branch's 2009 codification (https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-09506-6[Springer]) is the common modern reference
* SAM and Agile ID are the main contemporary alternatives for fast-moving, multimedia, and online-learning projects (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADDIE_model[ADDIE model, Wikipedia])

### Dreyfus Model of Skill Acquisition

***Full Name***: Dreyfus Model of Skill Acquisition according to Stuart E. and Hubert L. Dreyfus

***Also known as***: Five-Stage Model of Adult Skill Acquisition, Novice-to-Expert model

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Five stages***

- ***Novice***: Follows context-free rules rigidly; recognizes no situational nuance; needs explicit instructions
- ***Advanced Beginner***: Applies situational maxims drawn from experience; still rule-oriented but starts reading context
- ***Competent***: Plans consciously and sets goals; copes with complexity by deliberately choosing what matters; feels responsibility for outcomes
- ***Proficient***: Perceives situations holistically; intuition emerges, though responses are still decided analytically
- ***Expert***: Acts with fluid, intuitive mastery; perception and action merge; deliberates only when something unfamiliar appears

***Analytical-to-intuitive progression***: Skill develops from detached rule-following toward involved, intuitive pattern recognition — not by accumulating more rules

***Stage-matched instruction***: Each stage needs a different kind of guidance; novices want rules and recipes, experts want holistic context and are hindered by step-by-step rules

***Key Proponents***: Stuart E. and Hubert L. Dreyfus, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235125013_A_Five-Stage_Model_of_the_Mental_Activities_Involved_in_Directed_Skill_Acquisition["A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition"] (1980, UC Berkeley Operations Research Center for the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research); applied to nursing by Patricia Benner ("From Novice to Expert", 1984) and to software by Andy Hunt ("Pragmatic Thinking and Learning: Refactor Your Wetware", 2008)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Calibrating teaching or explanation depth to a learner's stage
* Designing mentoring and onboarding paths that move people from rules to intuition
* Diagnosing why rule-heavy documentation helps novices but frustrates experts
* Structuring competency frameworks and skill matrices for a team
* Framing how an LLM should adjust the granularity of its guidance to the user's expertise

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Bloom's Taxonomy
* Feynman Technique
* 4MAT

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Fernand Gobet and Philippe Chassy, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.3402/meo.v15i0.4846["The Dreyfus model of clinical problem-solving skills acquisition: a critical perspective"] and their 2008 paper in the _International Journal of Nursing Studies_ (45: 129-139) — argue there is no empirical evidence for discrete stages in the development of expertise, and that experts in fact use slow analytical problem-solving (e.g. look-ahead search in chess), contrary to the model's "experts act only intuitively" claim; they propose an alternative theory of intuition based on chunking

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The Dreyfus brothers later added a sixth stage of **mastery** and reframed the model (Rousse & Dreyfus, https://philarchive.org/archive/ROURTS["Revisiting the Six Stages of Skill Acquisition"]); training-data priors most often reflect the original five-stage version popularized by Benner and Hunt

### Genchi Genbutsu

***Full Name***: Genchi Genbutsu (現地現物) — "the actual place, the actual thing"

***Also known as***: go and see, go to gemba, go see for yourself, one of the five principles of the Toyota Way 2001

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Two Words, Two Demands***: Art Smalley reads the characters apart: 現地 (genchi) is "the actual place" where work happens; 現物 (genbutsu) is "the actual thing itself — not reports or descriptions of it". Both halves must be satisfied. Going to the place and then reading a dashboard there satisfies neither.

***Go Yourself***: The person who will decide is the person who must observe. Delegating the looking and receiving a summary reintroduces exactly the layer of abstraction the principle exists to remove.

***Gemba Is the Sibling Term***: **Gemba** (現場) is the actual place — "the scene", in the sense a Japanese journalist or detective would use. Smalley notes both terms share 現 (gen), "present" or "actual", and calls this "Toyota's linguistic emphasis on reality versus assumption". Genchi genbutsu is the practice; gemba is where it happens.

***The Ohno Circle***: The canonical illustration. Taiichi Ohno would chalk a circle on the factory floor and have an engineer stand in it and watch the process. Christoph Roser: "Often, a disciple stood in the circle for hours before Ohno was satisfied." The point was not endurance but perception — the premise is that most people do not see what is in front of them, and that hours of watching reveal what a walk-past cannot.

***Observation Before Hypothesis***: Genchi genbutsu sits upstream of every cause-hunting method. It is what makes a `five-whys` chain worth anything: without direct observation the first "why" is answered from memory, and every later one inherits the guess.

***Why This Matters for an LLM***: Named, it pushes toward reading the actual code, the actual log line, the actual trace, the actual failing test — before theorising. A model's default is to answer from the pattern it already carries, which is precisely the report-not-the-thing failure the principle targets. "Genchi genbutsu" is a short instruction to go and look first.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Before proposing a cause for any bug: read the failing output, not the description of it
* When a summary, ticket or handover is the only evidence available — the term names what is missing
* Requirements work, where what users say they do and what they do diverge
* Incident review, where the trace and the log are the genbutsu and the reconstruction is not
* Any time an explanation feels plausible and no one has yet looked

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "It means walking the factory floor" — the place is whatever place the work actually happens, including a terminal and a log
* ❌ "A gemba walk is genchi genbutsu" — a scheduled tour can be either the practice or a substitute for it
* ❌ "Go and see means go and check" — Smalley lists "confirming preexisting conclusions rather than observing openly" first among the common mistakes
* ❌ "One visit is enough" — "single visits instead of repeated observation" is another of Smalley's named failures
* ✓ "It is the observation step that `five-whys` depends on" — correct, and the reason the two belong together

## **Criticism**:

* **In practice it becomes theatre.** Annette Franz's critique is aimed at the practice as executed by leaders: when treated as an inspection, "employees perform. They hide problems, sanitize reality, and the walk becomes a staged event, not a learning exercise." Her sharper point concerns credibility: "When leaders repeatedly ask, 'What's getting in your way?' and nothing changes, credibility erodes fast." And without discipline, "Gemba collapses into performative leadership" — "Gemba becomes expensive theater." Franz's own conclusion is that the method is not the fault: leaders are. https://cx-journey.com/2026/03/gemba-walks-dont-fail-leaders-do.html[Franz, "Gemba Walks Don't Fail. Leaders Do."] (18 March 2026).
* **The observed change under observation.** The staged-event problem is not only a leadership failing; it is a measurement problem the principle does not solve. What genchi genbutsu delivers is the actual place under the condition of being watched, and nothing in the method separates the two.
* **The Ohno circle does not transplant.** Christoph Roser is direct about the limits of imitating it: "Not everybody is willing to observe a process for potentially hours on end. There is a risk of the trainee becoming upset about this 'waste of time.'" He adds the practical precondition that it "works only where workers have the time to answer your questions" and that you "must not interrupt their work", and argues for adapting the exercise rather than copying it. https://www.allaboutlean.com/chalk-circle/[Roser, "Taiichi Ohno's Chalk Circle"] (5 January 2016, updated 21 August 2025).
* **The story's provenance is thinly sourced.** Roser's account, like most, presents the chalk circle as established fact without documentary evidence. Treat it as a teaching legend that carries the idea, not as a verified episode.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Formally codified at Toyota.** Smalley records that when Toyota wrote down its management philosophy for a global workforce, genchi genbutsu became one of the five key principles of the Toyota Way 2001, alongside Challenge, Kaizen, Respect and Teamwork. https://artoflean.com/reference/genchi-genbutsu/[Smalley, "Genchi Genbutsu", TPS Encyclopedia].
* **The failure modes are catalogued, which is itself a sign of drift.** Smalley lists five recurring mistakes: confirming preexisting conclusions instead of observing openly; single visits instead of repeated observation; delegating the observation to subordinates; physical presence without active attention; and limiting the practice to factory floors. A principle needs such a list only once the ritual has outgrown the substance.
* **"Gemba walk" is now the dominant Western form of the term** — a scheduled leadership round rather than an engineer standing still for three hours. Both senses live in current training data; the walk is the one a model is likelier to produce unprompted.

### GTD — Getting Things Done

***Full Name***: Getting Things Done (GTD)

***Also known as***: GTD, GTD by David Allen, GTD Methodology

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Capture***: Collect everything that has your attention — tasks, ideas, commitments — into trusted external "inboxes" so nothing is held in your head

***Clarify***: Process each captured item: Is it actionable? If yes, define the next physical action. If no, trash it, incubate it, or file it as reference

***Organize***: Place clarified items into the right lists — Next Actions, Projects, Waiting For, Someday/Maybe, Calendar — so they are retrievable at the right moment

***Reflect***: Review your system regularly (Weekly Review) to keep it current, complete, and trusted

***Engage***: Choose which actions to take based on context, time available, energy, and priority

***Two-Minute Rule***: If an action takes less than two minutes, do it immediately rather than deferring it

***Projects List***: Any desired outcome requiring more than one action step is a "project" tracked on a dedicated list with at least one next action

***Contexts***: Next actions are tagged by context (e.g., @computer, @phone, @errands) to batch work efficiently

***Trusted System***: All commitments are stored externally so the mind is free to focus on doing rather than remembering

***Key Proponent***: David Allen ("Getting Things Done: The Art of Stress-Free Productivity")

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Managing a high volume of tasks, projects, and commitments across work and personal life
* Reducing mental load and anxiety caused by open loops (unfinished commitments)
* Setting up a reliable personal productivity and task management system
* Improving focus by clarifying next actions rather than vague to-do items
* Onboarding teams or individuals to structured workflow management
* Combining with note-taking systems such as P.A.R.A. or todo.txt

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* P.A.R.A. Method
* todo.txt-flavoured Markdown
* Definition of Done

### Hemingway Bridge

***Full Name***: Hemingway Bridge

***Also known as***: Stop Mid-Sentence Technique, Re-entry Point Strategy

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Stop Before You Are Finished***: End each work session deliberately before reaching a natural stopping point, while you still know exactly what comes next — preserving momentum for the next session

***Re-entry Point***: Leave a clear "bridge" to the next session: an unfinished sentence, a comment, a TODO note, or a short summary of the next steps so you can re-engage immediately without warm-up

***Creative Energy Management***: Avoid depleting all creative or cognitive energy in one session; stopping when energy is still high makes it easier to start again

***Reduce Blank-Page Anxiety***: By never fully stopping, you eliminate the paralysing "blank page" moment at the start of the next session

***Momentum Preservation***: The psychological state of "knowing what comes next" is transferred across time boundaries, keeping flow intact across interruptions

***Session Notes***: A brief note written at the end of a session ("next: implement X, blocked by Y") acts as an explicit Hemingway Bridge — a ready-made launchpad

***Key Proponent***: Ernest Hemingway (interviewed in George Plimpton (ed.), "The Paris Review Interviews"; practical elaboration by Steven Pressfield and others in the context of creative work)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Ending a coding, writing, or design session mid-task to ensure smooth re-entry next time
* Managing long-horizon creative or analytical projects across multiple sessions
* Combating procrastination and "blank page" paralysis at the start of work
* Pair programming or team handovers — leaving an explicit next-action note in comments or a ticket
* Daily work planning: close the day by writing tomorrow's first action
* Any knowledge work where cognitive warm-up cost is high

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* GTD — Getting Things Done
* P.A.R.A. Method
* todo.txt-flavoured Markdown

### P.A.R.A. Method

***Full Name***: P.A.R.A. Method (Projects, Areas, Resources, Archive)

***Also known as***: PARA Framework, Second Brain Organization System

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Projects***: Short-term efforts with a specific goal and deadline (e.g., "Launch website", "Write article")

***Areas***: Long-term responsibilities with a standard to maintain over time (e.g., "Health", "Finances", "Team Management")

***Resources***: Topics of ongoing interest or future relevance without a current action (e.g., "Machine Learning", "Design Patterns")

***Archive***: Inactive items from the other three categories — completed projects, dropped areas, or obsolete resources

***Actionability principle***: Items are organized by how actionable they are, not by topic or type

***Tool-agnostic***: Applicable to any note-taking or file management system (Notion, Obsidian, Roam Research, plain folders)

***Single source of truth***: Each piece of information belongs in exactly one of the four categories

***Key Proponent***: Tiago Forte ("Building a Second Brain")

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Organizing notes, documents, or files across tools
* Managing knowledge work with multiple concurrent projects
* Setting up a "Second Brain" personal knowledge management system
* Reducing time spent searching for information
* Separating actionable work from reference material
* Onboarding teams to a shared information architecture
* Structuring documentation repositories or wikis

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Diátaxis Framework
* todo.txt-flavoured Markdown

### todo.txt-flavoured Markdown

***Full Name***: todo.txt-flavoured Markdown Task Lists

***Also known as***: Enhanced Markdown Tasks, Markdown with todo.txt conventions

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Markdown task lists***: Standard GitHub-flavoured markdown syntax (`- [ ]` uncompleted, `- [x]` completed)

***Priority markers***: Uses todo.txt priority notation `(A)`, `(B)`, `(C)` where `(A)` is highest priority

***Project tags***: Prefixed with `+` to group related tasks (e.g., `+website`, `+semantic-anchors`)

***Context tags***: Prefixed with `@` to indicate location/tool/context (e.g., `@computer`, `@home`, `@research`)

***Key-value metadata***: Structured data pairs like `due:YYYY-MM-DD`, `priority:high`, or custom fields

***Date tracking***: Creation dates and completion dates in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD)

***Human readability***: Plain text format that remains readable without special tools

***Tool-agnostic***: Can be processed by both markdown renderers and todo.txt tools

***Searchable and filterable***: Easy to grep/search by tags, priorities, or metadata

[discrete]
## **Pattern Structure**:

```markdown
- [ ] (Priority) Task description +project @context key:value
- [x] YYYY-MM-DD (Priority) Completed task +project
```
[discrete]
## **Example Usage**:

```markdown
- [ ] (A) Review PR for +website @computer due:2024-02-03
- [x] 2024-02-01 (B) Update documentation +docToolchain
- [ ] (C) Research new feature +semantic-anchors @research
- [ ] Call team meeting @phone +project-planning due:2024-02-05
- [x] 2024-01-30 Fix bug in authentication +backend @computer
```
***Key Proponents***: Combines GitHub-flavoured Markdown task lists with Gina Trapani's todo.txt format

[discrete]
## **Original References**:

* GitHub-flavoured Markdown task lists
* todo.txt format specification by Gina Trapani

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Task management in markdown documentation
* Project planning and tracking in README files
* GitHub issues and pull request descriptions requiring structured task lists
* Personal productivity systems using plain text
* Documentation that combines narrative with actionable tasks
* When you need both human readability and programmatic parsing
* Team collaboration where tasks need clear priorities and contexts
* Generating consistent task list formats with LLMs

[discrete]
## **Benefits**:

* Leverages two well-established, widely recognized standards
* Renders nicely in GitHub, GitLab, and other markdown viewers
* Remains fully functional in plain text editors
* Enables rich metadata without sacrificing readability
* Facilitates both manual and automated task tracking

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The underlying todo.txt format is alive and canonical at https://todotxt.org/[todotxt.org] (Gina Trapani): one task per line, priorities as `(A)`, projects as `+project`, contexts as `@context`
* The prior is thin twice over: todo.txt itself is a single-maintainer niche ecosystem from the plain-text-productivity scene, and the **Markdown-flavoured** combination this anchor describes is a project-level convention on top — paste the concrete conventions into the prompt rather than relying on the name

---

## Meta

### Luhmann's System Theory

***Full Name***: Luhmann's Sociological System Theory (Luhmannsche Systemtheorie)

***Also known as***: Theory of Autopoietic Social Systems, Functional-Structural Systems Theory

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***System/Environment Difference***: A system defines itself by drawing a distinction (**Differenz**) between itself and its environment. "Es gibt kein System ohne Umwelt. Hier ist das System, dort die Umwelt. Wer das sagt, unterscheidet zwischen diesen beiden." (Luhmann, **Einführung in die Systemtheorie**, Kap. II)

***Operational Closure***: Systems reproduce themselves through their own operations. Social systems operate through communication, psychic systems through thought. No operation crosses the boundary. "Selbstreferentielle Geschlossenheit ist nur in einer Umwelt, ist nur unter ökologischen Bedingungen möglich."

***Autopoiesis***: Systems produce and reproduce their own elements. A system exists as long as operations connect to operations. "Ein System erhält sich dadurch, dass Operationen aneinander anschließen."

***Structural Coupling***: Systems cannot directly interact, but they can build expectation structures that make them sensitive to specific irritations from their environment. Language couples psychic and social systems.

***Double Contingency***: The foundational paradox of social interaction: "I will do what you want if you do what I want" — resolved only through the emergence of social systems. "Das gesamte Soziale kann als Antwort auf das Problem der doppelten Kontingenz gesehen werden." (**Soziale Systeme**, Kap. IV)

***Self-Reference / Self-Observation***: Systems observe themselves by distinguishing self-reference from external reference (**Fremdreferenz**). "Beobachten heißt: unterscheiden (-> differenzieren)."

***Communication as Operation***: Social systems consist of communication, not of people. Communication is the synthesis of information, utterance, and understanding.

***Complexity Reduction***: Systems reduce environmental complexity through selection. "Sinn" (meaning) is the medium through which psychic and social systems process complexity.

***Functional Differentiation***: Modern society differentiates into function systems (economy, law, politics, science, religion) each with their own binary code.

***Key Proponents***: Niklas Luhmann (**Soziale Systeme**, 1984; **Einführung in die Systemtheorie**, Vorlesung 1991/92, hg. v. Dirk Baecker), Humberto Maturana (autopoiesis, biological roots)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Analyzing complex socio-technical systems where boundaries are contested
* Designing system architectures that respect operational closure of subsystems
* Understanding why direct control often fails (systems can only be perturbed, not instructed)
* Modeling emergent behavior in multi-agent or organizational systems
* Identifying feedback loops and unintended consequences in automation design
* Distinguishing between the system's perspective and the observer's perspective

[discrete]
## **Relationship to Other Anchors**:

* Foundation for the System-Theoretic Semantic Anchors framework (see separate proposal)
* Complements Cynefin Framework (complexity classification) with operational theory
* Provides the theoretical basis for Semantic Contracts (structural coupling, see separate proposal)
* Contrasts with simpler input-output models of systems (e.g., early cybernetics)
* Related to Feynman Technique at the meta-level: Luhmann demands understanding systems through their own logic

***Historical Context***: Luhmann developed his theory across 30+ books and 500+ articles. The **Einführung in die Systemtheorie** is a transcribed lecture course from 1991/92 and is considered the most accessible entry point. His work fundamentally challenges common-sense notions of communication, causality, and control.

### Simon's Constructivism

***Full Name***: Simon's Introduction to System Theory and Constructivism

***Also known as***: Simon's Systemic Epistemology, Clinical Epistemology

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Systemic Thinking = System-Theoretic Explanation***: "Systemtheorie beschäftigt sich mit der 'Welt der Objekte'; aber sie isoliert sie nicht aus ihren realen Zusammenhängen, sondern setzt sie in Beziehung zueinander." Systemisches Denken ist systemtheoretisches Erklären — nicht nur Beschreiben. (Simon, **Einführung in Systemtheorie und Konstruktivismus**, Vorbemerkung)

***Emergent Properties***: "Systeme sind aus mehreren Teilen zusammengesetzte Einheiten, deren Eigenschaften emergent, d.h. nicht durch die schlichte Addition der Eigenschaften ihrer Teile herstellbar waren." (Kap. 1)

***Trivial vs. Non-Trivial Machines***: Trivial machines are predictable (same input → same output). Non-trivial machines depend on internal state — they are history-dependent and not fully predictable. Social systems are non-trivial machines. (Kap. 3.1)

***Cybernetics of Cybernetics (2nd Order)***: The observer is always part of the observed system. "Die Kybernetik der Kybernetik — der Beobachter wird in die Beobachtung einbezogen." (Kap. 3.2)

***Viability vs. Truth***: "Wahrheit vs. Viabilität — Die 'Passung' zwischen Landschaft und Landkarte." Knowledge is not "true" in an absolute sense, but viable if it enables successful operation in a given environment. (Kap. 4.5)

***Information as "Differences that Make a Difference"***: (Gregory Bateson) Information is not transmitted but created by the receiver. "Unterschiede, die Unterschiede machen." The Sender-Receiver model is replaced by circular causality. (Kap. 4.1)

***Beobachtung = Unterscheiden und Bezeichnen***: Every observation draws a distinction and names one side. The other side remains unmarked. (Kap. 4.3, following George Spencer-Brown)

***Operational Closure***: "Systeme sind operativ geschlossen und können nur nach ihrer eigenen Logik operieren." (Kap. 3.4)

***Perturbation vs. Instruction***: "Systeme können nicht instruiert, nur irritiert (perturbiert) werden." — A crucial principle for any intervention design. (Kap. 3.5)

***Structural Coupling + Co-Evolution***: Systems shape each other's environments over time, leading to coordinated structural drift without direct causality. (Kap. 5.1)

***Meaning Dimensions (Social, Factual, Temporal)***: Every communication (in Luhmann's sense) operates simultaneously in three dimensions: social (who), factual (what), temporal (when). (Kap. 6.4, following Luhmann)

***Key Proponents***: Fritz B. Simon (**Einführung in Systemtheorie und Konstruktivismus**, 2006, 8. Aufl. 2017), Humberto Maturana (autopoiesis), Gregory Bateson (cybernetics), Heinz von Foerster (constructivism), Ernst von Glasersfeld (radical constructivism)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Training teams in systemic thinking for complex problem-solving
* Designing interventions where direct control is impossible (organizations, families, ecosystems)
* Understanding why the same input produces different results in human systems
* Developing feedback-aware designs for socio-technical systems
* Distinguishing between explanation, description, and evaluation in requirements
* Building awareness of observer bias in system design and analysis

[discrete]
## **Relationship to Other Anchors**:

* Pedagogical bridge between Luhmann's System Theory and practical application
* Theoretical foundation for Systemic Consulting methods
* Provides the epistemological basis for the System-Theoretic Semantic Anchors framework (see separate proposal)
* "Ten Commandments of Systemic Thinking" (Kap. 7) are a direct precursor to Semantic Contracts (see separate proposal)
* Contrasts with purely technical systems theory (e.g., general systems theory, Bertalanffy)

***Quote***: "Regeln kann man leichter verändern als Menschen." (Fritz B. Simon)

### The Spectrum of Semantic Anchors

## What Qualifies as a Semantic Anchor

A term qualifies as a semantic anchor when it activates a rich, well-defined conceptual framework in the LLM's training data. The key differentiator is **definition depth** – not whether the anchor is about domain knowledge or interaction patterns.

A good semantic anchor is:

***Precise***: It references a specific, established body of knowledge or methodology with clear boundaries

***Rich***: It activates multiple interconnected concepts, not just a single instruction or directive

***Consistent***: Different users invoking it will get similar conceptual activation across contexts

***Attributable***: It can be traced to key proponents, publications, established practices, or documented standards

Semantic anchors exist on a spectrum from domain-heavy to interaction-heavy:

```
Domain-heavy ◄──────────────────────► Interaction-heavy
   arc42          Pyramid Principle        Socratic Method
   SOLID          Rubber Duck Debugging    BLUF
   DDD            Five Whys                Chain of Thought
```
The distinction isn't a strict category but rather a matter of emphasis. Most anchors have **both** dimensions:

***Pyramid Principle***: Domain knowledge about structured communication + behavior change in how output is structured

***TDD, London School***: Domain knowledge about testing + behavior change in how code is written

***Socratic Method***: Interaction pattern for dialogue + domain knowledge from philosophical tradition

The quality bar is the same across this spectrum – all anchors must be well-defined, rich, and activatable.

### Counter-Examples

Well-known terms that are **not** semantic anchors because they lack definition depth:

***"TLDR"***: Underspecified, no defined structure or methodology, vague instruction to "be short"

***"ELI5"***: Vague target level, no pedagogical framework, no consistent interpretation

***"Keep it short"***: Pure instruction, no conceptual depth or established methodology

***"Make it simple"***: Ambiguous directive without reference to specific simplification frameworks

These terms may be useful in conversation, but they don't activate rich conceptual frameworks the way true semantic anchors do.

The catalog itself is the list. Browse it on the [catalog home page](https://llm-coding.github.io/Semantic-Anchors/), filter it by category or role there, or read the [quality criteria](#/about) and the [rejected proposals](#/rejected-proposals) to see where the line is drawn in practice. Every measurement behind a tier rating is recorded in the [prior-test register](#/prior-tests).

---

## Problem Solving

### A3 Problem Solving

***Full Name***: A3 Problem Solving

***Also known as***: A3 thinking, the A3 management process, the A3 report

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***This Anchor Names the Method, Not the Paper Size***: "A3" is used in two different ways, and they get confused constantly. One is a **format** — a single sheet 297 × 420 mm, as in the X-Matrix of `hoshin-kanri`, which is "a single-page A3 artifact". The other, meant here, is a **problem-solving method** with a fixed narrative sequence, as referenced in `five-whys`. Anything printed on one big sheet is an A3 in the first sense. Only the sequence below is A3 problem solving.

***The Story Runs Left to Right***: Background — why this matters. Current condition, with data and a drawing. Goal, stated as a measurable target. Root cause analysis, usually `five-whys` or a fishbone. Countermeasures. Implementation plan with owners and dates. Follow-up: how you will know it worked, and what you learned. The Lean Enterprise Institute lists the same span: "the current situation, the nature of the issue, the range of possible counter-measures, the best countermeasure, the means (who will do what when) to put it into practice, and the evidence that the issue has actually been addressed."

***It Is PDCA on One Page***: Left half is Plan. Right half is Do, Check, Act. The paper enforces the cycle's order and makes a skipped step visible as a gap on the sheet.

***The Constraint Is the Method***: One sheet is not a stylistic preference. It forces selection, forbids the appendix, and makes an unclear problem statement impossible to hide behind volume. If the analysis does not fit, the problem is not yet understood.

***It Is a Dialogue, Not a Document***: In Shook's account the A3 is written iteratively, challenged by a mentor, and rewritten. The owner has responsibility without authority and must gain agreement by argument. LEI is explicit that it is "a management process learned through dialogue rather than merely a document", and that the systematic approach holds "regardless of whether they are guided by or record their findings on an A3 document."

***Key Proponents***: John Shook, whose _Managing to Learn: Using the A3 Management Process to Solve Problems, Gain Agreement, Mentor, and Lead_ (Lean Enterprise Institute, 2008) is the reference text; and Durward K. Sobek II with Art Smalley, _Understanding A3 Thinking_ (Productivity Press, 2008).

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* A recurring problem that needs an owner, a cause, and a check — not a ticket and a guess
* Incident and post-mortem write-ups where the discipline is to reach a cause and a countermeasure, not to narrate
* Proposals that must win agreement across teams without positional authority
* Coaching: the A3 is a mentoring instrument first, a report second
* As the container for `five-whys`, which supplies the cause-analysis box but nothing around it

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "An A3 is any one-page summary" — that is the format sense; the method is the sequence
* ❌ "The A3 is the deliverable" — Shook: "The A3 itself is nothing–it's just a blank piece of paper you use to tell a story"
* ❌ "Fill in the template and you are done" — the named failure mode, and Shook's own objection to templates
* ❌ "One pass is enough" — the method assumes rewriting under challenge
* ✓ "It is PDCA made visible on a single sheet" — a fair and useful compression

## **Criticism**:

* **The author's own warning is about the template.** John Shook, interviewed by Mark Graban: "I'm always skeptical of standard templates for something like that only because that tends to lean toward that tendency to see it as a fill-in-the-box exercise." And on where the difficulty actually lies: "You can learn to write an A3 in a day, but learning to use it as a management process takes much longer." https://www.leanblog.org/2009/01/john-shook-a3-problem-solving-managing-to-learn/[Graban, "John Shook on A3 Problem Solving and the Managing to Learn Process"] (6 January 2009). A method whose best-known proponent has to warn against its most common use is worth flagging as such.
* **Without a coach and a management system it does not take.** Mike Loughrin of Transformance Advisors lists why A3 efforts fail: organisations underestimate the process, treating it as "one piece of paper, one pencil, and one eraser"; they short-change coaching — "Many have not required a coaching role while others have not trained their leaders with the skills required for success"; there is no system for launching, monitoring and closing projects; and the methodology gets forced onto problems better suited to other approaches, with poor scoping leaving efforts to stagnate past 120 days. https://transformanceadvisors.com/portfolio/why-do-a3-fail/[Loughrin, "Why do A3 problem solving efforts often fail?"] (no date given on the page).
* **The power is claimed to sit outside the artifact, which makes the method hard to adopt piecemeal.** Sobek and Smalley: "The power of the A3 report, however, derives not from the report itself, but rather from the development of the culture and mindset required for the implementation of the A3 system." https://www.routledge.com/Understanding-A3-Thinking-A-Critical-Component-of-Toyotas-PDCA-Management-System/SobekII-Smalley/p/book/9781563273605[_Understanding A3 Thinking_, Productivity Press, 2008]. Read as criticism, it is an admission: buying the form buys nothing.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The two senses of "A3" both remain in active use**, including inside this catalog: `hoshin-kanri` uses A3 as a paper format for the X-Matrix, `five-whys` uses it as the problem-solving method. Neither is wrong. Say which one you mean, or a model will happily hand you a one-page layout when you asked for a root-cause discipline.
* **LEI still separates the thinking from the sheet.** Its lexicon defines A3 thinking as "a systematic approach to resolving problems" and notes that "someone can follow this systematic approach, regardless of whether they are guided by or record their findings on an A3 document." https://www.lean.org/lexicon-terms/a3-report/[LEI Lexicon, "A3 Report"].
* **No standard, no edition drift.** Unlike `dmaic` (ISO 13053) or `qfd` (ISO 16355), A3 carries no normative definition. _Managing to Learn_ (2008) remains the canonical text and the strongest prior; templates in the wild vary in their box count and labels, which is exactly what Shook objected to.

### Chain of Thought (CoT)

***Full Name***: Chain of Thought Prompting

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Step-by-Step Reasoning***: Explicitly show intermediate reasoning steps before reaching a conclusion

***Reasoning Transparency***: Make the thought process visible, not just the final answer

***Intermediate Representations***: Break complex problems into smaller, manageable steps

***Error Reduction***: Exposing reasoning allows detection of logical errors mid-process

***Complex Task Decomposition***: Handle multi-step problems that cannot be solved in one jump

***Zero-Shot CoT***: Simple prompt like "Let's think step by step" to trigger CoT behavior

***Few-Shot CoT***: Provide examples with reasoning chains to guide the model

***Self-Consistency***: Generate multiple reasoning paths and select most consistent answer

***Key Proponents***: Wei et al. (Google Research, 2022), "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models"

***Historical Context***: Breakthrough in LLM prompting research, significantly improved performance on reasoning tasks (math, logic, common sense)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Complex reasoning problems (multi-step math, logic puzzles)
* When you need to verify the reasoning process, not just the answer
* Debugging incorrect LLM outputs by seeing where reasoning went wrong
* Teaching or explaining complex topics where steps matter
* Problems requiring planning or strategy
* Any task where intermediate steps provide value

[discrete]
## **Related Research**:

* Tree of Thoughts (ToT): Extension allowing branching and backtracking
* Self-Consistency: Sample multiple reasoning paths
* Least-to-Most Prompting: Build up from simple to complex

[discrete]
## **Example Prompt Pattern**:

```
Problem: [Complex question]
Let's solve this step by step:
1. [First step]
2. [Second step]
...
Therefore: [Conclusion]
```
[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The core finding (Wei et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903[NeurIPS 2022]) is stable, but its practical relevance is cutoff-bound: reasoning models (late 2024 onward) internalise chain-of-thought during training — https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices[OpenAI's own docs] now advise against "think step by step" prompts for those models
* Treat CoT output as a useful but unreliable window into model reasoning: Turpin et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04388["Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think"] (2023) and https://www.anthropic.com/research/reasoning-models-dont-say-think[Anthropic's 2025 follow-up] show stated reasoning can be unfaithful to the actual decision factors — not a safety or audit guarantee

### Chesterton's Fence

***Full Name***: Chesterton's Fence

***Also known as***: The fence-and-gate parable; "don't remove a fence until you know why it was put up"

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **The parable moves the burden of proof onto the remover.** G.K. Chesterton, _The Thing_ (1929), chapter "The Drift from Domesticity": "There exists in such a case a certain institution or law; let us say for the sake of simplicity, a fence or gate erected across a road. The more modern type of reformer goes gaily up to it and says, 'I don't see the use of this; let us clear it away.' To which the more intelligent type of reformer will do well to answer: 'If you don't see the use of it, I certainly won't let you clear it away. Go away and think. Then, when you can come back and tell me that you do see the use of it, I may allow you to destroy it.'" Not seeing a reason is a fact about the observer, not about the fence.
* **The unexplained artifact is evidence, not noise.** Chesterton's supporting argument is the half that travels best into engineering: "The gate or fence did not grow there. It was not set up by somnambulists who built it in their sleep." A hard-coded seven-second retry delay, a feature flag that has been on for two years, a defensive check nobody can justify -- each one is a cheap record of a failure that once happened to somebody.
* **It buys a delay, not a veto -- and Chesterton wrote the exit clause himself.** Two sentences later in the same essay: "If he knows how it arose, and what purposes it was supposed to serve, he may really be able to say that they were bad purposes, or that they have since become bad purposes, or that they are purposes which are no longer served." A good-faith, timeboxed investigation that turns up nothing earns the removal. Take it out reversibly -- behind a flag, in a revertible commit -- and watch the signal that would tell you the fence was load-bearing.
* **It looks backwards, where second-order thinking looks forwards.** `second-order-thinking` asks "and then what?" about a change you are about to make. Chesterton's Fence asks "and why is this here?" about something already standing. The two compose: recover the reason first, then trace what removing it sets in motion.
* **The dig is a method, not an attitude.** `git log` and `git blame` on the line, `git log -S` on the unexplained string, the ticket or pull request that introduced it, the incident it followed, the on-call runbook and the alert definitions, and the author if they are still reachable. Operational documentation usually explains a strange line of code faster than the code does.
* **The effort scales with the blast radius.** An unused CSS class and a retry delay in a payment flow do not deserve the same archaeology. Let what breaks if you are wrong set the timebox.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Inheriting or modernising a system whose oddities nobody on the current team can explain -- the case the principle was made for
* Any cleanup list that already contains the words "safe", "obviously unused" or "quick win"
* Reviewing a pull request whose diff is mostly deletions
* Deprecating an API, a config flag, a cron job or a database column that appears to have no callers
* Joining a team and meeting a process that looks pointless from the outside
* As a brake on a static analyser -- or an LLM -- that confidently reports dead code

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "Never change anything you don't understand" -- the principle demands an investigation, not permanent preservation. Chesterton explicitly allows destruction once the purpose is known and found wanting.
* ❌ "The fence stays until someone proves it useless" -- that turns the burden into an unfalsifiable one, because nobody can prove the absence of a reason. The test is a serious attempt to find the reason, bounded in time.
* ❌ "It is an argument for tradition" -- in Chesterton's essay it was one. Applied to a codebase it is an argument about evidence: the artifact is the only surviving witness to a failure whose ticket is long closed.
* ❌ "Understanding it means reading the code" -- the reason is rarely in the code. It is in the incident, the contract, the regulator's letter, the vendor who used to time out.
* ✓ "It is a stopping rule for confident deletion" -- fair, and that is what makes it usable rather than merely wise.

## **Criticism**:

* **Reformers usually do see the use of the fence.** Paul Currion reads the original essay against itself: "The problem is that, even in Chesterton's day, none of the reformers he so clearly disdained failed to see the use of the fence; it was simply that they disagreed with people like Chesterton that that use was worth preserving the fence for." He also calls the framing gatekeeping rather than argument -- Chesterton "doesn't just want to have a debate about the anti-domestic drift; he wants to decide who is allowed to have that debate based on whether they meet his philosophical criteria", so "Chesterton's fence is being erected to exclude somebody". https://currion.net/2020/09/20/tearing-down-chestertons-fence/[Currion, "Tearing down Chesterton's fence"] (20 September 2020).
* **Invoked as a conversation-stopper, it is toothless.** Kevin Corcoran's objection is that the people arguing for removal have typically done the archaeology already: "Public choice theory meets Chesterton's injunction to understand what led to these regulatory fences being created." Where that is so, "invoking Chesterton's Fence is likewise toothless -- the person doing so only shows they are a step behind in the discussion." https://www.econlib.org/misusing-chestertons-fence/[Corcoran, "Misusing Chesterton's Fence", Econlib] (15 December 2022).
* **The removal process is itself a fence.** Stuart Armstrong's one-sentence post turns the principle on itself as "Chesterton's meta-fence": "in our current system (democratic market economies with large governments) the common practice of taking down Chesterton fences is a process which seems well established and has a decent track record, and should not be unduly interfered with (unless you fully understand it)". https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/WxDpeBi6aQAMH4BGB/stub-the-problem-with-chesterton-s-fence[Armstrong, LessWrong] (5 January 2016). This is the cuts-both-ways form: caution about removal is a policy too, and it has costs nobody counts.
* **The principle cannot tell a wise fence from an unjust one.** Arnold Kling: "Conservatives use the shorthand 'Chesterton's Fence' to describe their position." His counter-example is segregation -- "Racial segregation was wrong. But it was like a fence that had been in place for a long time. Does that mean it should be left in place?" -- and his conclusion is a repair rather than a rejection: the argument "has to be more nuanced than just 'never tear down the fence'". https://arnoldkling.substack.com/p/the-trouble-with-chestertons-fence[Kling, "The Trouble with Chesterton's Fence"] (25 August 2023).
* **No named German-language critique was found.** A German search returned only approving restatements. French, Spanish, Japanese and Chinese were not searched. That is a gap in our search, not in the discourse.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The name is not Chesterton's.** The string "Chesterton's fence" does not occur anywhere in _The Thing_; the https://www.gkc.org.uk/gkc/books/The_Thing.txt[full text at gkc.org.uk] carries the parable in "The Drift from Domesticity" and never the label. Chesterton wrote the parable, someone else named it. Who, and when, we could not establish from a citable source, so no coinage is claimed here.
* **The compressed version that circulates is also not his.** https://fs.blog/chestertons-fence/[Farnam Street] states it as "Do not remove a fence until you know why it was put up in the first place" -- shorter, sharper and not a sentence in the essay. The same page carries the caveat the short form loses: "The point is not that the status quo is always right, that every fence should remain standing." The https://www.lesswrong.com/w/chesterton-s-fence[LessWrong wiki entry] is the other main route by which the label spread, and it collects the counter-arguments alongside it.
* **Software adopted it as a rule about legacy code, not about institutions.** Oskar Dudycz's https://event-driven.io/en/chesterton_fence_and_software_architecture/[essay on Chesterton's Fence and software architecture] (17 August 2022) is representative of the genre: the fence becomes the line of code whose purpose is lost, and the reform becomes a refactoring. This is a genuine shift of subject -- Chesterton was defending the household, not a retry delay -- and it is the sense in which the anchor is used today.
* **The drift is worth naming in one direction only.** Nothing in the software reading contradicts the original argument; it narrows it. Where Chesterton's critics attack the essay's politics, the engineering use inherits none of it, because a payment service has no opponents to exclude.
* **A prior test on 2026-09-30 measured what naming it changes.** On a legacy-modernisation scenario that did not imply the principle, no baseline named it unprompted. A weak-tier model without the anchor called removing always-on feature flags a "safe, high-confidence win"; with the anchor it inserted an "Understand the fence" phase and asked whether the flags were finished rollouts or kill switches for a known bad vendor path. A strong-tier baseline was already cautious, and what the anchor added there was method -- read the runbook and the alert definitions before the code -- plus an explicit rule for when removal is earned. See the [prior-test register](#/prior-tests).

### Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC)

***Full Name***: Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication

***Also known as***: CERC -- but see _Common Misunderstandings_: the bare acronym does not carry the meaning

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **Be First.** An information vacuum does not stay empty. Communicating early, with a timestamp and an explicit account of what is not yet known, beats waiting for a complete picture.
* **Be Right.** Accuracy over completeness: separate what is confirmed from what is unknown from what is being investigated, and commit in advance to correcting what turns out wrong.
* **Be Credible.** Honesty and consistency over reassurance. Admitting uncertainty preserves the standing you will need for the next message.
* **Express Empathy.** Name the disruption and the distress before explaining the cause. People who feel unacknowledged stop reading.
* **Promote Action.** Give something concrete and feasible to do. Action restores a sense of control and displaces speculation.
* **Show Respect.** Address the audience as capable adults. Dismissing concerns as irrational forfeits the trust the other five principles are spending.
* **Communication under uncertainty is the design premise.** The framework assumes you must speak before the facts are in -- which is exactly the situation a status update during an unresolved incident is written in.
* **The crisis has a lifecycle.** Preparation, initial reaction, maintenance, resolution, evaluation. What the audience needs, and therefore what the message should carry, differs by phase.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Writing the first public statement about an incident whose cause is not yet known
* Status pages, customer notifications and internal updates while an outage is still unresolved
* Security disclosures, where the temptation to wait for certainty is strongest and most costly
* Preparing the communication plan before the incident, which is the phase the framework treats as primary

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Using the bare acronym.** "CERC" alone is not reliable vocabulary. Asked without context, a frontier model returns India's Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, Canada Excellence Research Chairs and a coastal engineering centre before it reaches this framework -- and in our measurement it did not reach it at all. Spell the name out. The prior-test register carries the evidence.
* **Reading "Be First" as speed over accuracy.** It is first **with what is known**, including the fact that little is. The two principles constrain each other rather than compete.
* **Treating empathy as a tone.** It is a content requirement -- naming the concrete effect on the reader -- not a softer register applied to the same sentences.

## **Criticism**:

* **The framework has almost never been tested, and that is the central objection.** Ann Neville Miller, Chad Collins, Lindsay Neuberger, Andrew Todd, Timothy L. Sellnow and Laura Boutemen, https://jicrcr.com/index.php/jicrcr/article/view/38["Being First, Being Right, and Being Credible Since 2002: A Systematic Review of Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) Research"], _Journal of International Crisis and Risk Communication Research_ (19 March 2021). They record the charge -- CERC "has been criticized as lacking the coherence and unity necessary to serve as a framework for research" -- and then measure it: "A total of 4,471 articles in 20 languages were screened, 400 full texts examined, and 19 articles included in the research and theory analysis, of which one tested tenets of the CERC model." Their conclusion: "CERC has rarely been theoretically tested, and we argue that reformulation of the propositions is necessary for empirical support of the model to proceed." The framework is distilled practice, not an empirically established model, and it should be named as such.
* **Its own custodian departed from it in the crisis that mattered most.** Molly A. Sauer, Shaun Truelove, Amelia K. Gerste and Rupali J. Limaye organise their analysis of the US COVID-19 response around the six principles and find the credibility principle broken by the CDC itself. On the revised school-reopening guidance of late July 2020: "This perceived bowing to political pressure, rather than relying on scientific rigor, was another blow to the CDC's credibility." https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9195491/["A Failure to Communicate? How Public Messaging Has Strained the COVID-19 Response in the United States"], _Health Security_ 19(1), 65--74 (18 February 2021). This is evidence about institutions under pressure rather than about the principles -- and it is the case every reader will have in mind.
* **No citable German-language criticism was found**, and no pass was run in French, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese or Korean. Given that the systematic review above screened 20 languages and still found near-nothing, thinness is plausible here rather than merely unmeasured -- but the honest statement remains: absent in our search.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **There is no single current edition of the manual.** The CDC now serves it as per-chapter PDFs with different years: Introduction to CERC (2018), The Psychology of a Crisis (2019), Messages and Audiences (2018), Community Engagement (2018), Crisis Communication Plans (2014), Spokesperson (2014), Working with the Media (2014). https://www.cdc.gov/cerc/php/cerc-manual/index.html[Manual index], page date stamp 20 November 2024. Citing "the 2018 edition" is therefore only partly right.
* **Older CERC links are probably stale.** The content moved to the `/cerc/php/...` URL scheme in the 2024 site reorganisation. The six-principle set itself appears in current CDC material carrying 2024 date stamps, so the framework is live rather than archived.
* **The model paper.** Reynolds B, Seeger MW, "Crisis and emergency risk communication as an integrative model", _Journal of Health Communication_ 10(1), 43--55 (2005). Attribution is split in practice and worth keeping split: the integrative model paper is Reynolds and Seeger; the manual, the training programme and the six-principle formulation are the CDC's as an institution.
* **Whether the principle wording drifted between the 2012, 2014 and 2018 chapter generations we did not establish.** The chapter structure demonstrably changed; the six principles appear stable, which is an observation and not a verified continuity.

### Decisional Balance Sheet

***Also known as***: Benjamin Franklin Analysis, Moral Algebra, Pros-and-Cons Sheet

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Four-Cell Matrix***: The full Janis & Mann form has four categories of consequence for each alternative — **utilitarian gains/losses for self**, **utilitarian gains/losses for significant others**, **self-approval/disapproval**, and **approval/disapproval from others**. Stretches "pros and cons" beyond instrumental outcomes into identity and social cost.

***Simplified Two-Column Form***: The everyday "pros vs cons" list popularised by Benjamin Franklin (1772 letter to Joseph Priestley). Strictly a degenerate case of the four-cell matrix — useful for quick decisions, lossy for complex ones.

***Weighting***: Each entry gets a numeric weight reflecting its importance. The decision is **not** a vote count — the discipline is to make trade-offs explicit, not to mechanise the choice.

***Resolving Ambivalence***: The artifact's primary purpose is **not** arithmetic but surfacing concerns the decider has not yet articulated. Listing the cons of a tempting option, or the pros of the rejected one, breaks the "all pros, no cons" framing that drives impulsive decisions.

***Decisional Conflict***: Janis & Mann's parent theory; high-stakes decisions produce stress that distorts judgment. The balance sheet is one of several debiasing techniques alongside vigilant information search and contingency planning.

***Motivational Interviewing Variant***: In the Prochaska–DiClemente **Stages of Change** model and Miller & Rollnick's **Motivational Interviewing**, the balance sheet is used to elicit change-talk: the client **says** the cons of staying the same and the pros of changing — moving them through ambivalence rather than persuading them.

***Limits***: The model is **deliberative**, not intuitive. It works poorly under time pressure and for decisions dominated by uncertainty (where Pugh Matrix or scenario-based methods fit better). It also doesn't surface options that aren't on the list — separate from the option-generation step.

***Key Proponents***: Irving Janis & Leon Mann ("Decision Making: A Psychological Analysis of Conflict, Choice, and Commitment", 1977 — the formal four-cell model). Benjamin Franklin (1772 letter, "moral algebra" — the informal pros/cons ancestor). William R. Miller & Stephen Rollnick ("Motivational Interviewing", 1991) for the clinical adaptation.

***Historical Context***: Franklin's pros/cons letter is one of the earliest documented decision-aid techniques in the Western tradition. Janis & Mann turned it into a research instrument in the 1970s; the simplified two-column form has spread through self-help, coaching, and Motivational Interviewing into mainstream use. Now a staple of decision coaching, financial advisory, and health-behaviour-change interventions.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Personal or career decisions where the alternatives are roughly comparable and the deciding factor is the decider's own clarity
* Coaching conversations where the client is **stuck in ambivalence** — the four-cell version surfaces concerns the simple pros/cons list misses
* Pre-mortem variant: pre-listing the "approval/disapproval from others" cell often predicts political resistance the team forgot to address
* Motivational Interviewing settings — health behaviour, addiction recovery, career changes
* Decision documentation in low-formality contexts where a full ADR is overkill but "we considered the alternatives" must be visible

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Pugh Matrix — scores alternatives against weighted criteria; complement when uncertainty or technical trade-offs dominate over personal/social cost
* ADR according to Nygard — captures architecture decisions with Context/Decision/Consequences; the balance sheet feeds the Consequences section
* MoSCoW — prioritisation among items chosen **after** the decision is made; the balance sheet helps decide **whether** to do the work at all

### Devil's Advocate

***Full Name***: Devil's Advocate (Latin: **Advocatus Diaboli**)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Systematic Counter-Argumentation***: Present opposing viewpoints even if not personally held

***Assumption Challenging***: Question premises and surface hidden assumptions

***Stress-Testing Ideas***: Identify weaknesses before they become problems

***Steelmanning***: Present the **strongest** version of the opposing argument, not a strawman

***Intellectual Honesty***: Separate idea evaluation from ego or political concerns

***Pre-Mortem Thinking***: Imagine failure scenarios to prevent them

***Dialectical Reasoning***: Thesis + Antithesis → Synthesis

***Risk Identification***: Surface potential problems proactively

***Key Origin***: Catholic Church canonization process (Promotor Fidei role, formalized 1587), secularized in critical thinking and decision-making

***Historical Context***: 400+ years as formalized practice in the Church, adopted widely in law, philosophy, business strategy, and red teaming

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Critical design or architecture decisions where failure is costly
* Security threat modeling (red teaming)
* Evaluating business strategies or proposals
* Pre-mortems before launching significant initiatives
* Code review where you want to challenge assumptions
* Risk assessment and contingency planning
* Any high-stakes decision where being wrong is expensive

[discrete]
## **Related Concepts**:

* Red teaming (security context)
* Pre-mortem analysis
* Dialectical reasoning
* Critical thinking frameworks
* Steelmanning (vs. strawmanning)

[discrete]
## **Example Prompt Pattern**:

```
I propose [idea/design/decision].
Play devil's advocate: What are the strongest arguments against this approach?
```

### DMADV

***Full Name***: Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, Verify

***Also known as***: DFSS, Design for Six Sigma

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Quality is Designed In, Not Inspected In***: DMADV exists because the cheapest place to remove a defect is the drawing board. Once a product or process is built, `dmaic` can only push its capability toward the limit the design allows. DMADV sets that limit.

***The Five Phases Owe Different Deliverables Than DMAIC's***: Same first three letters, different work:
* **Define** — the design mandate: customer segments, the business case, and the scope of what is being created. Not a defect to be reduced, but a gap to be filled.
* **Measure** — the Voice of the Customer translated into measurable CTQs (Critical to Quality) with targets and tolerances. There is no process to baseline yet, so "measure" means **quantify the requirement**, not the status quo.
* **Analyze** — generate and compare design **concepts** against the CTQs, then pick one. This is the phase where `pugh-matrix` and `kano-model` earn their keep.
* **Design** — the detailed design: parameters, tolerances, and a predicted capability for each CTQ, usually with `fmea` on the chosen concept and designed experiments on the critical parameters.
* **Verify** — build it, run pilot production, and demonstrate that the delivered thing meets the CTQs before handover to operations.

***Verify is Not Control***: DMAIC's last phase sustains a gain that already exists. DMADV's last phase proves a prediction. The question is not "is it still holding?" but "did the design do what the model said it would?" Handover to an operational control plan happens **after** Verify, which is where the two roadmaps meet.

***Predicted Capability Instead of Measured Capability***: Through Analyze and Design there is no **process** to measure, because it does not exist yet. Prototypes, DOE runs and simulations do produce data, but the capability of the future process is **predicted** from models — transfer functions, tolerance stacks, capability estimates — and only confirmed against the real thing in Verify. That gap between predicted and demonstrated capability is the method's core bet and the source of most of its criticism.

***Design Freeze as a Tollgate***: Like DMAIC, phases end in formal reviews and a project can be stopped at one. The tollgate at the end of Design is the expensive one: after it, changes cost an order of magnitude more.

***The Trigger That Picks DMADV***: Use DMADV when the process does not exist yet, or when an existing process is so far from the requirement that improving it cannot close the gap. If a capable process is merely running badly, DMADV is the wrong tool and `dmaic` is the right one.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing a new product, service or process where the quality target is fixed before the first prototype
* Replacing a process whose **entrenched** capability cannot reach the requirement, no matter how well it is tuned
* Translating fuzzy customer wishes into numeric, testable acceptance targets before the architecture is chosen — the CTQ step is useful far outside manufacturing
* Comparing design concepts on explicit criteria rather than on whoever argues loudest
* As the counterpart to `dmaic` in a portfolio: naming which of the two applies is itself a decision worth making out loud

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "DMADV and DMAIC differ only in the last two letters" — they differ in what Measure and Analyze **mean**. DMAIC measures a process; DMADV quantifies a requirement. DMAIC analyses causes; DMADV analyses concepts.
* ❌ "DFSS is a standardised roadmap like DMAIC" — it is not. DMADV, IDOV and DDICA all circulate under the DFSS label, and no single one won.
* ❌ "Verify means testing the finished product" — Verify means demonstrating the **predicted** capability on pilot output, against the CTQs fixed in Measure.
* ✓ "DMADV is a stage-gate design process with a statistics habit" — fair, and the reason it collides with design cultures that work by iteration.

## **Criticism**:

* **Applied to invention, it damages invention.** The most-cited case is 3M. Brian Hindo's report names DFSS explicitly as one of the two Six Sigma tools CEO James McNerney imported: "The other flavor is called Design for Six Sigma, or DFSS, which purports to systematize a new product development process." Post-it note inventor Art Fry "places the blame for 3M's recent lack of innovative sizzle squarely on Six Sigma's application in 3M's research labs", and 3M R&D vice-president Larry Wendling conceded: "We were letting, I think, the process get in the way of doing the actual invention." Successor CEO George Buckley "loosened the reins a bit by removing 3M research scientists' obligation to hew to Six Sigma objectives." https://effectuation.org/hubfs/Journal%20Articles/2016/06/3m-struggle-between-efficiency-and-creativity.pdf[Hindo, "At 3M, A Struggle Between Efficiency And Creativity", _BusinessWeek_, 11 June 2007].
* **The evidence points the same way beyond the anecdote.** The same report cites work by Wharton's Mary Benner and Harvard's Michael L. Tushman analysing patents in paint and photography firms before and after a quality drive: "after the quality push, patents issued based primarily on prior work made up a dramatically larger share of the total, while those not based on prior work dwindled." A design method that shifts output toward the incremental is a poor fit for the phase whose job is the non-incremental.
* **The translation tool at DMADV's heart produces numbers that do not mean what designers think they mean.** Andrew Olewnik and Kemper Lewis studied the House of Quality, the QFD matrix that converts customer attributes into engineering targets in the Measure phase, and concluded that "while the tool offers conceptual support to the design process, the quantitative information that results is largely invalid." http://www.emerald.com/ijqrm/article/25/2/125-146/139984[Olewnik & Lewis, "Limitations of the House of Quality to provide quantitative design information", _International Journal of Quality & Reliability Management_ 25(2), 2008, pp. 125–146].
* **Its optima are model optima.** The https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_for_Six_Sigma[Design for Six Sigma overview] states the standing objection to the statistical-modelling step plainly: even the best statistical model is an approximation to reality, so an estimated optimum need not be an actual optimum. DMADV inherits every weakness of the model it designs against, and it commits to that model before there is anything to measure.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **DMAIC was standardised; DMADV was not.** Six Sigma's improvement road became ISO 13053-1:2011, whose title says "Part 1: DMAIC methodology" — see `dmaic`.
