The design road has no comparable single roadmap: DMADV shares the DFSS label with IDOV (identify, design, optimise, verify) and DDICA, among others. Anyone who says "we run DFSS" has said less than they think.
* **The name still travels better than the practice.** DMADV remains the canonical answer to "what is the design-side counterpart of DMAIC?" and that is the prior a model reliably serves. Which phases a given organisation actually runs varies far more than the acronym suggests.
* **Its tools outlived the roadmap.** QFD, `pugh-matrix`, design `fmea` and designed experiments are all in routine use in product development without anyone invoking DMADV. As an anchor, DMADV is most useful as the **name of the sequence**; the individual tools have their own, stronger priors.

### DMAIC

***Full Name***: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control

***Also known as***: the Six Sigma improvement cycle, DMAIC roadmap

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Five Gated Phases***: The cycle runs in a fixed order, and each phase owes a defined deliverable before the next begins:
* **Define** — the business problem, goal, scope and timeline, captured in a project charter with the customer's CTQs (Critical to Quality)
* **Measure** — a baseline of current performance, with operational definitions and a check that the measurement system itself is trustworthy
* **Analyze** — root causes, identified and **validated** against the data, not merely proposed
* **Improve** — solutions that address those causes, piloted before rollout
* **Control** — a control plan that holds the gain: monitoring, response plans, ownership

***Measurement Before Improvement***: The gate between Measure and Analyze is the method's backbone. No improvement is proposed before a baseline exists, so the effect can be demonstrated rather than asserted.

***Root Cause Before Solution***: Analyze is deliberately separated from Improve, which forces causes to be established before remedies are designed — the opposite of the usual reflex to solution first.

***Tollgate Reviews***: Phase transitions are formal reviews, not soft handovers. A project can be stopped at a gate.

***The Control Phase is the Differentiator***: Most improvement approaches end when the fix ships. DMAIC treats sustaining the gain as its own phase, typically with SPC control charts — this is where the anchor meets `spc`, `control-chart-shewhart` and `nelson-rules`.

***DMADV, the Sibling***: DMAIC improves an **existing** process. For a new product or process design, Six Sigma uses DMADV (Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, Verify), also called DFSS. Naming the wrong one sends the output down the wrong road.

***PDCA Lineage***: The Six Sigma project methodologies are inspired by W. Edwards Deming's Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle; DMAIC is its phase-gated, measurement-heavy descendant.

***Key Proponents***: Bill Smith, who introduced Six Sigma at Motorola in 1986; Mikel J. Harry; General Electric, where Jack Welch made it central to business strategy in 1995.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Improving an existing process whose performance is unsatisfactory but whose cause is unknown
* Any task where the temptation is to jump straight to solutions — DMAIC forces a baseline and a validated cause first
* Quality and reliability work that has to **stay** fixed, because the Control phase is explicit
* Structuring an improvement initiative into reviewable stages with named deliverables
* As the frame around `spc`: DMAIC is the project, SPC is what runs in its Control phase

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "DMAIC is for manufacturing only" — ISO 13053-1 explicitly covers service and transactional processes
* ❌ "DMAIC designs new processes" — that is DMADV; DMAIC improves existing ones
* ❌ "The phases can be reordered or skipped" — the gates are the method; without Measure before Improve it is just a to-do list
* ✓ "DMAIC is PDCA with gates and statistics" — a fair summary, and the basis of one of its criticisms

## **Criticism**:

* **Not original.** Quality expert Joseph M. Juran, via the https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Sigma[Six Sigma overview]: "there is nothing new there. It includes what we used to call facilitators. They've adopted more flamboyant terms, like belts with different colors." The core loop is Deming's PDSA under new branding.
* **It can suppress the work it measures.** A _BusinessWeek_ report on James McNerney's introduction of Six Sigma at 3M found it stifled creativity, and the method was withdrawn from the research function. _Design News_ editor John Dodge: "excessive metrics, steps, measurements and Six Sigma's intense focus on reducing variability water down the discovery process." Variance reduction is the wrong objective where variance is the point.
* **Most projects fail.** A 2010 _Wall Street Journal_ figure cited in the same overview puts the failure rate of Six Sigma projects above 60%.
* **The statistics are contested.** Statistician Donald J. Wheeler dismissed the 1.5-sigma shift — the assumption underpinning the "3.4 defects per million" headline — as "goofy" (2004). Over-reliance on statistical method and misreading of p-values are recurring complaints.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* DMAIC is unusual among management methods in being **standardised**: https://www.iso.org/standard/52901.html[ISO 13053-1:2011] ("Quantitative methods in process improvement — Six Sigma — Part 1: DMAIC methodology") specifies best practice for each phase, the project roles, and their training; Part 2 covers the tools per phase. Its scope explicitly includes service and transactional processes, not only manufacturing.
* In practice the dominant contemporary form is **Lean Six Sigma**, which pairs DMAIC's measurement discipline with Lean's focus on flow and waste. The prior most training data serves is the five-phase DMAIC cycle as described here.

### Double Diamond

***Full Name***: Double Diamond Design Process Model

***Also known as***: 4Ds Model, Design Council Double Diamond

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Two Diamonds, Four Phases***: **Discover → Define → Develop → Deliver**. Each diamond is one divergent-convergent cycle. The first diamond explores and frames the **problem**; the second diamond explores and ships the **solution**.

***Discover (Divergent, Problem Space)***: Broad research — interviews, observation, immersion, data analysis. Goal: widen the understanding of what's actually going on, not jump to causes.

***Define (Convergent, Problem Space)***: Synthesize findings into a sharp problem statement. The famous slogan: **"Are we solving the right problem?"** — the diamond ends with a problem worth solving, not a list of features.

***Develop (Divergent, Solution Space)***: Generate many candidate solutions — sketches, prototypes, co-design workshops. Diverge widely before narrowing; resist solution fixation.

***Deliver (Convergent, Solution Space)***: Test, refine, ship. The chosen concept is iterated until it's production-ready; failed candidates are explicitly killed rather than left lingering.

***Design the Right Thing, Then Design the Thing Right***: The canonical summary. The first diamond addresses "right thing" (problem worth solving); the second addresses "thing right" (solution that works).

***Divergent Before Convergent***: A hard discipline at every phase. Premature convergence — picking the obvious problem or obvious solution — is the failure mode the model is designed to prevent.

***Iteration, Not Waterfall***: The diamonds are not strictly linear. Learnings in Develop frequently send the team back to Discover or Define. The 2019 **Framework for Innovation** update made this explicit.

***Mindsets and Principles***: The Design Council pairs the four phases with four principles (Put people first, Communicate visually and inclusively, Collaborate and co-create, Iterate, iterate, iterate) — the diamonds without the mindset is just process theater.

***Key Proponents***: UK Design Council (originally published 2005; expanded as **Framework for Innovation** in 2019). Built on the divergent-convergent tradition of J.P. Guilford (1956) and Béla H. Bánáthy.

***Historical Context***: Developed by the Design Council in 2005 after research into how leading design organizations actually worked. The 2019 update reframed it as a system-level innovation framework, adding the principles, key roles, and explicit iteration arrows. Adopted broadly in UX, service design, government innovation (UK GDS, NHS, Danish Mindlab), and design education.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Framing UX or service design projects when the team is at risk of jumping to solutions
* Innovation workshops and design sprints — the diamonds give a shared visual model for sequencing divergent and convergent work
* Discovery phases of product development when the problem itself is not yet well understood
* Teaching design thinking — the model is more concrete than abstract "design thinking" because it names the four moves
* Communicating **why** a discovery phase is necessary to stakeholders who want to skip straight to delivery

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Jobs to be Done — sharpens the **Define** output by reframing customer needs as functional, emotional, and social jobs
* Problem Space (NVC) — separates needs from strategies; complements the first-diamond discipline of staying in problem space
* XY Problem — anti-pattern that the first diamond is designed to prevent (solving Y before understanding X)
* MVP — the **Deliver** output is often shaped as an MVP to validate the chosen solution against the defined problem

### Fermi Estimation

***Also known as***: Order-of-Magnitude Estimation, Back-of-the-Envelope Calculation, Fermi Problem, Guesstimation

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Decomposition***: Break an unknown quantity into a chain of smaller sub-quantities you can each estimate with some confidence

***Order-of-magnitude reasoning***: Reason in powers of ten; aim to land the right power of ten rather than an exact figure

***Bracketing***: For each sub-quantity, pick a plausible lower and upper bound, then take the geometric mean of the bounds as the estimate

***Error cancellation***: Independent over- and under-estimates tend to cancel, so the product of many rough guesses is often within a factor of 2-3 of the true value

***Sanity check / sizing***: Use the estimate to test whether a claim, design, or measured number is even plausible before investing in precision

***The piano-tuner problem***: Fermi's classic teaching example — "How many piano tuners are there in Chicago?" — solved by chaining population, pianos per household, tuning frequency, and tuner throughput

***Key Proponents***: Enrico Fermi (estimated the Trinity-test yield by dropping paper scraps in the blast wave, landing within an order of magnitude); Lawrence Weinstein and John A. Adam (https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691129495/guesstimation["Guesstimation: Solving the World's Problems on the Back of a Cocktail Napkin"], Princeton University Press, 2008)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Sizing a system before committing to detailed analysis (capacity, cost, traffic)
* Build-vs-buy and feasibility checks where exact numbers are unavailable
* Interview and whiteboard estimation problems
* Validating a surprising metric or vendor claim against rough physical limits
* Prompting an LLM to sanity-check a quantitative estimate by decomposing it and reasoning in powers of ten

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* First Principles Thinking
* MECE
* Five Whys

### Feynman Technique

***Full Name***: Feynman Technique (also Feynman Learning Method)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Explain Simply***: Teach the concept in simple language as if to a beginner (traditionally "explain to a 12-year-old")

***Identify Gaps***: When you struggle to explain, you've found gaps in your understanding

***Return to Source Material***: Go back and re-learn the parts you couldn't explain clearly

***Simplify and Use Analogies***: Refine explanation using plain language and concrete examples

***Iterative Refinement***: Repeat the cycle until you can explain clearly and simply

***No Jargon Hiding***: Inability to avoid jargon signals lack of true understanding

***Active Learning***: Transform passive reading into active teaching

***Metacognition***: Become aware of what you don't know

***Key Attribution***: Richard Feynman (Nobel Prize-winning physicist, 1965), famous for making complex physics accessible

***Historical Context***: Feynman was renowned for his teaching ability and his belief that deep understanding meant being able to explain simply. The "technique" is a formalization of his learning approach.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Learning new technical concepts or frameworks
* Validating your understanding before using knowledge in practice
* Preparing to teach or present a topic
* Debugging conceptual confusion
* Code review where you explain your design choices simply
* Documentation writing (if you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it)

[discrete]
## **Four Steps (Canonical Form)**:

1. **Choose a concept**: Pick the topic you want to understand
1. **Teach it to a child**: Write an explanation in simple terms
1. **Identify gaps and review**: Where you struggle, study more
1. **Simplify and analogize**: Refine your explanation, use examples

[discrete]
## **Related Concepts**:

* Rubber Duck Debugging (explaining to understand)
* Learning by teaching
* Active recall
* Elaborative interrogation
* Plain language movement

***Quote***: "If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough." (Often attributed to Einstein, but embodies Feynman's philosophy)

### First Principles Thinking

***Full Name***: First Principles Thinking

***Also known as***: Reasoning from First Principles, Reasoning from Fundamentals

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Reduce to fundamentals***: Break a problem down to the basic truths that cannot be deduced from anything more fundamental, then reason upward from those

***Reason vs. analogy***: Contrast with reasoning by analogy ("we do it this way because that's how it's done") — first principles rebuild the answer from the ground up

***Challenge inherited assumptions***: Each "requirement" or "constraint" is interrogated: is it a law of nature, or merely convention/legacy that can be discarded?

***Ground-up synthesis***: After identifying the irreducible elements, recombine them into a solution unconstrained by how the problem was solved before

***Cost of the method***: Powerful but expensive — reserve it for high-stakes or stuck problems; reasoning by analogy is fine for routine decisions

***Key Proponents***: Rooted in Aristotle (the "first cause"/archē); sharpened by René Descartes' methodical doubt; popularized in modern engineering discourse (e.g. Elon Musk's cost-of-batteries example)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* A problem feels blocked because "that's just how it's done"
* Re-examining requirements, cost structures, or architecture constraints
* High-stakes design decisions where analogy may mislead
* Teaching learners to separate fundamental truths from convention

[discrete]
## **When NOT to Use**:

* Routine decisions where established patterns are good enough — the method is costly
* When proven best practices already encode hard-won fundamentals

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Feynman Technique — explain from fundamentals to expose gaps
* Socratic Method — question assumptions to reach bedrock
* Five Whys — drill from symptom toward a root cause

### Five Whys (Ohno)

***Full Name***: Five Whys Root Cause Analysis

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Iterative Causal Analysis***: Ask "Why?" repeatedly (typically ~5 times) to drill down to root causes

***Root Cause vs. Symptom***: Distinguish between surface symptoms and underlying causes

***Causal Chain***: Each answer becomes the subject of the next "Why?" question

***Actionable Root Cause***: Continue until you reach a cause that can be acted upon

***Simplicity***: No complex tools or statistical analysis required

***Team-Based Investigation***: Collaborative exploration of causal relationships

***Avoiding Blame***: Focus on process failures, not individual fault

***Countermeasure Identification***: Once root cause is found, design interventions

***Key Proponent***: Taiichi Ohno (Toyota Production System, 1950s)

***Historical Context***: Core tool in Lean Manufacturing and Toyota Production System (TPS), foundational to continuous improvement (Kaizen)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Incident post-mortems in software/DevOps
* Debugging when surface fixes don't resolve the issue
* Process improvement initiatives
* Understanding recurring problems
* Quality defect analysis
* Any situation where symptoms are clear but causes are not

[discrete]
## **Related Concepts**:

* Kaizen (continuous improvement)
* Root Cause Analysis (RCA)
* Fishbone Diagram (Ishikawa) – complementary tool
* A3 Problem Solving (Toyota)
* DevOps post-mortem culture

[discrete]
## **Pitfall to Avoid**:

* Stopping too early at a symptom rather than root cause
* Pursuing a single causal chain when multiple factors contribute (use Fishbone Diagram for complex causality)
* Blame-focused questioning rather than system-focused

[discrete]
## **Example Application**:

```
Problem: Website is down
Why? → Database connection failed
Why? → Connection pool exhausted
Why? → Long-running queries not timing out
Why? → No query timeout configured
Why? → Default configuration was never reviewed for production
Root Cause: Configuration review process missing
Countermeasure: Establish pre-production configuration checklist
```
[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Alan J. Card, https://qualitysafety.bmj.com/content/26/8/671["The problem with '5 whys'"] (BMJ Quality & Safety, 2017) — no evidence of effectiveness despite wide institutional adoption; the technique pushes investigators down a single linear causal path and its results are not reproducible across teams
* John Allspaw, https://www.kitchensoap.com/2014/11/14/the-infinite-hows-or-the-dangers-of-the-five-whys/["The Infinite Hows (or, the Dangers of the Five Whys)"] (2014) — "why" questions invite blame and narrative bias in complex systems; he proposes asking "how" about the conditions instead
* The deeper objection: in complex systems a single root cause often does not exist — incidents emerge from interacting contributing factors, which a five-step linear chain cannot represent

### FMEA

***Full Name***: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis

***Also known as***: FMECA (Failure Mode, Effects and Criticality Analysis) when a criticality step is added; Design FMEA (DFMEA) and Process FMEA (PFMEA) by scope

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Bottom-Up, Not Top-Down***: FMEA starts at the component or process step and asks what can fail **here**, then traces the effect outward. Fault tree analysis works the other way, from an undesired event down to its causes. Picking the wrong direction produces a plausible-looking document that answers a question nobody asked.

***Three Questions Per Failure Mode***: For every way an item can fail, the analysis records its **effect** (what the customer or system notices), its **cause** (why it happens), and its **controls** (what prevents it or detects it). These are separate columns because they have separate remedies: prevention attacks the cause, detection attacks the escape.

***Three Ratings, and What Used to Be Done With Them***: Each failure mode is rated for Severity, Occurrence and Detection, classically on a 1–10 scale. The traditional Risk Priority Number is their product — RPN = S × O × D — used to rank what gets fixed first. That multiplication is where the method's central controversy sits; see Criticism and Current Status.

***Prevention Beats Detection***: A control that stops a failure mode from occurring is worth more than one that catches it afterwards, and the rating scheme is meant to reflect that. Systems that chase a low RPN often improve Detection because it is cheapest, which lowers the number without lowering the risk.

***Forward-Looking, Unlike Root Cause Analysis***: `five-whys` and `ishikawa-diagram` work backwards from something that already happened. FMEA works forwards from something that has not happened yet, which makes it a sibling of `premortem` in intent and of `stride` in structure — both enumerate failure modes against a model before there is damage to investigate.

***A Living Document, Not a Deliverable***: An FMEA that is written once for an audit and never reopened has lost its function. Its value is in being revisited when the design, the process or the field data change.

***Key Milestones***: Procedures were described in 1949 in the US military document MIL-P-1629, revised as MIL-STD-1629A in 1980; NASA contractors applied variants across Apollo, Viking, Voyager and Skylab; Ford introduced FMEA after the Pinto affair and extended it to process FMEA; AIAG published the first automotive FMEA standard in 1993.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing or changing something whose failure is expensive, dangerous or hard to reverse
* Before a launch, migration or cutover, to enumerate failure modes while there is still time to add controls
* Safety and regulatory work, where an auditable record of considered failure modes is itself a requirement — see `iec-61508-sil-levels`
* In software: dependency and interface failure analysis, resilience reviews, and anything where "what happens when this call never returns?" needs a written answer
* As the risk counterpart to `dmaic`: FMEA is a standard tool in its Analyze and Improve phases

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "FMEA finds the root cause of an incident" — it is a prospective method. For an incident that already happened, use `five-whys` or `ishikawa-diagram`.
* ❌ "A low RPN means low risk" — a severity-10 failure mode with a low RPN is still a severity-10 failure mode. The number hides exactly what matters most.
* ❌ "FMEA covers combined failures" — used bottom-up it finds single-point failure modes. Failures that require two subsystems to fail together are largely invisible to it.
* ❌ "RPN is what FMEA is" — the automotive standard has dropped RPN in favour of Action Priority. The ratings survived; the multiplication did not.
* ✓ "FMEA is a structured pessimism exercise with an audit trail" — fair, and the reason it pairs well with `premortem`.

## **Criticism**:

* **The RPN ranks things wrongly, by construction.** The https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Failure_mode_and_effects_analysis[FMEA overview] states the defect precisely: "The multiplication of the severity, occurrence and detection rankings may result in rank reversals, where a less serious failure mode receives a higher RPN than a more serious failure mode." Rank reversal is not an error in applying the method; it follows from multiplying ordinal ratings.
* **Arithmetic on ordinal scales is not a small sin.** Michael Krisper catalogues the problem class that the RPN belongs to — "ordinal scales, semi-quantitative arithmetics, range compression, risk inversion, ambiguity, and neglection of uncertainty" — across 24 documented problems with ordinal risk matrices, and argues for fully quantitative risk assessment instead. https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.05440[Krisper, "Problems with Risk Matrices Using Ordinal Scales", arXiv:2103.05440, 2021].
* **The replacement drew its own criticism, from FMEA practitioners.** Richard Harpster argued against the AIAG-VDA design FMEA before it shipped, holding that its structure/function/failure-tree approach is "both ineffective as a risk management tool and very inefficient", that it "more closely resembles a fault tree analysis than a Design FMEA process", and that engineers "will not spend the time and effort to develop verifyable functions/requirements for each of the sub-assemblies". https://www.qualitydigest.com/inside/risk-management-column/case-against-aiag-vda-dfmea-013118.html[Harpster, "The Case Against the AIAG-VDA DFMEA", _Quality Digest_, 31 January 2018].
* **Complexity is a risk of its own.** Carl S. Carlson, author of _Effective FMEAs_, lists five concerns with the new handbook: it "adds considerable new terminology and other complexities", it "consumes valuable time on potentially lower-risk tasks", "enforcing causes at next lower level can miss important causes", it was published before a corresponding standard existed, and it "does an inadequate job of clearly identifying high-risk interfaces". https://accendoreliability.com/reviewing-aiag-vda-fmea-handbook/[Carlson, "Reviewing AIAG / VDA FMEA Handbook", Accendo Reliability, 1 December 2022]. His point is that complexity can bury the high-risk items it was meant to surface.
* **Used alone it does not carry the weight put on it.** The same FMEA overview reports that in healthcare the method showed "limited validity when used in isolation", with scoping and organisational boundaries strongly affecting the result. Where the boundary is drawn decides what the analysis can find.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The automotive world replaced RPN with Action Priority in 2019.** The AIAG & VDA FMEA Handbook, first edition, was published in June 2019 and replaced AIAG's 4th-edition FMEA manuals and VDA Volume 4. Mary Rowzee describes the change: "the recommended method of combining these three indices into a single composite value is no longer the risk priority number" — instead a three-axis reference table assigns each failure mode a high, medium or low Action Priority. https://www.qualitydigest.com/inside/lean-article/understanding-aiag-vda-s-fmea-process-and-approach-061820.html[Rowzee, "Understanding AIAG-VDA's FMEA Process and Approach", _Quality Digest_, 18 June 2020]. A second source puts it flatly: "the Risk Priority Number or RPN has been eliminated. It has been replaced by the AP or Action Priority process." https://quality-one.com/aiag-vda-fmea/[Quality-One, AIAG & VDA FMEA].
* **The handbook also reorganised the method into seven steps** — planning and preparation, structure analysis, function analysis, failure analysis, risk analysis, optimisation, results documentation — which is a different shape from the column-by-column worksheet most training data describes (Rowzee, as above).
* **RPN has not disappeared outside automotive.** The generic standards remain in use — IEC 60812 for FMEA and FMECA, SAE J1739 in the automotive space — and RPN is still the dominant prior in most non-automotive material. When a prompt says "FMEA", expect the model to reach for Severity × Occurrence × Detection unless Action Priority is named.
* **Consequence for prompting:** naming the edition matters here more than for most anchors. "FMEA" gets the classic worksheet; "AIAG & VDA FMEA (2019)" gets seven steps and Action Priority. The two produce different artefacts.

### Genchi Genbutsu

***Full Name***: Genchi Genbutsu (現地現物) — "the actual place, the actual thing"

***Also known as***: go and see, go to gemba, go see for yourself, one of the five principles of the Toyota Way 2001

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Two Words, Two Demands***: Art Smalley reads the characters apart: 現地 (genchi) is "the actual place" where work happens; 現物 (genbutsu) is "the actual thing itself — not reports or descriptions of it". Both halves must be satisfied. Going to the place and then reading a dashboard there satisfies neither.

***Go Yourself***: The person who will decide is the person who must observe. Delegating the looking and receiving a summary reintroduces exactly the layer of abstraction the principle exists to remove.

***Gemba Is the Sibling Term***: **Gemba** (現場) is the actual place — "the scene", in the sense a Japanese journalist or detective would use. Smalley notes both terms share 現 (gen), "present" or "actual", and calls this "Toyota's linguistic emphasis on reality versus assumption". Genchi genbutsu is the practice; gemba is where it happens.

***The Ohno Circle***: The canonical illustration. Taiichi Ohno would chalk a circle on the factory floor and have an engineer stand in it and watch the process. Christoph Roser: "Often, a disciple stood in the circle for hours before Ohno was satisfied." The point was not endurance but perception — the premise is that most people do not see what is in front of them, and that hours of watching reveal what a walk-past cannot.

***Observation Before Hypothesis***: Genchi genbutsu sits upstream of every cause-hunting method. It is what makes a `five-whys` chain worth anything: without direct observation the first "why" is answered from memory, and every later one inherits the guess.

***Why This Matters for an LLM***: Named, it pushes toward reading the actual code, the actual log line, the actual trace, the actual failing test — before theorising. A model's default is to answer from the pattern it already carries, which is precisely the report-not-the-thing failure the principle targets. "Genchi genbutsu" is a short instruction to go and look first.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Before proposing a cause for any bug: read the failing output, not the description of it
* When a summary, ticket or handover is the only evidence available — the term names what is missing
* Requirements work, where what users say they do and what they do diverge
* Incident review, where the trace and the log are the genbutsu and the reconstruction is not
* Any time an explanation feels plausible and no one has yet looked

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "It means walking the factory floor" — the place is whatever place the work actually happens, including a terminal and a log
* ❌ "A gemba walk is genchi genbutsu" — a scheduled tour can be either the practice or a substitute for it
* ❌ "Go and see means go and check" — Smalley lists "confirming preexisting conclusions rather than observing openly" first among the common mistakes
* ❌ "One visit is enough" — "single visits instead of repeated observation" is another of Smalley's named failures
* ✓ "It is the observation step that `five-whys` depends on" — correct, and the reason the two belong together

## **Criticism**:

* **In practice it becomes theatre.** Annette Franz's critique is aimed at the practice as executed by leaders: when treated as an inspection, "employees perform. They hide problems, sanitize reality, and the walk becomes a staged event, not a learning exercise." Her sharper point concerns credibility: "When leaders repeatedly ask, 'What's getting in your way?' and nothing changes, credibility erodes fast." And without discipline, "Gemba collapses into performative leadership" — "Gemba becomes expensive theater." Franz's own conclusion is that the method is not the fault: leaders are. https://cx-journey.com/2026/03/gemba-walks-dont-fail-leaders-do.html[Franz, "Gemba Walks Don't Fail. Leaders Do."] (18 March 2026).
* **The observed change under observation.** The staged-event problem is not only a leadership failing; it is a measurement problem the principle does not solve. What genchi genbutsu delivers is the actual place under the condition of being watched, and nothing in the method separates the two.
* **The Ohno circle does not transplant.** Christoph Roser is direct about the limits of imitating it: "Not everybody is willing to observe a process for potentially hours on end. There is a risk of the trainee becoming upset about this 'waste of time.'" He adds the practical precondition that it "works only where workers have the time to answer your questions" and that you "must not interrupt their work", and argues for adapting the exercise rather than copying it. https://www.allaboutlean.com/chalk-circle/[Roser, "Taiichi Ohno's Chalk Circle"] (5 January 2016, updated 21 August 2025).
* **The story's provenance is thinly sourced.** Roser's account, like most, presents the chalk circle as established fact without documentary evidence. Treat it as a teaching legend that carries the idea, not as a verified episode.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Formally codified at Toyota.** Smalley records that when Toyota wrote down its management philosophy for a global workforce, genchi genbutsu became one of the five key principles of the Toyota Way 2001, alongside Challenge, Kaizen, Respect and Teamwork. https://artoflean.com/reference/genchi-genbutsu/[Smalley, "Genchi Genbutsu", TPS Encyclopedia].
* **The failure modes are catalogued, which is itself a sign of drift.** Smalley lists five recurring mistakes: confirming preexisting conclusions instead of observing openly; single visits instead of repeated observation; delegating the observation to subordinates; physical presence without active attention; and limiting the practice to factory floors. A principle needs such a list only once the ritual has outgrown the substance.
* **"Gemba walk" is now the dominant Western form of the term** — a scheduled leadership round rather than an engineer standing still for three hours. Both senses live in current training data; the walk is the one a model is likelier to produce unprompted.

### Ishikawa Diagram

***Full Name***: Ishikawa Cause-and-Effect Diagram

***Also known as***: fishbone diagram, cause-and-effect diagram, Fishikawa

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***One Effect, Many Branches***: The problem statement sits at the head of the fish. A spine runs to it, and labelled bones branch off, each carrying causes of one kind, with sub-causes branching off those. The shape exists to hold **parallel** causes side by side.

***The Division of Labour With Five Whys***: `five-whys` follows one causal chain downward and is at its best when the chain is real and single. The fishbone spreads across several chains at once and is the tool for problems with contributing factors rather than a cause. Running 5 Whys on a multi-factor problem produces a confident answer about one branch; running a fishbone on a simple chain produces five near-empty branches. Choose by the shape of the causality, not by habit.

***Categories as Memory Aids***: The branch labels are prompts, not a taxonomy. The manufacturing set is the 5 Ms — Manpower, Machine, Material, Method, Measurement — extended to 8 with Mission, Management and Maintenance. Services use 4–5 Ss (Surroundings, Suppliers, Systems, Skill, Safety); product marketing uses 8 Ps. Software teams routinely invent their own set, and that is within the method rather than a deviation from it.

***Structured Brainstorming, Not Evidence***: What the diagram produces is a **list of suspects**. It does not rank them, does not test them and does not tell you which one acted. The step that follows — going to the data — is not part of the diagram, which is why so many fishbones end where the real work should have started.

***Sub-Causes are Where the Value Is***: A branch with one word on it has recorded a category, not a cause. The technique earns its keep two and three levels down, where "Method" becomes a specific step performed in a specific wrong way.

***One of the Seven Basic Tools***: The fishbone diagram sits alongside the check sheet, histogram, Pareto chart, graphs, scatter diagram and stratification. Together with PDCA and the QC-story format, this set became the foundation of _kaizen_ in Japan.

***Key Proponent***: Kaoru Ishikawa, who popularised the technique in the 1960s while pioneering quality management at Kawasaki Heavy Industries' shipyards; the basic concept goes back to the 1920s.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Incident and defect analysis where several factors plausibly contributed and no single chain explains the outcome
* Early in an investigation, to widen the candidate set before narrowing it — the opposite move from `five-whys`
* Group settings, where the branches give quieter participants a structured place to contribute
* In the Analyze phase of `dmaic`, as the standard generator of cause hypotheses that the data then confirms or kills
* Whenever a team has already converged on one explanation and needs to see what else is on the board

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "The fishbone finds the root cause" — it generates candidates. Evidence decides, and the diagram contains none.
* ❌ "You must use the 6 Ms" — the categories are prompts. A set that fits the domain beats a memorised one.
* ❌ "It replaces 5 Whys" — they answer different shapes of question. Parallel causes: fishbone. One chain: `five-whys`. Often both, in that order.
* ❌ "A filled diagram is a finished analysis" — a filled diagram is a hypothesis list that has not been tested yet.
* ✓ "It is `mece` thinking applied to causes" — fair as an aspiration; the categories overlap in practice, which is one of the criticisms below.

## **Criticism**:

* **It offers no definition of what it is looking for.** Mark Paradies of TapRooT lists the gaps bluntly: "there is no guidance for building the bones of the fish. The building of the bone structure depends on the knowledge of the investigator", the technique lacks "any guidance for what a 'root cause' is", and selecting causes by voting "is simply the team's opinion. It doesn't prove that the selected cause caused the incident." He adds that the method "provide[s] no guidance to help investigators develop effective corrective actions". https://taproot.com/fishbone-diagram-root-cause-analysis-pros-cons/[Paradies, "Fishbone Diagram Root Cause Analysis — Pros & Cons", 7 October 2020].
* **Forcing an incident into a fixed shape is not analysis.** Mark Galley of ThinkReliability objects to the premise itself: "The premise of the fishbone is there is one single effect for a given problem", which "does not reflect the nature of real problems". On the categories: "Making the incident fit into a predefined shape is contrived, not scientific" — the incident already happened and therefore has a structure of its own, which the template overwrites. https://blog.thinkreliability.com/updating-the-fishbone-diagram-cause-and-effect-analysis-improved[Galley, "Updating the Fishbone Diagram", 1 February 2021].
* **Brainstorming displaces evidence-gathering.** Galley's practical objection is about where the hour goes: rather than speculating, investigators should "spend that time gathering specific evidence to support or disprove the possible causes". A diagram full of unverified branches can feel like progress while producing none.
* **It cannot surface what the room does not know.** Because the branches come from the participants, the diagram inherits their blind spots and has no mechanism to reveal the omission. Paradies makes the same point about investigators without human-factors training guessing at causes. This limitation is structural, not a matter of facilitation skill.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Canonical and unchanged.** The diagram is documented as "one of the seven basic tools of quality control", with Ishikawa popularising it in the 1960s at the Kawasaki shipyards. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishikawa_diagram[Ishikawa diagram overview]. There is no edition drift here: the 1960s tool and the tool taught today are the same tool.
* **The category sets multiplied, the method did not.** 5 Ms, 8 Ms, 8 Ps and 4–5 Ss all circulate (same source), and teams invent domain-specific sets freely. When precision matters, name the category set in the prompt — otherwise expect the manufacturing 6 Ms by default.
* **Its place in the quality canon is documented and stable.** Ronald D. Moen and Clifford L. Norman list the seven basic tools — "check sheet, histograms, Pareto chart, fishbone diagram, graphs, scatter diagrams and stratification" — and trace them, together with the PDCA cycle and the QC-story format, to the foundation of _kaizen_ in Japan. https://qicentral.rcpch.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/9/2021/10/Moen-and-Norman-on-Deming-circling-back-ph556x.pdf[Moen & Norman, "Circling Back", _Quality Progress_, November 2010, ASQ].
* **The criticism comes from the RCA profession, not from quality management.** The sharpest objections are raised by practitioners who sell structured root-cause methods and who position the fishbone as the thing their approach replaces. That does not make the objections wrong — the missing definition of "root cause" and the absent evidence step are real — but it explains where the discourse lives and why quality-management sources report none of it.

### Kaizen

***Full Name***: Kaizen (改善) — kai, "change", plus zen, "for the better"; conventionally rendered "continuous improvement"

***Also known as***: continual improvement, gemba kaizen, daily kaizen; popularised in the West by Masaaki Imai (1930–2023), founder of the Kaizen Institute (1985)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Small, Continuous, By Everyone***: The unit is the small change made by the person doing the work, repeated without end. Imai's most-quoted formulation, as reported by Mark Graban: "Kaizen is everyone, everywhere, every day." The improvement is not delegated to a specialist function.

***Kaikaku Is the Deliberate Contrast***: **Kaikaku** (改革) is radical, discontinuous change — Jim Womack glosses it as "the Japanese word for revolution, in contrast with kaizen, which is incremental improvement". The pair is what keeps kaizen precise: without kaikaku as its opposite, "continuous improvement" drifts into meaning any change at all. Womack's own position is sequential: "lean transformation will always need to begin with evolution: kaizen and model lines…These create the basic stability", and only afterwards "we really do need to go fast".

***Standardise the Gain, Then Improve From the New Standard***: The second thing that keeps the term precise. An improvement that is not written into the standard is not kaizen; it is a good day. Art Smalley: "Permanent conditions change when the gains get built into standards and held by an operating system that runs daily", with "standardized work as the mechanism connecting daily management to daily improvement — not as a document in a binder". Standard and improvement alternate: the standard is the floor the next improvement starts from, never a freeze.

***A Habit, Not a Project***: Graban summarises Imai's position: "Not a project. Not an event. A daily practice, distributed across the entire organization, expected of everyone — not delegated to a kaizen office or a specialist team."

***It Needs Something to Look At***: Kaizen without `muda-mura-muri` has no diagnosis and without `genchi-genbutsu` no evidence. It is the habit; those supply what the habit examines.

***In Software***: The `boy-scout-rule` is kaizen scoped to a file. Retrospective actions that actually change the working agreement are kaizen; retrospective actions that produce a list are not, because nothing was standardised.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Framing improvement as an everyday obligation of the whole team rather than a quarterly initiative
* Distinguishing a small, reversible, local change from a redesign — say kaizen or say kaikaku, and the conversation separates
* Any improvement effort where the gain will evaporate unless the new way becomes the documented default
* As the daily counterpart to a project-shaped method such as `dmaic`, and as the cultural ground under `toyota-kata`

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "Kaizen means a week-long improvement workshop" — that is a kaizen event, a Western packaging, and the thing the criticism below targets
* ❌ "Kaizen is any improvement" — kaikaku exists precisely so that the word keeps meaning **incremental**
* ❌ "Kaizen is the opposite of standardisation" — it depends on it; without a standard there is nothing to improve from and no way to hold a gain
* ❌ "Kaizen is a Toyota tool" — it is a management philosophy that Imai generalised well beyond manufacturing
* ✓ "It is a habit that produces small, standardised changes made by the people doing the work" — accurate

## **Criticism**:

* **The event replaced the habit.** Art Smalley's critique is aimed squarely at the packaged form: "Kaizen events most commonly fail because organizations never make the transition from running improvement events to building an operating and management system that sustains results daily." And on the arithmetic of the format itself: "A one-week event cannot change permanent conditions on its own. At most it is a vehicle for local change and learning." His conclusion is the line the criticism turns on: "The event is not the system. The daily discipline is the system." https://artoflean.com/gemba-coach/why-does-kaizen-fail/[Smalley, "Why Does Kaizen Fail?", Art of Lean].
* **"Kamikaze kaizen".** Smalley reports that Jim Womack coined the term for such efforts — "intense bursts of activity with no lasting effect other than a fiery death". We verified this quotation only in Smalley's article, not in an original Womack publication; treat it as attributed via Smalley.
* **Imai himself was frustrated by how the West took it up.** In his foreword to _Healthcare Kaizen_, quoted by Graban: "I am profoundly frustrated with the slow pace at which Kaizen strategy has been embraced by the business community", and "Embracing Kaizen is a long-term journey. It is not a flavor of the month and requires the cultural change, commitment and self-discipline that needs to be sustained over many decades." https://www.leanblog.org/2023/06/in-memoriam-masaaki-imai-the-father-of-kaizen-1930%E2%81%A0-%E2%81%A02023/[Graban, "In Memoriam: Masaaki Imai"] (16 June 2023).
* **Continuous improvement without respect for people is the standard failure.** Bob Emiliani: Fake Lean is "the technical application of 'Continuous Improvement' tools and methods, invariably in a zero-sum fashion"; Real Lean requires both continuous improvement **and** respect for people. https://bobemiliani.substack.com/p/back-story-real-vs-fake-lean[Emiliani, "The Backstory: Real vs. Fake Lean"] (13 September 2013).

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The founding text is _Kaizen (Ky'zen), the Key to Japan's Competitive Success_** — Masaaki Imai, Random House Business Division, New York, 1986, 259 pages. The widely cited later edition is published by McGraw-Hill; the title is often given without the "(Ky'zen)" of the original.
* **The more influential book is the second one.** _Gemba Kaizen: A Commonsense, Low-Cost Approach to Management_ (McGraw-Hill, 1997) moved the emphasis to the actual place of work and won the Shingo Research Prize in 1999. Imai's last book was _Strategic KAIZEN_ (McGraw-Hill, 2021). He died on 12 June 2023, aged 92.
* **The trademarked form is a live complication.** The Kaizen Institute, which Imai founded in 1985, writes the term as KAIZEN™ in its own material. The word is simultaneously generic Japanese vocabulary, a management philosophy and a consultancy's brand — worth knowing when a source's capitalisation looks odd.
* **"Kaizen event" remains the dominant Western usage** despite the criticism above, and it is the sense a model is likeliest to reach for. Naming daily kaizen, or naming kaikaku as the contrast, is what steers it back.

### Luhmann's System Theory

***Full Name***: Luhmann's Sociological System Theory (Luhmannsche Systemtheorie)

***Also known as***: Theory of Autopoietic Social Systems, Functional-Structural Systems Theory

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***System/Environment Difference***: A system defines itself by drawing a distinction (**Differenz**) between itself and its environment. "Es gibt kein System ohne Umwelt. Hier ist das System, dort die Umwelt. Wer das sagt, unterscheidet zwischen diesen beiden." (Luhmann, **Einführung in die Systemtheorie**, Kap. II)

***Operational Closure***: Systems reproduce themselves through their own operations. Social systems operate through communication, psychic systems through thought. No operation crosses the boundary. "Selbstreferentielle Geschlossenheit ist nur in einer Umwelt, ist nur unter ökologischen Bedingungen möglich."

***Autopoiesis***: Systems produce and reproduce their own elements. A system exists as long as operations connect to operations. "Ein System erhält sich dadurch, dass Operationen aneinander anschließen."

***Structural Coupling***: Systems cannot directly interact, but they can build expectation structures that make them sensitive to specific irritations from their environment. Language couples psychic and social systems.

***Double Contingency***: The foundational paradox of social interaction: "I will do what you want if you do what I want" — resolved only through the emergence of social systems. "Das gesamte Soziale kann als Antwort auf das Problem der doppelten Kontingenz gesehen werden." (**Soziale Systeme**, Kap. IV)

***Self-Reference / Self-Observation***: Systems observe themselves by distinguishing self-reference from external reference (**Fremdreferenz**). "Beobachten heißt: unterscheiden (-> differenzieren)."

***Communication as Operation***: Social systems consist of communication, not of people. Communication is the synthesis of information, utterance, and understanding.

***Complexity Reduction***: Systems reduce environmental complexity through selection. "Sinn" (meaning) is the medium through which psychic and social systems process complexity.

***Functional Differentiation***: Modern society differentiates into function systems (economy, law, politics, science, religion) each with their own binary code.

***Key Proponents***: Niklas Luhmann (**Soziale Systeme**, 1984; **Einführung in die Systemtheorie**, Vorlesung 1991/92, hg. v. Dirk Baecker), Humberto Maturana (autopoiesis, biological roots)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Analyzing complex socio-technical systems where boundaries are contested
* Designing system architectures that respect operational closure of subsystems
* Understanding why direct control often fails (systems can only be perturbed, not instructed)
* Modeling emergent behavior in multi-agent or organizational systems
* Identifying feedback loops and unintended consequences in automation design
* Distinguishing between the system's perspective and the observer's perspective

[discrete]
## **Relationship to Other Anchors**:

* Foundation for the System-Theoretic Semantic Anchors framework (see separate proposal)
* Complements Cynefin Framework (complexity classification) with operational theory
* Provides the theoretical basis for Semantic Contracts (structural coupling, see separate proposal)
* Contrasts with simpler input-output models of systems (e.g., early cybernetics)
* Related to Feynman Technique at the meta-level: Luhmann demands understanding systems through their own logic

***Historical Context***: Luhmann developed his theory across 30+ books and 500+ articles. The **Einführung in die Systemtheorie** is a transcribed lecture course from 1991/92 and is considered the most accessible entry point. His work fundamentally challenges common-sense notions of communication, causality, and control.

### Morphological Box

***Full Name***: Morphological Analysis / Morphological Box (German: Morphologischer Kasten)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Multi-dimensional decomposition***: Break complex problem into independent parameters/dimensions

***Variant enumeration***: Identify possible values/options for each parameter

***Matrix construction***: Organize parameters and variants in table/box form

***Combinatorial exploration***: Systematically examine combinations of variants

***Constraint filtering***: Eliminate infeasible or contradictory combinations

***Novel solution discovery***: Find non-obvious solutions through systematic recombination

***Complete solution space***: Ensure all possibilities are considered

***Structured creativity***: Systematic approach to innovation and ideation

***Key Proponent***: Fritz Zwicky (1940s-1960s, California Institute of Technology)

***Historical Context***: Developed for aerospace engineering problems (jet engines, spacecraft propulsion), now widely applied in product development, system design, and innovation management.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Exploring design alternatives for complex systems
* Product feature combination analysis
* Technology selection with multiple dimensions
* Architecture decision-making with independent parameters
* Innovation workshops and ideation sessions
* Requirements engineering for product variants
* Solution space mapping before evaluation

[discrete]
## **Example Application**:

```
Problem: Design a developer documentation system
Parameters:
├─ Format: Markdown, AsciiDoc, reStructuredText, API-first
├─ Hosting: GitHub Pages, Netlify, Read the Docs, S3+CloudFront
├─ Generator: Static (Hugo, Jekyll), Dynamic (Docusaurus), Custom
└─ Versioning: Git-based, Version selector, Branch-per-version

Matrix generates 4 × 4 × 3 × 3 = 144 possible combinations
Filter by constraints (e.g., "AsciiDoc + Hugo not well-supported")
→ Identify ~20 feasible solutions for evaluation with Pugh Matrix
```
[discrete]
## **Related Concepts**:

* MECE Principle (for parameter independence)
* Pugh Matrix (for evaluating generated alternatives)
* Design of Experiments (DOE)
* Combinatorial design
* Solution space exploration

[discrete]
## **Complementary Tools**:

* Use **Morphological Box** to generate alternatives
* Then apply **Pugh Matrix** to evaluate and select best option
* Use **MECE** to ensure parameter independence

[discrete]
## **Pitfalls to Avoid**:

* Parameters that are not independent (violates combinatorial logic)
* Too many parameters leading to combinatorial explosion
* Stopping at matrix creation without exploring combinations
* Forgetting to filter out infeasible combinations

### Muda, Mura, Muri

***Full Name***: Muda (無駄), Mura (斑), Muri (無理) — waste, unevenness, overburden; the "three Ms" of the Toyota Production System

***Also known as***: the 3Ms, the three evils, the seven wastes (muda only), TIMWOOD / TIMWOODS (muda only)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Anchor the Triple, Not Muda Alone***: This is the whole reason the anchor exists. Naming only waste hides what produces the waste. Muda is the symptom that is easy to see and easy to count; mura and muri are the conditions that regenerate it after every clean-up.

***The Three, Defined***: The Lean Enterprise Institute's lexicon:
* **Muda** — "Any activity that consumes resources without creating value for the customer."
* **Mura** — "Unevenness in an operation; for example, a gyrating schedule not caused by end-consumer demand but rather by the production system, or an uneven work pace in an operation causing operators to hurry and then wait."
* **Muri** — "Overburdening equipment or operators by requiring them to run at a higher or harder pace with more force and effort for a longer period of time than equipment designs and appropriate workforce management allow."

***The Causal Chain Runs Mura → Muri → Muda***: Jim Womack argues for reversing the conventional recital order: "I would tell them to have it read 'Mura, muri, muda.'" His reason is the mechanism itself — "The inevitable result is that mura creates muri that undercuts previous efforts to eliminate muda." Unevenness forces people and machines past their design point; overburden then manufactures the very waste that was eliminated last quarter.

***The Seven Wastes***: Ohno's categories are transporting, inventory, motion, waiting, over-production, over-processing and defects. Over-production is traditionally treated as the worst, because it generates most of the others.

***The Eighth Waste Is a Later Addition***: "Unused skills" was appended to the original seven, "as resolving this waste is a key enabler to resolving the others". The mnemonic "TIM WOOD" covers the seven; "TIM WOODS", with the S for skills, covers eight. The eighth is not Ohno's.

***Type One and Type Two Muda***: The lexicon distinguishes waste that cannot be removed quickly (rework a current process cannot avoid) from waste that kaizen can remove at once. The distinction stops "eliminate all waste" from being an instruction nobody can follow.

***In Software***: Mura is the release train that ships nothing for three weeks and everything on Thursday; muri is the sprint committed at 110% capacity; muda is the rework, the queue, the half-finished branch. Attacking the rework without touching the batching is the mistake the triple names.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Whenever a "waste elimination" or efficiency effort is being planned, to force the question of what regenerates the waste
* Capacity and scheduling discussions — mura and muri are the vocabulary that batching and overcommitment otherwise lack
* Retrospectives where the same waste keeps returning after being removed
* As the diagnostic layer under `kaizen`: kaizen is the habit, the three Ms are what it looks for

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "Lean is about eliminating waste" — that is muda only, and Womack's argument is that muda-first is the wrong order
* ❌ "There are eight wastes" — there are Ohno's seven plus a later, widely adopted eighth; the distinction matters when citing him
* ❌ "Muri means working hard" — it means being required to run past the design point of the person or machine, which is a property of the system, not of effort
* ❌ "Mura is just variation" — it is unevenness **manufactured by the system itself**, not demand variation from the customer
* ✓ "Fix mura first and much of the muda stops coming back" — this is Womack's point exactly

## **Criticism**:

* **The conventional ordering teaches the wrong reflex.** Womack's essay is itself a criticism of how the three Ms are usually taught and used — muda first, as a hunt for visible waste, with mura and muri as footnotes. He locates the failure in the sequence: "mura creates muri that undercuts previous efforts to eliminate muda", so a muda-first programme is structurally condemned to repeat itself. https://www.lean.org/the-lean-post/articles/mura-muri-muda/[Womack, "Mura, Muri, Muda?", Lean Enterprise Institute] (6 July 2006).
* **Muri, read from the shop floor, is the point of the system rather than a defect in it.** Jane Slaughter's account of "management by stress" describes a system tuned so that "The ideal state is achieved when the plant is running with all stations just on the line between green and yellow" — that is, deliberately at the edge of overburden, using the operator's inability to keep up as the signal for where to improve next. On this reading, muri is not an accident the method removes but a lever the method applies. https://www.multinationalmonitor.org/hyper/issues/1990/01/slaughter.html[Slaughter, "Management by Stress", _Multinational Monitor_, January/February 1990].
* **Waste-hunting without the people half is the common failure mode.** Bob Emiliani's Real Lean / Fake Lean distinction names it: Fake Lean is "the technical application of 'Continuous Improvement' tools and methods, invariably in a zero-sum fashion", while Real Lean is "the application of both 'Continuous Improvement' and 'Respect for People'". His summary of what actually happened: "Lean intends to correct two big problems in organizations: bad processes and bad management. But it usually corrected only one – bad processes." https://bobemiliani.substack.com/p/back-story-real-vs-fake-lean[Emiliani, "The Backstory: Real vs. Fake Lean"] (13 September 2013).

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Womack's reordering has not displaced the conventional recital.** "Muda, mura, muri" remains the common sequence in training material and in most model output, twenty years after the essay. Expect a model to produce the muda-first order and the seven wastes list unless the causal chain is named explicitly.
* **"The seven wastes" now usually means eight.** TIMWOODS, with unused skills or unused human potential added, is the version most current material teaches. Attributing all eight to Ohno is a common and avoidable error.
* **Type One / Type Two muda is fading from popular usage** even though it remains in the Lean Enterprise Institute lexicon. It is the distinction that makes waste lists actionable, and it is the first thing dropped in short-form summaries.

### Occam's Razor

***Full Name***: Occam's Razor (also spelled Ockham's Razor)

***Also known as***: Law of Parsimony, Principle of Parsimony, _Lex Parsimoniae_, "Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity"

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Core rule***
Among competing hypotheses that explain the same observations equally well, prefer the one that requires the fewest assumptions. The razor **shaves off** unnecessary entities, causes, or mechanisms.

**What it is *not***
* Not a rule to be brief or terse — that is a stylistic choice, not an epistemic one.
* Not a proof that the simpler answer is **true** — only a guide to which hypothesis to prefer, investigate first, or commit to under uncertainty.
* Not a licence for KISS-style solution simplification — Occam operates at the level of **explanations**, KISS at the level of **solutions**. They overlap but are not the same razor.

***How it is used***
* As a **selection filter** under uncertainty — when two stories fit the data, start with the one that assumes less.
* As a **debugging heuristic** — before assuming a bug requires a race condition plus caching layer plus stale DNS, check whether a single off-by-one explains everything.
* In **architecture decisions** — a design that needs three new components to justify itself is evidentially weaker than one that reuses existing pieces.
* In **diagnostic reasoning** — prefer explanations grounded in the system's known mechanics over ones that require novel failure modes.

***Limits and counters***
The razor is a **prior**, not a verdict. Reality is frequently non-parsimonious, and "simpler" is relative to a chosen ontology. Einstein's corollary — "_as simple as possible, but no simpler_" — warns against under-fitting. Pair Occam with evidence, not as a substitute for it.

***Key Proponents***: William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347, _Summa Logicae_, _Quodlibetal Questions_); the principle predates Ockham in Aristotle and Scotus but carries his name due to his repeated methodological use of it. Modernised by Bertrand Russell and formalised as minimum-description-length / Bayesian simplicity priors in 20th-century philosophy of science.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Debugging: triage competing theories of a bug before instrumenting for all of them
* Architecture review: challenge proposals that introduce new components to explain observed requirements
* Root-cause analysis: pair with Five Whys to avoid stopping at an elaborate but unjustified explanation
* Incident response: the outage likely has **one** cause matching the data, not a conspiracy
* Requirements clarification: pick the interpretation that requires fewest hidden assumptions about the user
* LLM prompting: ask the model to prefer the explanation with the fewest moving parts when diagnosing

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* KISS Principle - Sibling razor applied to **solutions** rather than **explanations**
* YAGNI - Applies parsimony to future requirements: don't build what you can't justify
* Five Whys - Occam helps pick which "why" to pursue when the chain forks
* MECE Principle - Both disciplines of hypothesis hygiene; MECE ensures coverage, Occam ranks by parsimony
* Devil's Advocate - Devil's Advocate stress-tests the hypothesis Occam has selected

### PDCA

***Full Name***: Plan-Do-Check-Act

***Also known as***: the Deming cycle, the Deming wheel, the Shewhart cycle; PDSA (Plan-Do-Study-Act) in Deming's own wording

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Four Steps, Repeated Forever***: The loop is deliberately small and deliberately endless:
* **Plan** — state the problem, form a hypothesis about cause and remedy, and decide how the result will be judged
* **Do** — carry out the change, preferably on a small scale
* **Check** — compare the observed result with what was expected
* **Act** — standardise the change if it worked, or return to Plan if it did not

***The Scientific Method, Shrunk to Fit a Shop Floor***: PDCA is an experiment loop: hypothesis, trial, evaluation, decision. Its ancestor is Shewhart's 1939 sequence of specification, production and inspection, which he bent from a straight line into a circle precisely because "these three steps must go in a circle instead of in a straight line".

***Small Scale First***: The Do step is meant to be a **test**, not a rollout. Running the change on a small scale is what keeps a failed hypothesis cheap — and what makes the Check step interpretable at all.

***Act Means Standardise or Loop***: The step most often skipped. A successful change that is not written into the standard decays; a failed change that is not fed back into Plan teaches nothing. Act is where the loop either compounds knowledge or leaks it.

***The Engine Under Kaizen***: PDCA, the seven basic quality tools and the QC-story format became the foundation of _kaizen_ in Japan. When a text says "continuous improvement" without naming a method, PDCA is usually what it means.

***Ancestor of the Phase-Gated Cycles***: `dmaic` is PDCA with gates, measurement discipline and statistics bolted on; `dmadv` is the same lineage applied to design. Both descend from this four-step loop.

***Deming Preferred "Study"***: Deming warned that "check" is misleading, because the English word means "to hold back". His own late formulation is PDSA — Plan-Do-Study-Act — where Study asks what was **learned**, not merely whether the target was hit. See Current Status: the naming split is not cosmetic.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Any improvement where the remedy is a hypothesis rather than a known fix
* Small, reversible changes that can be tested before they are committed — the loop's economics depend on the test being cheap
* As the frame for retrospectives, incident follow-ups and process experiments that would otherwise end at "we should do better"
* Where an organisation needs a shared vocabulary for "we tried it, here is what we learned" — PDCA gives the four slots
* As the structural skeleton of a management system: ISO 9001:2015 and its siblings are organised around exactly these four steps

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "Deming invented PDCA" — he did not. Japanese executives recast his 1950 Deming wheel into PDCA in 1951; Deming later wrote, "How the PDCA ever came into existence I know not."
* ❌ "PDCA and PDSA are two names for one thing" — Deming himself denied it: asked how the QC circle and the Deming circle relate, he answered, "They bear no relation to each other."
* ❌ "Check means verify the deliverable" — Check compares result with **prediction**. Without a prediction recorded in Plan, there is nothing to check against.
* ❌ "One pass through the cycle is a PDCA" — the method is the repetition. A single loop is an experiment, not an improvement system.
* ✓ "PDCA is the scientific method wearing work clothes" — fair, and the reason its critics measure it against scientific standards.

## **Criticism**:

* **Almost nobody runs it as specified.** Michael J. Taylor and colleagues reviewed 73 peer-reviewed healthcare articles that claimed to apply PDSA and found that only **two** met all five core principles of the method. "Less than 20% (14/73) fully documented the application of a sequence of iterative cycles", and "only 15% (7/47) reported the use of quantitative data at monthly or more frequent data intervals to inform progression of cycles." Their conclusion is blunt: "the varied practice compromises its effectiveness as a method for improvement." https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3963536/[Taylor, McNicholas, Nicolay, Darzi, Bell & Reed, "Systematic review of the application of the plan–do–study–act method to improve quality in healthcare", _BMJ Quality & Safety_ 23(4), 2014, pp. 290–298]. The finding cuts both ways: it is a criticism of practice, and it makes claims of PDCA's effectiveness hard to evaluate, since what was measured was rarely the method.
* **Deming rejected the version everyone uses.** Ronald D. Moen and Clifford L. Norman document the objection from the source. In a letter of 17 November 1990, Deming wrote: "Be sure to call it PDSA, not the corruption PDCA." He "warned his audiences that the PDCA version is frequently inaccurate because the English word 'check' means 'to hold back'". https://qicentral.rcpch.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/9/2021/10/Moen-and-Norman-on-Deming-circling-back-ph556x.pdf[Moen & Norman, "Circling Back", _Quality Progress_, November 2010, ASQ]. Calling PDCA "the Deming cycle" attributes to Deming a cycle he publicly disowned.
* **The two cycles are aimed at different levels.** At a US Government Accounting Office roundtable, Deming was asked how the QC circle and the Deming circle relate: "They bear no relation to each other. The Deming circle is a quality control program. It is a plan for management. … Maybe you could say that the Deming circle is for management, and the QC circle is for a group of people that work on faults encountered at the local level" (same source). Teams that adopt PDCA for strategy are using a local fault-fixing loop for a job it was not shaped for.
* **Check without prediction degrades into review.** The gap Moen, Nolan and Provost closed in 1991 by requiring prediction and theory in the Plan step is exactly the gap the Taylor review measured twenty years later: cycles run without recorded predictions and without data over time cannot produce the deductive-inductive interplay that makes the loop scientific.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The naming split is documented, and the popular name is the "corrupted" one.** Moen and Norman lay out the lineage: Shewhart's cycle (1939) → Deming wheel (1950, JUSE seminar: design, production, sales, research) → Japanese QC's PDCA (1951, per Masaaki Imai, with no individual ever claiming authorship) → Ishikawa's expanded PDCA for TQC (1985) → Deming's Shewhart cycle (1986) → Deming's PDSA, "the Shewhart Cycle for Learning and Improvement" (1993). PDCA won the popularity contest; PDSA carries Deming's intent.
* **The split is now regional and professional, not resolved.** Healthcare quality improvement writes PDSA, following Deming and the Model for Improvement that Langley, Nolan and colleagues built on the PDSA cycle in 1994. Manufacturing, Lean and the ISO management-system world write PDCA. Both priors are strong; a prompt that needs the learning emphasis should say PDSA and say why.
* **PDCA is embedded in the ISO management-system standards.** ISO 9001:2015 names the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle explicitly in its introduction and organises its requirement clauses along it — planning (6) as Plan, support and operation (7, 8) as Do, performance evaluation (9) as Check, improvement (10) as Act. https://the9000store.com/articles/iso-9000-tips-plan-do-check-act/[Overview of the ISO 9001:2015 PDCA structure]. That embedding is why the four-letter form will not go away, whatever Deming wrote.

### Premortem

***Full Name***: Project Premortem

***Also known as***: Pre-mortem, prospective hindsight exercise

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **The failure is a premise, not a possibility.** The group is told the plan has already failed, comprehensively, and is asked why. This is the whole technique; everything else is staging.
* **Prospective hindsight.** Explaining an event stated as fact produces more concrete reasons than speculating about an event that might happen.
* **Before commitment, not after.** A postmortem examines a corpse; a premortem examines a plan that can still be changed.
* **Everyone writes first.** Each participant lists reasons independently before anything is shared, so the most senior voice does not set the frame.
* **Round-robin collection.** Reasons are read out one per person per turn, which surfaces the quiet objections that a free discussion buries.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Before committing to a plan that is hard to reverse -- a migration, a re-platforming, a fixed-date release
* When a team has converged suspiciously fast and nobody is arguing
* When the people who see the risks report to the people who made the plan
* As a complement to a risk register: the register lists known risks, the premortem generates the ones nobody wrote down

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Softening the question.** Asking "what could go wrong?" instead of "it failed -- why?" reverts the exercise to ordinary risk brainstorming and loses the effect the technique is named for.
* **Treating it as pessimism.** The purpose is to license dissent, not to kill the plan. It usually ends with a modified plan, not a cancelled one.
* **Running it after the decision.** Once commitment is public, the findings have nowhere to go.

## **Criticism**:

* **The evidence chain is weaker than the citation suggests.** Behavioural economist Jason Collins documents that the widely repeated "30 percent" figure does not say what it is used to say. https://corporate.jcx.au/premortem[Collins] traces it to Mitchell, Russo and Pennington (1989), whose result is that prospective hindsight increases the **number** of reasons generated -- and notes explicitly: "Mitchell, Russo, and Pennington (1989) did not assess the quality of the reasons." The common paraphrase, that the technique improves the ability to **correctly identify** reasons by 30 percent, originates in Klein's 2007 restatement rather than in the study.
* **The academic literature is thin.** Collins states it plainly: "The academic literature on the premortem is thin." The technique's standing rests largely on practitioner reports and on Klein's own 2010 study with Veinott and Wiggins, not on independent replication.
* **No independent methodological critique was found.** A search in English and German turned up no failed replication, no meta-analysis, and no peer-reviewed critique of the technique itself. Note the frame: the journals where such an evaluation would most plausibly sit -- work on structured analytic techniques in _Intelligence and National Security_ and the _International Journal of Intelligence and CounterIntelligence_ -- are paywalled and were not read. This is an absence in our search, not a demonstrated absence in the literature.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Established and unchanged.** Klein's own description in https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/seeing-what-others-dont/202101/the-pre-mortem-method[Psychology Today] (January 2021) matches the 2007 original; there is no revised edition or successor method to drift toward. He dates the technique's origin to roughly three decades before that writing, with the first formal description in "Performing a Project Premortem", _Harvard Business Review_ 85(9), 18–19, September 2007.
* **The failure modes Klein names are execution errors, not limits.** He lists three: softening the question, running it too slowly, and letting a senior participant dominate instead of going round-robin. These are the author's caveats about his own method, which is a different thing from independent criticism.

### Second-Order Thinking

***Full Name***: Second-Order Thinking

***Also known as***: Second-level thinking (Howard Marks); second- and third-order consequences (Ray Dalio)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **And then what?** The first-order effect is the one the decision was made for. The second-order effect is what happens once people adapt to the first.
* **First-order effects are visible and immediate; second-order effects are delayed and often dominant.** The delay is why they lose arguments they should win.
* **Chains, not lists.** The move is to follow one consequence into the next, rather than to enumerate more consequences at the same level.
* **The consequences that decide the outcome are usually behavioural.** Rules change incentives, incentives change behaviour, and behaviour produces the effect nobody planned.
* **Applies to the status quo too.** Not acting has second-order effects as well, and they are easy to omit because nothing appears to happen.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Evaluating a policy or process change that people will adapt to -- review rules, quality gates, on-call schedules, incentive structures
* Assessing a technical decision whose cost arrives later than its benefit
* Whenever a proposal's argument consists entirely of its immediate effect
* As a counterweight when a metric is about to become a target

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Adding more items instead of going deeper.** Twenty first-order effects are still first-order. One consequence followed three steps is the technique.
* **Treating it as an argument against acting.** It changes what you decide, not whether you decide. Inaction gets the same analysis.
* **Confusing it with risk analysis.** A risk is an event that may or may not occur. A second-order effect is a consequence a decision sets in motion once people adapt to it -- likely rather than certain, but systematic rather than accidental, and nobody has reacted to it yet.

## **Criticism**:

* **No named critique of the term itself was found.** A search in English and German produced no cited author arguing that second-order thinking is trivial, unfalsifiable or unusable. What search engines return as criticism -- analysis paralysis, time cost, context dependence -- appears in advice blogs without attribution and does not qualify.
* **The literature that popularised it is contested.** The criticism lands on the mental-models genre rather than on this term. Cedric Chin names Farnam Street directly in https://commoncog.com/the-mental-model-fallacy/["The Mental Model Fallacy"]: "The mental model fallacy is that it's worth it to read descriptions of mental models, written and aggregated by non-practitioners, in the pursuit of self-improvement and success", and adds that "the most valuable mental models do not survive codification". Richard Hughes-Jones argues in https://www.richardhughesjones.com/mental-models/["The Mental Models Paradox"] that such frameworks "make us smarter but only up to a point, after which they can actually constrain our thinking". Data scientist Boris Gorelik reviews Parrish's _The Great Mental Models_ at https://gorelik.net/2020/02/12/book-review-great-mental-models-by-shane-parrish[two out of five], calling it "ambitious but yet shallow".
* **None of those three critics discusses second-order thinking.** They criticise the packaging, not this entry. The distinction matters, and readers should not take the citations as a verdict on the technique.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The name that works is not the name in the sources.** Howard Marks contrasts "first-level" with "second-**level** thinking" in https://cup.columbia.edu/book/the-most-important-thing/9780231153683/[_The Most Important Thing_] (Columbia University Press, 2011). Ray Dalio's principle reads https://www.principles.com/principles/7658aec7-c3f6-4248-8cc6-57aa84b0a955/["Consider second- and third-order consequences, not just first-order ones"]. Neither writes "second-order thinking". That phrasing belongs to the popularisers, chiefly https://fs.blog/second-order-thinking/[Farnam Street], which adopts it as its own heading while stating plainly that Marks "calls it second-level thinking" and quoting Dalio on "second- and third-order consequences" -- the rename is deliberate and documented on the page that performs it.
