***Twelve "drawers"***: A lightweight template of twelve sections, deliberately mirroring arc42's structure, for capturing agile requirements without drifting into heavyweight specification. Fill only the drawers a project actually needs.

***01 Business Goals***: Why the product exists and what success looks like

***02 Stakeholders***: Who has an interest in the system and what they expect

***03 Scope***: What is in and out — the system boundary

***04 Product Backlog***: Features, user stories, and product ideas

***05 Supporting Models***: Diagrams and models that clarify the requirements (context, data, processes)

***06 Quality Requirements***: Quality goals and scenarios — the focus that sets req42 apart from pure backlog management

***07 Constraints***: Conditions that limit design and implementation decisions

***08 Domain Terminology***: Shared vocabulary; a glossary

***09 Assets***: Existing things to reuse or protect

***10 Teams***: Who builds the product

***11 Roadmap***: Planned sequence of delivery over time

***12 Risks / Assumptions***: Open risks and the assumptions the plan rests on

***Pairs with arc42***: req42 documents the requirements (the "what" and "why"); arc42 documents the architecture (the "how"). The two share authorship, structure, and tooling, so they combine seamlessly.

***Docs-as-code***: Distributed as an AsciiDoc template built with the arc42 generator; version-controllable, diffable, and toolchain-friendly. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (free and open source).

***Key Proponents***: Dr. Peter Hruschka and Markus Meuten (https://req42.de). Hruschka is a principal of the Atlantic Systems Guild, IREB founding member, and co-creator of arc42; req42 also draws on the Volere requirements tradition.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Documenting requirements in an agile context without abandoning structure
* Giving a product backlog a frame for quality requirements, constraints, and risks — not just user stories
* Pairing a requirements document with an arc42 architecture document so both share structure and tooling
* Lightweight, docs-as-code requirements that live next to the code in version control

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* arc42 Architecture Documentation
* EARS Requirements Syntax
* Cockburn Use Cases
* Docs-as-Code

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* Far less widely known than its sibling arc42. An LLM recognizes "req42" mainly **because** of arc42's name and structure; the training-data prior on req42's own twelve-section content is thin, so the model may extrapolate from arc42 rather than recall req42 accurately. Verify section names against the source (https://docs.req42.de, https://github.com/Hruschka/req42-framework) rather than trusting recall.
* Actively maintained as a free, open-source template (CC BY-SA 4.0) on https://github.com/Hruschka/req42-framework[GitHub], with section-level guidance at https://docs.req42.de — the same docs-as-code model as arc42.

### SIPOC

***Full Name***: Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers

***Also known as***: COPIS when filled out in reverse; high-level process map; process scoping diagram

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Five Columns, One Page***: Every SIPOC is the same table. **Suppliers** provide the **Inputs**; the **Process** — five to seven steps, no more — turns them into **Outputs**; the **Customers** receive them. The one-page limit is not a convention, it is the tool. A SIPOC that needs a second page has become a process map and lost its job.

***Its Job is Drawing the Boundary***: SIPOC answers "where does this process start and stop, and who is on each side?" before anyone argues about what is wrong inside it. In `dmaic` it belongs to the Define phase, and it is also a standard opener for kaizen events.

***Process First, Then Outward***: The usual fill order is P → O → C → I → S: name the process steps, then what comes out, then who receives it, then what goes in, then who supplies it. Starting with Suppliers invites a shopping list; starting with the Process keeps the scope honest.

***Customers are Plural and Named***: The Customers column forces the question of **who exactly** receives each output — internal handover partners included. Most scoping arguments turn out to be disagreements hiding in this column.

***Boundary Objects, Not Detail***: Inputs and Outputs are the things that cross the boundary: documents, data, decisions, material. Anything that never crosses the line belongs inside the Process column or nowhere.

***COPIS Reverses the Reading***: "To emphasize putting the needs of the customer foremost, the tool is sometimes called COPIS and the process information is filled out in reverse order by starting with the customer and working upstream to the supplier." Same five columns, opposite direction, different conversation: COPIS starts from what the customer needs and asks what must be true upstream.

***Where it Sits Among the Tools***: SIPOC scopes, `ishikawa-diagram` hypothesises causes inside that scope, and detailed process mapping comes later. Using SIPOC for any of the other two jobs is the most common way to waste it.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* At the start of a process improvement effort, before the problem statement is fixed — the scope argument is cheaper on one page
* Whenever "the process" means different things to different people in the room
* For system boundaries in software work: SIPOC maps cleanly onto "who calls us, what do they send, what do we return, who consumes it"
* As a Define-phase artefact in `dmaic`, and to frame the customer side of `dmadv` before CTQs are written
* As a warm-up before `event-storming` or detailed modelling, to agree what is in and out of scope

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "A SIPOC is a process map" — it is deliberately the opposite: five to seven steps, no branching, no swim lanes. Detail is someone else's tool.
* ❌ "Customers means paying customers" — it means whoever receives an output, mostly colleagues.
* ❌ "COPIS is a different tool" — same table, reversed reading order, customer-first.
* ❌ "Once drawn, it is done" — the SIPOC is a scoping agreement, and scoping agreements go stale.
* ✓ "SIPOC is a boundary contract in table form" — fair, and it explains why the arguments it triggers are the point rather than a delay.

## **Criticism**:

* **Most of them are decoration.** Christian Loyer, then plant manager at Ecolab, writes that the large majority of SIPOCs have no real meaning and make no difference in continuous improvement projects, because they are "not detailed enough" and "not integrated at all" — the columns are filled in but never linked, so nobody can say which supplier feeds which input, or which step produces which output. https://www.processexcellencenetwork.com/lean-six-sigma-business-performance/articles/the-integrated-sipoc-the-full-power-of-system-thin[Loyer, "Using an Integrated SIPOC for Better Results", Process Excellence Network, 3 June 2011].
* **Clarity is mistaken for understanding.** The tool's tidiness is itself a hazard: a finished SIPOC can give the impression that the process is understood when only its most general elements have been captured. "Using SIPOC alone won't stop problems occurring within processes", and "it's very simplistic, so it only serves as a starting point for process mapping". https://thinkinsights.net/consulting/sipoc-process-analysis[Think Insights, "SIPOC Process Analysis"].
* **It inherits the blind spots of whoever is in the room.** "Your SIPOC model is only as good as the people who created it. If key people are missing when its created then it's likely important items will be missing" (same source). The tool has no mechanism that surfaces its own omissions — a weakness it shares with every brainstorming-based artefact, including `ishikawa-diagram`.
* **The named criticism is thin, and that is worth saying.** We found no academic or book-length critique of SIPOC specifically; the objections above come from practitioner writing. Our search covered English and German sources only. That is a limit of our search, not evidence that no critique exists.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Old, stable, and unowned.** SIPOC "was in use at least as early as the total quality management programs of the late 1980s" and continues in use today; it is described as a simplification of Philip Crosby's process model. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIPOC[SIPOC overview]. No single author claims it, which is one reason the five column names are stable while everything around them varies.
* **Its home is the Define phase.** The tool "is often presented at the outset of process improvement efforts such as kaizen events or during the 'define' phase of the DMAIC process" (same source). That is the prior a model will serve: ask for a SIPOC and expect a Six Sigma-flavoured scoping table.
* **COPIS is a live variant, not a historical footnote.** Customer-first ordering is the standard answer where the improvement is driven by customer need rather than by internal defects. Naming COPIS instead of SIPOC changes which column the conversation starts in — a small prompt lever with a real effect.
* **Practitioner extensions circulate.** Integrated and augmented forms — linking the columns to each other, or adding requirements and measures — exist precisely because the plain five-column table stops short. None has displaced the original five letters.

### User Story Mapping

***Full Name***: User Story Mapping according to Jeff Patton

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Narrative flow***: Horizontal arrangement of user activities

***User activities***: High-level tasks users perform

***User tasks***: Steps within activities

***Walking skeleton***: Minimal end-to-end functionality first

***Release planning***: Horizontal slices for releases

***Prioritization by value***: Vertical ordering by importance

***Shared understanding***: Collaborative mapping builds team alignment

***Big picture view***: See the whole journey, not just backlog items

***Opportunity for conversation***: Stories as placeholders for discussion

***Key Proponent***: Jeff Patton ("User Story Mapping", 2014)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Planning new products or major features
* When backlog feels overwhelming or fragmented
* Release planning for incremental delivery
* Onboarding team members to product vision

---

## Software Architecture

### ADR according to Nygard

***Full Name***: Architecture Decision Records according to Michael Nygard

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Lightweight documentation***: Short, focused records

***Standard structure***
* Title
* Status (proposed, accepted, deprecated, superseded)
* Context (forces at play)
* Decision (what was chosen)
* Consequences (both positive and negative)

***Immutability***: ADRs are never deleted, only superseded

***Version control***: ADRs stored with code

***Decision archaeology***: Understanding why past decisions were made

***Evolutionary architecture***: Supporting architecture that changes over time

***Key Proponent***: Michael Nygard

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* All software projects (low overhead, high value)
* Distributed teams needing shared understanding
* When onboarding new team members
* Complex systems with evolving architecture

### arc42 Architecture Documentation

***Full Name***: arc42 Architecture Documentation Template

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***12 standardized sections***: From introduction to glossary

***Section 1***: Introduction and Goals

***Section 2***: Constraints

***Section 3***: Context and Scope

***Section 4***: Solution Strategy

***Section 5***: Building Block View

***Section 6***: Runtime View

***Section 7***: Deployment View

***Section 8***: Crosscutting Concepts

***Section 9***: Architecture Decisions (ADRs)

***Section 10***: Quality Requirements

***Section 11***: Risks and Technical Debt

***Section 12***: Glossary

***Pragmatic documentation***: Document only what's necessary

***Multiple formats***: AsciiDoc, Markdown, Confluence, etc.

***Key Proponents***: Gernot Starke, Peter Hruschka

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Medium to large software projects
* When stakeholder communication is critical
* Long-lived systems requiring maintainability

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The current release is template version https://arc42.org/download[9.0] (July 2025); the 12-section structure has been stable for many years — v9's main change splits Section 10 into a quality-requirements overview (10.1) and detailed scenarios (10.2)
* What evolves is the material around the skeleton: help texts, translations, the tips-and-examples site https://docs.arc42.org/home/[docs.arc42.org], and the https://quality.arc42.org/[arc42 quality model (Q42)] — a prior trained on v7/v8 material knows the section structure correctly but misses the Section-10 split and Q42

### ATAM

***Full Name***: Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method

***Also known as***: Architecture Evaluation, ATAM Review

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Utility Tree***: Hierarchical decomposition of system quality goals into concrete, prioritized quality attribute scenarios (e.g., Performance → Response Time → "Search results returned in < 1s under peak load")

***Quality Attribute Scenarios***: Testable, concrete expressions of quality requirements consisting of stimulus, source, environment, artifact, response, and response measure

***Architectural Approaches***: Design decisions and patterns (e.g., caching, replication, layering) used to achieve quality attributes

***Sensitivity Points***: Architectural decisions that significantly affect one specific quality attribute

***Tradeoff Points***: Architectural decisions that affect two or more quality attributes in conflicting ways — the core insight of ATAM

***Risks and Non-risks***: Identified architectural decisions that may (risks) or demonstrably will not (non-risks) lead to future problems

***Nine-step process***: Presentation of ATAM → presentation of business drivers → presentation of architecture → identification of architectural approaches → generation of utility tree → analysis of architectural approaches → brainstorming scenarios → analysis of scenarios → presentation of results

***Key Proponents***: Rick Kazman, Mark Klein, Paul Clements (SEI / Carnegie Mellon University)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Evaluating a software architecture before major investment in implementation
* When multiple stakeholders have conflicting quality requirements (e.g., performance vs. security)
* During architecture reviews of safety-critical or high-availability systems
* When making buy-vs.-build decisions or selecting between competing architectural styles

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* arc42 Architecture Documentation
* ADR according to Nygard
* Quality Attribute Scenario

### Bulkhead Pattern

***Full Name***: Bulkhead, a stability pattern from Michael T. Nygard's _Release It!_

***Also known as***: resource isolation, compartmentalisation, pool isolation; at infrastructure scale, cell-based architecture

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Partition the Resource, Not the Call***: A bulkhead gives each dependency, tenant or workload its own slice of a finite resource -- threads, connections, memory, processes, instances -- so that one slow or failing consumer can only exhaust its own slice. Microsoft's Azure Architecture Center states the goal in one line: "Isolate the elements of an application into pools so that if one element fails, the others continue to function."

***The Name Is the Design***: From a ship's hull. Azure: "This pattern is named after the sectioned partitions (bulkheads) of a ship's hull. If the hull of a ship is compromised, only the damaged section fills with water, which prevents the ship from sinking." The ship still takes damage. It does not sink.

***The Line Against Circuit Breaker***: A circuit breaker **stops calling** a dependency that keeps failing. A bulkhead **caps how much of the system** any one dependency can consume, whether it fails or merely gets slow. They answer different failure modes and are normally combined -- Azure lists the combination explicitly: "consider combining bulkheads with retry, circuit breaker, and throttling patterns."

***Two Implementation Forms***: A **thread-pool bulkhead** gives each dependency its own executor, so a hanging downstream call blocks only that pool -- the classic Hystrix form. A **semaphore bulkhead** caps concurrent calls on the caller's own thread, with no extra pool. Resilience4j documents the trade: its `SemaphoreBulkhead` "should work well across a variety of threading and I/O models. It is based on a semaphore, and unlike Hystrix, does not provide 'shadow' thread pool option" -- and therefore "it is up to the client to ensure correct thread pool sizing that will be consistent with bulkhead configuration."

***The Same Idea at Infrastructure Scale***: Separate pods, clusters, accounts or regions per tenant or criticality tier. Azure treats this as the same pattern under a second name: the approach is "also known as a _cell-based architecture_."

***Timeouts Are a Precondition***: A bulkhead bounds how many calls can be stuck at once. Without a timeout, "stuck" means forever, and the partition fills up and stays full. The bulkhead then contains the damage instead of preventing it.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing a service that fans out to dependencies with different latency profiles -- a slow third-party payment API next to a fast internal catalogue
* Separating critical from best-effort consumers of the same service, so a batch job cannot starve interactive traffic
* Multi-tenant systems, where the question is which blast radius a single noisy tenant gets
* Reviewing an incident in which one dependency took the whole process down: the missing control is usually a bulkhead, not a retry
* Together with `circuit-breaker` and timeouts, as the stability-pattern set rather than one pattern alone

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "A bulkhead and a circuit breaker do the same job" -- one limits concurrency, the other limits repeated failures; a system with only a breaker still dies of a slow dependency that never fails outright
* ❌ "A bulkhead prevents the failure" -- it bounds the blast radius; the partitioned workload still degrades
* ❌ "Finer partitioning is always safer" -- Azure asks you to "determine the level of granularity for the bulkheads" and to weigh "the overhead in terms of cost, performance, and manageability"
* ❌ "Netflix invented it" -- Netflix popularised it through Hystrix and then moved away from that form; the pattern is Nygard's
* ✓ "A bulkhead is a cap on how much of my system one dependency may consume" -- accurate, and it explains why the hard part is choosing the number

## **Criticism**:

* **Static partitioning buys isolation with wasted capacity, and Microsoft prints the condition under which that trade fails.** The Azure Architecture Center lists when not to use the pattern: "Less efficient use of resources might not be acceptable in the project" and "The added complexity isn't necessary." Reserved capacity that sits idle in one partition while another queues is the cost of the guarantee. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/bulkhead[Microsoft, "Bulkhead Pattern", Azure Architecture Center] (page updated 19 September 2026).
* **The static number is the real objection, and it comes from the organisation that popularised the pattern.** Netflix's own `concurrency-limits` project exists because fixed limits have to be guessed and then go stale: "in large distributed systems that auto-scale this value quickly goes out of date and the service falls over by becoming non-responsive." https://github.com/Netflix/concurrency-limits[Netflix, _concurrency-limits_ README]. Netflix's stated reason for retiring Hystrix is the same shift, toward "more adaptive implementations".
* **The thread-pool form lost its default status on cost grounds.** Resilience4j, the successor Netflix names, makes the semaphore the plain case and drops Hystrix's "shadow" thread pool, pushing pool sizing back to the caller. The extra threads, context switches and memory of a pool per dependency were a price the follow-on library chose not to pay by default. https://resilience4j.readme.io/docs/bulkhead[Resilience4j, Bulkhead documentation].

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **A named pattern in the book, verified in the second edition.** The Pragmatic Bookshelf table of contents for _Release It!_ Second Edition (2018) lists the Stability Patterns as "Timeouts, Circuit Breaker, Bulkheads, Steady State, Fail Fast". https://pragprog.com/titles/mnee2/release-it-second-edition/[_Release It!_ Second Edition, Pragmatic Bookshelf]. The publisher page covers the second edition only; the first edition (2007) is where the stability patterns first appeared.
* **Hystrix is done; Resilience4j is the named successor.** The Netflix README states: "Hystrix is no longer in active development, and is currently in maintenance mode", with no further issue review, merges or releases, and points new projects at Resilience4j while existing ones stay on 1.5.18. https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix[Netflix/Hystrix]. Polly covers .NET.
* **Naming the term changes the answer.** On a neutral logistics-platform resilience task, one of three no-anchor baselines on `claude-haiku-4-5` proposed bulkheads unprompted and two did not. The term is worth naming.
* **The attribution does not survive the weak tier.** Asked who created the pattern, the same model answered `creator=Netflix (collective); year=2011` -- Hystrix's popularisation, not Nygard 2007. This entry carries the attribution the model does not.

### C4-Diagrams

***Full Name***: C4 Model for Software Architecture Diagrams

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Four levels of abstraction***

- ***Level 1 - Context***: System in its environment (users, external systems)
- ***Level 2 - Container***: Applications and data stores that make up the system
- ***Level 3 - Component***: Components within containers
- ***Level 4 - Code***: Class diagrams, entity relationships (optional)

***Zoom in/out***: Progressive disclosure of detail

***Simple notation***: Boxes and arrows, minimal notation overhead

***Audience-appropriate***: Different diagrams for different stakeholders

***Supplementary diagrams***: Deployment, dynamic views, etc.

***Key Proponent***: Simon Brown

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Communicating architecture to diverse stakeholders
* Onboarding new team members
* Architecture documentation and review
* Replacing or supplementing UML

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The four levels (System Context, Container, Component, Code) and the supporting diagrams (system landscape, dynamic, deployment) are stable; https://c4model.com/[c4model.com] remains actively maintained by Simon Brown with edits into 2026
* In September 2024 the site was rewritten from a single long page into a multi-page reference with new guidance (modelling microservices, queues and topics, a review checklist) — a prior trained on the old one-pager misses this guidance and the sharpened https://c4model.com/tooling[diagramming-vs-modelling] framing around tooling such as Structurizr

### CAP Theorem

***Full Name***: CAP Theorem (Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance)

***Also known as***: Brewer's Theorem

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***The three properties***: **Consistency** (every read sees the most recent write), **Availability** (every request gets a non-error response), **Partition tolerance** (the system keeps working despite dropped/delayed messages between nodes)

***The trade-off***: When a network partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability — it cannot have both during the partition

***Partitions are not optional***: Real networks partition, so P is a given; the genuine design choice is CP vs AP behaviour **while partitioned**

***Common misreading***: "Pick 2 of 3" is a simplification; outside a partition a system can be both consistent and available

***PACELC extension***: Else (no partition), trade Latency against Consistency — captures the everyday tuning that CAP alone omits (Abadi, 2012)

***Key Proponents***: Eric Brewer (2000 conjecture, PODC keynote); formally proved by Seth Gilbert & Nancy Lynch (2002); PACELC by Daniel Abadi (2012)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Choosing or evaluating a distributed datastore (CP vs AP behaviour)
* Framing a concrete consistency/availability trade-off for a feature
* Reasoning about behaviour during network partitions and failover
* Explaining why strong consistency costs availability or latency

[discrete]
## **When NOT to Use**:

* For single-node systems with no replication (no partitions to tolerate)
* As a crude "2 of 3" slogan — prefer the partition-time framing or PACELC

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Event-Driven Architecture — eventual consistency as an AP design choice
* Fallacies of Distributed Computing — the network assumptions CAP makes explicit

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Eric Brewer himself, https://www.infoq.com/articles/cap-twelve-years-later-how-the-rules-have-changed/["CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed"] (IEEE Computer, 2012) — the "2 of 3" formulation is misleading; the trade-off is narrower and more nuanced than the slogan suggests
* Martin Kleppmann, https://martin.kleppmann.com/2015/05/11/please-stop-calling-databases-cp-or-ap.html["Please stop calling databases CP or AP"] (2015) — CAP's formal definitions are too narrow to classify real systems; many databases are neither CP nor AP under the theorem's own terms
* Alternative named in the discourse: reason with precise consistency models (linearizability, causal consistency, etc.) and the PACELC framing instead of the CP/AP dichotomy

### Circuit Breaker

***Also known as***: Circuit Breaker stability pattern

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Closed state***: Normal operation; calls pass through to the protected resource while the breaker counts failures

***Open state***: Once failures cross the threshold the breaker trips; further calls fail immediately (fail-fast) without invoking the protected call, preventing resource exhaustion and cascading failure

***Half-open state***: After a reset timeout the breaker tentatively lets a trial call through to probe whether the dependency has recovered; success closes the breaker, failure re-opens it

***Failure threshold***: Configured count or rate of failures that trips the breaker from closed to open

***Fail-fast***: Returning an error instantly instead of blocking on a call known to be failing, freeing threads and connections

***Fallback***: The client-side strategy when the breaker is open — return cached data, a default, a queued request, or a graceful error

***Composes with***: Pairs with timeout (bound each call), retry (recover from transient faults), and bulkhead (isolate failures) as a stability-pattern set

***Key Proponents***: Michael Nygard ("Release It!", Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2007), who introduced it as a stability pattern; Martin Fowler (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html[bliki: CircuitBreaker]), who popularized it further

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Calls across a network boundary to a remote service or dependency that can become slow or unavailable
* Microservice architectures where one failing service must not cascade into a system-wide outage
* Integrations with third-party APIs of uncertain reliability
* Any operation that can exhaust threads, connections, or other bounded resources while waiting on a stuck dependency
* Prompting an LLM to add resilience to inter-service communication

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Fallacies of Distributed Computing
* CAP Theorem
* Event-Driven Architecture

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The reference Java implementation in training-data priors is often Netflix Hystrix, which is now frozen. Its https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix[README] states: "Hystrix is no longer in active development, and is currently in maintenance mode." (final stable release 1.5.18, November 2018)
* Netflix's own guidance points elsewhere: "we intend to continue using Hystrix for existing applications, and to leverage open and active projects like resilience4j for new internal projects. We are beginning to recommend others do the same." (https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix[Netflix/Hystrix])
* https://resilience4j.readme.io/[Resilience4j] is the maintained successor in the Java/Spring ecosystem and is recommended by Spring Cloud as the default circuit breaker
* In service-mesh deployments, circuit breaking is increasingly handled at the infrastructure layer by the sidecar proxy (e.g. https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/circuit_breaking[Envoy circuit breaking], used by https://istio.io/latest/docs/tasks/traffic-management/circuit-breaking/[Istio]) rather than in application code

### Clean Architecture

***Full Name***: Clean Architecture according to Robert C. Martin

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***The Dependency Rule***: Dependencies only point inward

***Concentric circles***: Entities → Use Cases → Interface Adapters → Frameworks & Drivers

***Independent of frameworks***: Architecture doesn't depend on libraries

***Testable***: Business rules testable without UI, database, or external elements

***Independent of UI***: UI can change without changing business rules

***Independent of database***: Business rules not bound to database

***Independent of external agencies***: Business rules don't know about outside world

***Screaming Architecture***: Architecture reveals the intent of the system

***SOLID principles***: Foundation of the architecture

***Key Proponent***: Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob")

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Enterprise applications with complex business logic
* Systems requiring long-term maintainability
* When team size and turnover are high
* Projects where business rules must be protected from technology changes

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Jimmy Bogard, https://www.jimmybogard.com/vertical-slice-architecture/["Vertical Slice Architecture"] (2018) — calls the "traditional layered/onion/clean architecture" monolithic in its approach and appropriate for only a minority of requests, criticizing mock-heavy tests and abstractions "around concepts that really shouldn't be abstracted"; his alternative is Vertical Slice Architecture
* Derek Comartin, https://codeopinion.com/clean-architecture-and-indirection-no-thanks/["'Clean Architecture' and indirection. No thanks."] (CodeOpinion) — dismisses canonical Clean Architecture examples as "useless indirection": the layering adds cost without paying for itself in typical systems
* The critiques converge: the dependency rule imposes a fixed indirection tax on every feature, while most changes cut across all layers anyway — the coupling Vertical Slice Architecture organizes around instead

### Conway's Law

***Full Name***: Conway's Law

***Also known as***: The Mirroring Hypothesis

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Homomorphic force***: "Any organization that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure" — system boundaries mirror team boundaries

***Communication paths***: Interfaces in the software appear wherever two teams must coordinate; the cost and friction of cross-team communication shapes where modules are split

***Inverse Conway Maneuver***: Deliberately structure teams to match the desired architecture, rather than letting an accidental org chart dictate the system

***Team Topologies***: Modern operationalization (Skelton & Pais) — stream-aligned, platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem teams sized for a manageable cognitive load

***Sociotechnical view***: Architecture is not purely technical; org design and system design are two sides of the same decision

***Key Proponents***: Melvin E. Conway ("How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation 1968); popularized by Fred Brooks ("The Mythical Man-Month"); modern form in Matthew Skelton & Manuel Pais ("Team Topologies", 2019)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Planning team structure for a new system or a re-architecture
* Diagnosing why module boundaries are awkward or why integration is painful
* Justifying microservice/bounded-context splits along team lines
* Reviewing whether the org chart is fighting the intended architecture

[discrete]
## **When NOT to Use**:

* As a deterministic prediction — it is a strong tendency, not a law of physics
* For tiny single-team systems where there is only one communication path

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Domain-Driven Design — bounded contexts as team-aligned boundaries
* Cohesion Criteria — module cohesion that team boundaries should respect
* Vertical Slice Architecture — slices that map to stream-aligned teams

### CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

***Also known as***: CQS at architectural scale

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Command Query Separation (CQS)***: Bertrand Meyer's principle — methods either change state (commands) or return data (queries), never both

***Commands***: Write operations that change state and return void; represent intent as immutable command objects

***Queries***: Read operations that return data with no side effects; safe to retry and cache

***Separate read/write models***: Independent data models optimized for their respective purpose

***Eventual consistency***: Read model may lag behind write model; acceptable trade-off for scalability

***Event-based synchronization***: Domain events propagate changes from write side to read side projections

***Independent scalability***: Read and write sides can be scaled, deployed, and optimized independently

***Event sourcing optional***: CQRS does not require event sourcing; the patterns are complementary but independent

***Key Proponents***: Greg Young (coined CQRS), Bertrand Meyer (CQS origin, "Object-Oriented Software Construction", 1988), Udi Dahan

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Systems with asymmetric read/write workloads
* Complex domains where read and write models diverge significantly
* Event-sourced systems requiring materialized views
* High-performance systems needing independent scaling of reads and writes
* Collaborative domains with task-based UIs

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Domain-Driven Design - Often combined with CQRS for complex domains
* Hexagonal Architecture - Ports and adapters complement CQRS separation
* Fowler Patterns - CQRS builds on enterprise application patterns

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Martin Fowler, https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html[bliki: CQRS] — warns that "for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity", a "significant mental leap" that pays off only in specific bounded contexts, not as a default pattern
* Udi Dahan, one of CQRS's main proponents, opens https://udidahan.com/2011/04/22/when-to-avoid-cqrs/["When to avoid CQRS"] (2011) with "Most people using CQRS (and Event Sourcing too) shouldn't have done so" — and adds that CQRS "should not be your top-level architectural pattern"
* Greg Young himself pushed back on scope creep in https://web.archive.org/web/20121129063556/http://codebetter.com/gregyoung/2012/09/09/cqrs-is-not-an-architecture-2/["CQRS is not an Architecture"] (2012, archived): CQRS is a pattern applied inside a single component, not an architectural style for a whole system

### CUPID Properties

***Full Name***: CUPID -- the back story to five properties of joyful code

***Also known as***: The CUPID properties, joyful code

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **Properties, not principles.** A principle is a rule you either follow or break. A property is a quality code has more or less of, and that you move toward. This is the distinction the term is built on, and the one most often lost when it is summarised.
* **Composable.** Small surface area, few dependencies, clear intent -- so the code is easy to pick up, reuse and combine with things its author never saw.
* **Unix philosophy.** Does one thing well. Close to single responsibility, but stated from the outside: about what the code does, not about why it would have to change.
* **Predictable.** Does what you expect. Behaves consistently, is deterministic where it can be, and is observable enough that you can tell its internal state from its outputs.
* **Idiomatic.** Feels natural. Follows the conventions of its language, framework and team, so the next reader spends attention on the problem rather than on the style.
* **Domain-based.** Names, structure and boundaries follow the problem domain rather than technical layers or framework concepts.
* **Positioned against SOLID, not on top of it.** North's argument is that SOLID's criteria are met or missed at the level of a class, while what makes code pleasant to work in is a set of overlapping qualities that reinforce each other.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Reviewing a module whose problems are qualities rather than rule violations -- a class that breaks no principle and is still unpleasant to work in
* As a vocabulary for code review, where "this is hard to compose" is a more useful sentence than a principle acronym
* When SOLID has become a checklist and the discussion has stopped being about the code

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Reading the D as "Domain-driven".** It is **Domain-based**. The pull toward DDD is strong enough that weaker language models make this substitution reliably -- see the prior-test register. CUPID's D is a statement about naming and structure, not an endorsement of a method.
* **Reading the I as "Intelligible".** It is **Idiomatic**. Intelligibility is a consequence North argues for, not the property he named.
* **Treating them as five boxes to tick.** They are deliberately not binary, and a scorecard turns them back into the thing they were proposed against.

## **Criticism**:

* **The properties are hard to tell apart from the principles they replace.** Stephan Roth, author of _Clean C++_, measures CUPID against his own test for a good principle -- it must give real orientation, be applicable by the team unaided, build shared understanding, be practicable, and be visible in the code afterwards. His verdict: "Dan Norths CUPID-Eigenschaften sind oberflächlich betrachtet nicht falsch, erfüllen aber meines Erachtens diese Qualitätskriterien für gute Prinzipien nicht immer." The concrete complaint is a confusion the acronym invites: "Zudem dürfte es herausfordernd für Anwendende sein, zu unterscheiden, was denn jetzt der genaue Unterschied beispielsweise zwischen Single Responsibility (aus SOLID) und Single Purpose (aus CUPID) ist." He adds that the underlying idea is not in dispute anyway -- "Es wird wohl eine weitgehend unumstrittene Vorstellung in unserer Disziplin darüber geben, dass kleine Module/Klassen mit einer klar definierten Aufgabe besser sind als große ‚Gemischtwarenläden'." https://www.developer-world.de/dwx-insights/testing-quality/solid-versus-cupid-gegner-verbuendete[Roth, developer-world.de] (16 June 2025). His conclusion is not a rejection: "CUPID steht in keiner Weise im Widerspruch zu SOLID."
* **The five letters are a selection, not a derivation -- and North says so.** From the canonical article: "Because CUPID is a backronym, I had several candidates for each letter. I chose these five because they feel 'foundational' somehow". A reader who expects the set to be complete or minimal is expecting something the author did not claim.
* **One frequently misattributed source.** Jeroen De Dauw's https://www.entropywins.wtf/blog/2017/02/17/why-every-single-argument-of-dan-north-is-wrong/["Why Every Single Argument of Dan North is Wrong"] (2017) is a defence of SOLID against North's earlier talk. It predates CUPID by five years and does not mention it. It is worth reading for the dispute CUPID grew out of, and it is not a critique of CUPID.
* **No citable criticism was found on the angle that matters most in review** -- that a property you move toward cannot be checked the way a rule can. North pre-empts it in the article with his "properties of properties", but we found nobody taking up the argument. English and German were searched; other languages were not, so this is an absence in our search rather than in the discourse.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The property set has not changed since publication.** The canonical article, https://dannorth.net/blog/cupid-for-joyful-coding/["CUPID: for joyful coding"], is dated 10 Feb 2022 and lists the five verbatim: "Composable: plays well with others / Unix philosophy: does one thing well / Predictable: does what you expect / Idiomatic: feels natural / Domain-based: the solution domain models the problem domain in language and structure". It is preceded by https://dannorth.net/blog/cupid-the-back-story/["CUPID: the back story"] (16 Mar 2021), which tells the origin and deliberately withholds the five.
* **The promised follow-ups are unverified.** North writes "I will expand on each property in future articles so that this one does not get any longer." We did not confirm that any were published -- which is a gap in our check, not evidence that none exist.
* **A dedicated site, https://cupid.dev/[cupid.dev], restates the same five with the same one-line definitions.** Its own description calls it "based on an article by Daniel Terhorst-North". Whether North maintains it could not be established from the page.

### Defense in Depth

***Full Name***: Defense in Depth -- military doctrine adapted to information security; the reference text for the information-assurance reading is the NSA paper "Defense in Depth: A practical strategy for achieving Information Assurance in today's highly networked environments"

***Also known as***: layered security, layered defense, the castle model, defence in depth

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Independence, Diversity, Assumed Failure***: Three conditions decide whether a set of controls is defence in depth or just a pile. **Independence**: a layer must not fail for the same reason as its neighbour. **Diversity**: different mechanisms, so one exploit does not pass through all of them. **Assumed failure**: every layer is designed on the premise that the one in front of it has already been breached. A set of correlated controls -- same vendor, same parser, same identity provider, same misconfiguration -- is one layer wearing several names. This is the part of the idea the term does not reliably carry (see Current Status), so state it rather than assume it.

***Nobody Owns the Phrase***: This is weaker attribution than most entries in this catalog. The concept is military doctrine -- trade space for time, make the attacker spend resources rather than stopping them at a single line -- adapted to information security. The NSA paper is the citable information-assurance formulation; the safety-engineering counterpart is James Reason's Swiss cheese model of accident causation, where the holes in individual layers only matter when they line up. This entry quotes no primary Reason text, having verified none, so it gives neither year nor page for the model.

***The NSA Formulation Is Not a Stack of Boxes***: The paper's organising claim is that information assurance "requires a balanced focus on three primary elements: People, Technology and Operations" -- so training, policy and incident response are layers in the same sense as a firewall. Its first recommended principle is "Defense in Multiple Places", on the reasoning that "adversaries can attack a target from multiple points using either insiders or outsiders". It calls itself a "best practices" strategy that "recommends a balance between the protection capability and cost, performance, and operational considerations".

***Layers Are Weighted, Not Uniform***: The same paper tells you to "specify the security robustness (strength and assurance) of each Information Assurance component as a function of the value of what's it is protecting and the threat at the point of application", with the example that "it's often more effective and operationally suitable to deploy stronger mechanisms at the network boundaries than at the user desktop". Defence in depth is therefore a budgeting argument, not an instruction to harden everything equally.

***Detection and Recovery Are Layers Too***: If every layer may fail, something must notice. Monitoring, alerting, incident response and backups belong in the decomposition, not as an afterthought to prevention.

***Relation to Least Privilege***: `least-privilege` is what makes a layer's failure survivable -- it bounds what the attacker reaches after the breach. Defence in depth is the arrangement; least privilege sizes each compartment.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing a control set for a single risky operation -- file upload, document rendering, deserialisation, arbitrary code execution
* Reviewing a security design for correlated failure: which two layers die to the same bug
* Sandboxing and isolation decisions, where the question is what the next layer assumes
* Bridging security and safety thinking next to `fmea` and `poka-yoke`
* After a `stride` threat model, to decide how many independent controls each high-rated threat gets

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "More controls means more depth" -- correlated controls are one layer; the count is of **independent** failures required, not of products
* ❌ "Defence in depth is about the network perimeter" -- the NSA formulation puts People and Operations alongside Technology
* ❌ "It is only prevention" -- detection, response and recovery are layers
* ❌ "Zero Trust replaced it" -- Zero Trust removes trust in network location; it does not say how many independent controls a given operation needs
* ✓ "Name each layer, say what it catches when the previous one fails, and show the two are not correlated" -- the form that makes the term mean something

## **Criticism**:

* **The sharpest charge is that the strategy fails against an adversary who cannot be removed.** Prescott Small, in a SANS/GIAC paper, argues from the breaches of RSA, HBGary and others that "Defense in Depth, as practiced, is unsustainable and the examples show that the enemy cannot be eliminated permanently", and goes further: "Knowing that Defense in Depth, as practiced, actually renders the organization more vulnerable is vital to understanding that there must be a shift in attitudes and thinking to better address the risks faced in a more effective manner." His replacement is a posture he calls Sustained Cyber-Siege Defense. https://www.sans.org/white-papers/33896/[Small, "Defense in Depth: An Impractical Strategy for a Cyber World"] (SANS Institute, 20 February 2012). The paper attacks the practice rather than the principle -- which is the same move the independence requirement above makes, arrived at from the other side.
* **The literature defines it and then stops.** Phil Venables, writing on his own site, charges that the body of guidance offers no design principles at all: "There is a huge number of possible arrangements of controls to achieve defense in depth with little in the way of principles to guide us in how controls should be arrayed." On the standard texts: "Most of the content is essentially a variant of the definition I just gave, together with examples of the need to deploy multiple controls...Most of the examples are given without much discussion of why they are effective." He also finds the Swiss cheese model too flat -- it "does not support defense in depth working at multiple dimensions from policy and governance to technical controls" -- and warns that the linear reading "leads to viewing risk and risk mitigation as a simple chain of events without being able to look at the wider system which induced the design factors that led to the event." https://www.philvenables.com/post/defense-in-depth[Venables, "Defense in Depth"] (21 May 2022).
* **Read as a shopping list, it produces the opposite of security.** Armin Recha names the failure mode directly: "Der zentrale Denkfehler vieler Security-Strategien liegt darin, Defense in Depth als Einkaufsliste zu betrachten" -- the central error is treating defence in depth as a shopping list. And on what that yields: "Im schlimmsten Fall entsteht eine trügerische Sicherheit. Formal sind alle notwendigen Komponenten vorhanden, operativ fehlt jedoch die Fähigkeit, Angriffe sauber einzuordnen und kontrolliert zu reagieren" -- at worst a deceptive sense of security, every required component formally present while the ability to classify and answer an attack is missing. https://www.security-insider.de/defense-in-depth-integration-resilienz-security-architekturen-a-21c61d9d2fe7f7a10fc504d970587f5c/[Recha, "Defense in Depth: Integration statt Einkaufsliste für Resilienz", _Security-Insider_] (8 April 2026). Recha is Regional Vice President DACH at Fastly, so read the piece as a vendor's argument -- the objection stands on its own, the framing is interested.
* **The staffing cost is the practical objection.** Jochen Koehler argues the strategy is unreachable for most organisations as practised: "Ohne massiven personellen Aufwand können die allerwenigsten Unternehmen diesen Ansatz praktisch und vor allem erfolgreich umsetzen", and "Unternehmen müssen begreifen, dass mehr Tools nicht zwangsläufig mehr Sicherheit bedeuten" -- without massive staffing very few organisations can run the approach successfully, and more tools do not automatically mean more security. https://www.iavcworld.de/security/9443-defense-in-depth-klingt-gut-aber-ist-es-das-auch.html[Koehler, "Defense in depth: Klingt gut, aber ist es das auch?", _iavcworld_] (21 November 2023). Koehler is VP EMEA Sales at Ontinue; same caveat.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The NSA paper survives only in the Internet Archive, and it carries no date.** The nsa.gov URL it was published under is dead; the five-page document is retrievable through a Wayback Machine snapshot captured on 11 April 2016 (`web.archive.org/web/20160411062620/https://www.nsa.gov/ia/_files/support/defenseindepth.pdf`). The quotations above come from that file. The commonly repeated date of "around 2000" is a secondary claim: the document itself prints no date, version or revision. Anyone citing it as a dated standard is citing something the paper does not say.
* **Naming it adds layers the baseline omits.** Measured on `claude-haiku-4-5` on 3 October 2026 against a document-rendering task: with the anchor named, two of two runs produced sandboxed preview rendering and an explicitly layered decomposition; without it, zero of two did.
* **The premise does not come with the name.** In the same measurement, "assume breach" appeared in only one of the two anchored runs. The independence and assumed-failure requirement is therefore not reliable in the prior, which is why this entry states it in Core Concepts instead of leaving it to the model.

### Domain-Driven Design according to Evans

***Full Name***: Domain-Driven Design according to Eric Evans

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Ubiquitous Language***: Shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts

***Bounded Context***: Explicit boundaries where a model is defined and applicable

***Aggregates***: Cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit

***Entities***: Objects defined by identity, not attributes

***Value Objects***: Immutable objects defined by their attributes

***Repositories***: Abstraction for object persistence and retrieval

***Domain Events***: Significant occurrences in the domain

***Strategic Design***: Context mapping, anti-corruption layers

***Tactical Design***: Building blocks (entities, value objects, services)

***Model-Driven Design***: Code that expresses the domain model

***Key Proponent***: Eric Evans ("Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software", 2003)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Complex business domains with intricate rules
* Long-lived systems requiring deep domain understanding
* When business and technical teams need close collaboration
* Systems where the domain logic is the core value

### Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe/Woolf)

***Full Name***: _Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions_ -- Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Addison-Wesley Signature Series, 2003. The catalog lives at https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/[enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com]

***Also known as***: EIP, the Hohpe/Woolf patterns, the messaging pattern language

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***The Four Integration Styles Come Before Any Pattern***: The book opens by comparing **File Transfer**, **Shared Database**, **Remote Procedure Invocation** and **Messaging**, and argues for messaging on the grounds of coupling -- in time, in location and in data format. That comparison is part of the anchor: naming EIP should produce the choice of style, not only a list of patterns. A design that never considered the other three styles has skipped the book's first chapter.

***Sixty-Five Patterns in Six Categories***: The catalog states its own size: "This pattern catalog includes 65 integration patterns that we collected from integration projects and updated over two decades." The categories follow a message's journey -- **Messaging Channels**, **Message Construction**, **Message Routing**, **Message Transformation**, **Messaging Endpoints**, **System Management**. The categories are the usable abstraction; the full list of sixty-five is a reference, not something to recite.

***The Handful That Carries Most Designs***: **Message Channel** -- the named pipe a sender writes to without knowing the receiver. **Message Router** -- a component that decides a message's destination from its content, keeping the decision out of both endpoints. **Message Translator** -- the seam where one system's format becomes another's. **Competing Consumers** -- several consumers on one channel, which is how messaging buys throughput and failover. **Dead Letter Channel** -- where a message goes when it cannot be delivered, so a failure becomes an inspectable object instead of a loss. **Canonical Data Model** -- one shared format at the boundary, so _n_ systems need _n_ translators and not _n²_.

***Pipes and Filters Is the Base Metaphor***: Every routing and transformation pattern is a filter wired into a pipe. This is what makes the patterns composable: a Content Enricher followed by a Content-Based Router followed by a Splitter is a legitimate design, and each piece can be tested on its own.

Not the Same Anchor as `event-driven-architecture`:: Both entries name Hohpe and Woolf, and the split matters. Event-driven architecture is an architectural **style**: the system reacts to events, state is distributed, consistency is eventual. EIP is the named **vocabulary** for building any messaging solution -- request/reply integration between a shop and an invoicing system is EIP territory and is not event-driven at all. Reach for EDA to decide how a system should behave; reach for EIP to name the parts once it does.

***The Icon Language Is Part of Why It Travels***: Each pattern has a drawn symbol, and the site still distributes them: "You can create design documents using our icon language by downloading the Visio stencil or using the OmniGraffle stencil created by one of our readers." A pattern language with a notation gets drawn on whiteboards, and the names survive because the pictures do.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing integration between systems you do not own, where the vocabulary has to be shared with another team
* Naming the parts of an existing messaging flow before changing it -- most undocumented integrations turn out to be a router plus two translators
* Error design: `Dead Letter Channel`, Invalid Message Channel and Idempotent Receiver answer questions that otherwise surface in production
* Deciding integration style at all, by making File Transfer, Shared Database and RPC explicit alternatives instead of defaults
* Reading Apache Camel or Spring Integration code and configuration, which use the pattern names as API

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "EIP means build an ESB" -- the patterns say nothing about where they run; the same Message Router can be a Camel route, a Lambda, a Kafka Streams stage or a `switch` statement
* ❌ "EIP is event-driven architecture" -- EIP covers request/reply and batch integration too; EDA is one style you can build with it
* ❌ "You need all 65" -- six categories and roughly six patterns carry most designs; the rest is a reference catalog
* ❌ "It is a 2003 book, so it is obsolete" -- the names map directly onto today's platforms; what aged are the code examples, not the patterns
* ✓ "EIP is the vocabulary for messaging design; EDA is a style" -- accurate, and the reason both entries exist

## **Criticism**:

* **The microservices community rejected the architecture the patterns were usually implemented in.** James Lewis and Martin Fowler open their definition of microservices with exactly this target: "When building communication structures between different processes, we've seen many products and approaches that stress putting significant smarts into the communication mechanism itself. A good example of this is the Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), where ESB products often include sophisticated facilities for message routing, choreography, transformation, and applying business rules." Their alternative is "smart endpoints and dumb pipes", and their footnote is blunter: "We can't resist mentioning Jim Webber's statement that ESB stands for 'Erroneous Spaghetti Box'." Note what the objection does and does not hit. Routing, transformation and choreography are EIP patterns; the criticism is of putting them in central middleware, not of the patterns themselves. But the 2003 pattern language is what the ESB vendors sold, and a model that reaches for EIP will suggest middleware-resident routing unless told otherwise. https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices.html[Lewis and Fowler, "Microservices", 25 March 2014]
* **Hohpe's own follow-up names the gap: the patterns describe single messages, not conversations.** His _Conversation Patterns_ work states the limitation directly: "Asynchronous Messaging is a great way for distributed systems to communicate while maintaining loose coupling. Sending a single message isn't always enough for a meaningful exchange, though: a request expects a response; a certificate exchange may be needed for initial authentication; an order message is supposed to lead to a payment message, and if something goes wrong, additional messages may be needed to handle or correct errors." Request-Response with Retry, Lease Renewal, Compensating Action and Tentative Operation live in that second language, not in the 2003 book. The page is also still labelled "Work in progress. Last update: Jan 2017", so the acknowledged gap has stayed open for roughly two decades. https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/conversation/[Hohpe, "Conversation Patterns"]
* **What we did not find, and where we looked.** No named German-language critique of the pattern language turned up; German-language results are book reviews and introductions. Languages searched: English, German. The substantive criticism is English and architectural -- it concerns centralised middleware, not the pattern catalog.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The prior produces the vocabulary unprompted, and cites its source.** In a clean-room test on `claude-haiku-4-5` (2026-10-03), naming Enterprise Integration Patterns on a neutral logistics-platform brief produced Request/Reply, Publish/Subscribe, Canonical Message Format and Message Translator without being asked for patterns, and the model referred to "Hohpe and Woolf's notation" without being asked for a source. The no-anchor baseline named none of them. This is the strongest of the three priors tested that day.
* **There is no second edition, and saying so is not a quibble.** The 2003 Addison-Wesley edition is still the only one. The _Conversation Patterns_ work is announced as Volume 2 of the series and remains unpublished, work in progress on the site rather than a shipped book (checked 2026-10-03). Cite "the 2003 edition" or "the online catalog"; never "the second edition".
* **The pattern count is confirmed, and the catalog is not the 2003 book.** The site states 65 patterns and carries the copyright line "© 2003, 2023" together with "updated over two decades" (checked 2026-10-03). A citation of "the 2003 book, 65 patterns" is correct about the count; it is not safe to assume the printed edition and today's online catalog say the same thing about any individual pattern.
* **The names outlived the platforms.** Apache Camel and Spring Integration expose EIP pattern names as API, which is why the vocabulary still resolves for anyone reading integration code. The infrastructure under it has turned over -- message brokers, Kafka, serverless functions, managed queues -- while the pattern names did not change, which is the usual sign of a pattern language that was written at the right level.

### Event-Driven Architecture

***Also known as***: EDA, Message-Driven Architecture

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Event producers and consumers***: Components communicate by emitting and reacting to events rather than direct calls

***Publish-subscribe***: Producers publish events without knowing which consumers will process them

***Asynchronous decoupling***: Sender and receiver operate independently in time; no blocking request-response

***Message queue***: Intermediary that buffers events between producers and consumers (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka)

***At-least-once delivery***: Most messaging systems guarantee delivery but may deliver duplicates, requiring idempotent consumers

***Eventual consistency***: System state converges over time rather than being immediately consistent after each operation

***Event notification***: Lightweight event signals that something happened; consumers decide whether to act

***Event-carried state transfer***: Events carry enough data for consumers to process without calling back to the producer

***Choreography vs. orchestration***: Events can trigger distributed workflows implicitly (choreography) or via a central coordinator (orchestration)

***Key Proponents***: Gregor Hohpe, Bobby Woolf ("Enterprise Integration Patterns", 2003), Martin Fowler ("What do you mean by Event-Driven?", 2017)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Systems requiring loose coupling between components
* Workloads with asynchronous processing pipelines
* Architectures that need independent scaling of producers and consumers
* Distributed systems where components must evolve independently

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Domain-Driven Design - Domain events are a DDD building block
* Hexagonal Architecture - Message queues as driven adapters
* Clean Architecture - Events cross architectural boundaries via interfaces

### Event Storming according to Alberto Brandolini

***Full Name***: Event Storming

***Also known as***: EventStorming (Brandolini)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Domain events on a timeline***: Model the domain as past-tense **domain events** (orange stickies) placed left-to-right on a wide wall, reconstructing how the business actually unfolds over time

***The colour notation***: A fixed sticky vocabulary — orange = Domain Event, blue = Command, yellow = Aggregate, lilac = Policy (reactive "whenever… then…"), green = Read Model, pink = External System, red = Hotspot (conflict, question, assumption)

***Three levels***: **Big Picture** (explore the whole domain with all stakeholders), **Process Modeling** (zoom into one flow: command → event → policy → command), **Design Level** (aggregates, commands and events detailed enough to drive implementation)

***Pivotal events***: Events that mark phase transitions or boundaries — strong candidates for **bounded context** seams

***Hotspots***: Make conflicts, unknowns and assumptions explicit on the wall instead of glossing over them — they become the agenda

***Chaotic exploration → enforced timeline***: Everyone adds events in parallel first (diverge), then the group orders and de-duplicates them into a coherent line (converge)

***Key Proponents***: Alberto Brandolini (first run 2012, "Introducing EventStorming" blog post 2013; Leanpub book, continuously updated)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Kicking off a Domain-Driven Design effort — discovering bounded contexts and aggregate boundaries collaboratively
* Aligning business and engineering on a shared, visual domain model
* Before deciding on an event-driven or CQRS architecture — discover the events/commands first
* **Reverse Event Storming** on legacy systems (well suited to an AI agent): extract state transitions → map to Domain Events → cluster into Aggregates → surface Bounded Contexts

[discrete]
## **When NOT to Use**:

* Trivial CRUD domains with no meaningful process or business rules
* Solo modeling where the collaborative, cross-role discovery — the whole point — is absent

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Domain-Driven Design — the vocabulary (aggregates, bounded contexts) Event Storming discovers; often the on-ramp to DDD
* User Story Mapping — activity-centric mapping vs. event-centric discovery
* CQRS — commands and read models found on the wall feed a later CQRS decision
* Event-Driven Architecture — the modeling step that precedes deciding how events are routed

### Fallacies of Distributed Computing

***Full Name***: The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing

***Also known as***: Deutsch's Fallacies, Fallacies of Networked Computing

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***The eight false assumptions***: (1) The network is reliable. (2) Latency is zero. (3) Bandwidth is infinite. (4) The network is secure. (5) Topology doesn't change. (6) There is one administrator. (7) Transport cost is zero. (8) The network is homogeneous

***Why it matters***: Each assumption is comfortable in local development and false in production; building on them produces systems that fail under real network conditions

***As an audit checklist***: Invoke the list to interrogate a distributed design — for each fallacy, ask what happens when the real-world opposite is true (retries, timeouts, backpressure, encryption, service discovery, capacity limits, protocol negotiation)

***Mitigation cues***: Reliability → retries/idempotency; latency → batching/locality; security → zero-trust; topology → service discovery; homogeneity → explicit contracts and versioning

***Key Proponents***: L. Peter Deutsch (first seven, Sun Microsystems, c. 1994); James Gosling added the eighth ("the network is homogeneous"); early items credited to Bill Joy and Tom Lyon

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Reviewing or hardening a distributed/microservice design
* Writing resilience requirements (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers)
* Onboarding developers moving from monolith to distributed thinking
* Post-incident analysis of network-related outages

[discrete]
## **When NOT to Use**:

* For purely in-process, single-machine logic with no network calls
* As a substitute for measuring your actual network's behaviour

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* CAP Theorem — the consistency/availability consequence of partitions
* Event-Driven Architecture — async patterns that assume unreliable networks
* Hexagonal Architecture — isolating network adapters behind ports

### 4+1 View Model according to Kruchten

***Full Name***: The "4+1" View Model of Software Architecture -- Philippe Kruchten, "Architectural Blueprints -- The '4+1' View Model of Software Architecture", _IEEE Software_ 12(6), November 1995, pp. 42-50 (https://doi.org/10.1109/52.469759[doi:10.1109/52.469759])

***Also known as***: Kruchten's 4+1, the 4+1 views, the RUP architecture views, 4+1-Sichtenmodell

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***One View, One Named Audience***: Each view exists because a specific group asks a specific question. The **logical view** answers the end user's question about functionality. The **development view** (also implementation view) answers the programmer's question about code organisation -- modules, packages, layers, build. The **process view** answers the integrator's question about runtime: concurrency, distribution, performance, fault tolerance. The **physical view** (also deployment view) answers the system engineer's question about which hardware runs what. The audience is part of the model, not an afterthought.

***The "+1" Is the Cross-Check, Not a Fifth Topic***: The scenarios -- a small set of key use cases -- are deliberately redundant with the four views. They are used twice: to **discover** architectural elements while the architecture is being designed, and to **validate** the four views against each other afterwards. A scenario that cannot be walked through all four views has found an inconsistency. This is the mechanism that makes 4+1 more than a filing system.

What Separates It From `arc42` and `c4-diagrams`:: All three describe a system through several views, and the three overlap heavily in content. Two things are 4+1's own. First, the explicit stakeholder-per-view mapping: the model names who each view is for, so a view with no reader is a defect. Second, the scenarios as the consistency check **between** views. `c4-diagrams` instead supplies one zoom hierarchy with a fixed notation; `arc42` supplies a twelve-chapter document structure in which the building block, runtime and deployment views descend from the same idea.

***Lineage -- RUP, Then the Standard***: 4+1 came out of Kruchten's work at Rational and became the architecture description of the Rational Unified Process. The idea of describing a system through stakeholder-specific views was then generalised in IEEE 1471-2000 and its successor ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 as the **view / viewpoint** distinction: a viewpoint is the reusable template, a view is one application of it. Rozanski and Woods state the move plainly: "The IEEE standard makes this idea generic (and does not specify one set of views or another) by proposing the concept of a viewpoint."

***The Diagram Vocabulary Is UML-Era***: The paper and all its teaching material speak UML: class and sequence diagrams for the logical view, component and package diagrams for the development view, activity diagrams for the process view, deployment diagrams for the physical view, use case diagrams for the scenarios. Naming the anchor therefore pulls UML with it. That is the vocabulary of the model, not a defect in it, but it is worth knowing before a model picks notation on your behalf.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Structuring a first architecture description when the team has no agreed view set, and the stakeholders are known
* Auditing an existing architecture document for a missing audience -- a document with no process view usually means nobody asked the integrator
* Forcing consistency between views: write the scenarios, then walk each one through all four views
* Teaching why multiple views exist at all, before introducing `arc42` or `c4-diagrams` as the modern container
* Reading older architecture documents, RUP artefacts and ISO 42010 wording, where the vocabulary is already in use

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "4+1 means five documents" -- it means five **views** of one architecture; they may live in five chapters of one document, and a view without a reader should be dropped
* ❌ "The scenarios are the use case chapter" -- they are the cross-check; their job is to expose contradictions between the other four views
* ❌ "4+1 is the same as arc42 or C4" -- arc42 is a document structure and C4 a notation hierarchy; 4+1 is a stakeholder-to-view mapping plus a consistency mechanism
* ❌ "Physical view means the server diagram" -- it is the mapping of software elements onto nodes, which includes availability and installation, not a network drawing
* ✓ "4+1 is a view set; ISO 42010 is the grammar for view sets" -- accurate, and the reason the model survives as vocabulary even where its UML diagrams do not

## **Criticism**:

* **The standard that formalised the idea declined to keep the view set.** IEEE 1471 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 adopted Kruchten's central move -- stakeholder-driven views -- and then deliberately refused to prescribe which views. Rozanski and Woods, authors of _Software Systems Architecture_, describe the sequence directly: "In his introductory paper, Kruchten defined four standard views, namely, Logical, Process, Physical, and Development," after which "The IEEE standard makes this idea generic (and does not specify one set of views or another) by proposing the concept of a viewpoint." A fixed set of four is exactly what the standard treats as the part not to generalise. https://www.viewpoints-and-perspectives.info/home/viewpoints/[Rozanski and Woods, "Views and Viewpoints", viewpoints-and-perspectives.info]
* **Two concerns the four views do not carry: data and operations.** The Rozanski and Woods catalog answers 4+1 with seven viewpoints -- Context, Functional, Information, Concurrency, Development, Deployment, Operational. Information and Operational have no counterpart among Kruchten's four: there is no view that owns the data model, and none that owns running the system in production. Teams using 4+1 on information systems add these themselves, which is the practical argument for the newer catalogs. Same source as above.
* **What we did not find, and where we looked.** No named, published critique of 4+1 with a verifiable quotation turned up in English or German searching -- not from Philippe Kruchten in retrospect, not from Simon Brown, not from the arc42 authors (Stefan Zörner's embarc comparison of arc42 against alternatives discusses Simon Brown's C4 and Software Guidebook, and does not treat 4+1). The criticism of 4+1 is structural rather than polemical: it is carried by what the successors changed. Languages searched: English, German. Other languages were not searched, so this is a frame, not a proof of absence.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The prior is strong and correctly attributed.** In a clean-room test on `claude-haiku-4-5` (2026-10-03) a neutral logistics-platform brief that named no method produced no view vocabulary at all; naming the 4+1 View Model produced all five views together with their audiences. The weak tier attributes Kruchten 1995 correctly and with high confidence. The model is one of the rare cases where the term alone restructures the answer.
* **The citation itself has drifted.** Crossref's record for `doi:10.1109/52.469759` gives _IEEE Software_ 12(6), 1995, pp. 42-50, matching the German Wikipedia entry's "Band 12, Nr. 6, November 1995, S. 42-50". Kruchten's own bibliography lists the same DOI as "pp. 45-50" (https://philippe.kruchten.com/architecture/[philippe.kruchten.com/architecture]). Use 42-50.
* **It lives on as vocabulary, not as a template.** The stakeholder-per-view idea is now standard through ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, and the views themselves reappear inside `arc42` (building block, runtime, deployment) and `c4-diagrams`. What has aged is the notation layer: a model naming 4+1 today still reaches for UML diagram types, which may not be what the project uses.

### GoM

***Full Name***: Grundsätze ordnungsmäßiger Modellierung (Principles of Proper Modeling)

***Also known as***: GoM Principles, Principles of Well-formed Modeling

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Correctness (Richtigkeit)***: The model must accurately reflect the reality it represents — both syntactically (follows notation rules) and semantically (describes the real subject matter truthfully)

***Relevance (Relevanz)***: A model should include only elements that are relevant to the intended purpose; unnecessary details reduce usability

***Economic Efficiency (Wirtschaftlichkeit)***: The benefit gained from a model must justify the effort and cost of creating and maintaining it

***Clarity (Klarheit)***: The model must be understandable to its intended audience; layout, notation, and level of detail must support comprehension

***Comparability (Vergleichbarkeit)***: Models of the same subject should follow consistent conventions so they can be meaningfully compared

***Systematic Design (Systematischer Aufbau)***: Models should be constructed using a consistent, structured approach to enable reuse and integration across a model landscape

***Key Proponents***: Jörg Becker, Michael Rosemann, Rolf Schütte ("Grundsätze ordnungsmäßiger Modellierung", WIRTSCHAFTSINFORMATIK, 1995)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Evaluating or reviewing the quality of business process models (BPMN, EPC)
* Establishing modeling standards within an organization or project
* Enterprise architecture modeling to ensure consistent, reusable model artifacts
* ERP implementation projects requiring traceable and auditable process documentation
* Assessing whether a model is fit for its intended purpose
* Onboarding teams to structured modeling practices

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* arc42 Architecture Documentation
* C4 Diagrams
* Morphological Box

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The canonical reference is Becker, Rosemann & Schütte, "Grundsätze ordnungsmäßiger Modellierung", Wirtschaftsinformatik 37(5), 1995, pp. 435–445 — no DOI exists; stable records: https://dblp.org/rec/journals/wi/BeckerRS95.html[dblp] and the https://www.wi.uni-muenster.de/de/forschung/publikationen/3436[University of Münster publication page]
* The prior is thin: a German-language-only academic paper from the Wirtschaftsinformatik community with virtually no English-language footprint — supply the six principles in the prompt rather than relying on the term

### Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)

***Also known as***: Ports and Adapters, Onion Architecture (variant)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Hexagonal structure***: Core domain at the center, isolated from external concerns

***Ports***: Interfaces defining how the application communicates

***Adapters***: Implementations that connect to external systems

***Dependency inversion***: Dependencies point inward toward the domain

***Technology independence***: Core logic doesn't depend on frameworks or infrastructure

***Primary/Driving adapters***: User interfaces, APIs (inbound)

***Secondary/Driven adapters***: Databases, message queues (outbound)

***Testability***: Easy to test core logic in isolation

***Symmetry***: All external interactions are treated uniformly

***Key Proponent***: Alistair Cockburn (2005)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Applications requiring high testability
* Systems that need to support multiple interfaces (web, CLI, API)
* When you want to defer infrastructure decisions
* Microservices with clear domain boundaries

### ISO/IEC 25010

***Full Name***: ISO/IEC 25010 — Systems and Software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product Quality Model

***Also known as***: SQuaRE Quality Model, Software Product Quality Model, ISO 25010

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:
