* Annual or multi-year strategic planning when alignment across many teams is the critical risk
* Translating a vision or mission into measurable, accountable work
* Scaling an organization where local optimization is starting to dominate over global goals
* Lean transformations — Hoshin Kanri is the strategy-layer counterpart to Kaizen at the operational layer
* As an alternative to OKRs when the organization needs explicit cause-and-effect links and stronger accountability than quarterly self-set objectives provide

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Kotter's 8-Step Change Model — large-scale transformation framework; Hoshin Kanri is the recurring discipline that operationalizes a Kotter-style vision year after year
* MoSCoW — tactical prioritization within the hoshin's improvement priorities
* Kano Model — feature classification that often feeds the customer-facing leg of the X-Matrix

### Impact Mapping

***Full Name***: Impact Mapping according to Gojko Adzic

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Four levels***: Goal → Actors → Impacts → Deliverables

***Goal***: Business objective (Why?)

***Actors***: Who can produce or prevent desired impact? (Who?)

***Impacts***: How can actors' behavior change? (How?)

***Deliverables***: What can we build? (What?)

***Visual mapping***: Mind-map style collaborative diagram

***Assumption testing***: Make assumptions explicit

***Scope management***: Prevent scope creep by linking to goals

***Roadmap alternative***: Goal-oriented rather than feature-oriented

***Key Proponent***: Gojko Adzic ("Impact Mapping", 2012)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Strategic planning for products or projects
* When stakeholders disagree on priorities
* Aligning delivery with business outcomes
* Avoiding building features that don't serve business goals

### Jobs To Be Done (JTBD)

***Full Name***: Jobs To Be Done Framework (Christensen interpretation)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Job definition***: Progress people want to make in a particular context

***Functional job***: Practical task to accomplish

***Emotional job***: How people want to feel

***Social job***: How people want to be perceived

***Hire and fire***: Customers "hire" products to do a job, "fire" when inadequate

***Context matters***: Jobs exist in specific circumstances

***Competition redefined***: Anything solving the same job is competition

***Innovation opportunities***: Unmet jobs or poorly served jobs

***Job stories***: Alternative to user stories focusing on context and motivation

***Key Proponents***: Clayton Christensen, Alan Klement, Bob Moesta

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Product discovery and innovation
* Understanding why customers choose solutions
* Identifying true competition
* Writing more meaningful user stories
* Market segmentation based on jobs, not demographics

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Two schools claim the same term: Alan Klement documents in https://jtbd.info/know-the-two-very-different-interpretations-of-jobs-to-be-done-5a18b748bd89["Know the Two — Very — Different Interpretations of Jobs to be Done"] that Christensen/Moesta's **Jobs-as-Progress** and Ulwick's **Jobs-as-Activities** (Outcome-Driven Innovation) are incompatible interpretations that confuse practitioners
* Even the origin is contested: Ulwick's Strategyn states that https://strategyn.com/jobs-to-be-done/history-of-jtbd/["JTBD was created by Tony Ulwick in 1990"] and merely popularized by Christensen (https://hbr.org/2016/09/know-your-customers-jobs-to-be-done["Know Your Customers' 'Jobs to Be Done'"], HBR 2016)
* The bare acronym therefore activates two conflicting priors — say "JTBD (Christensen, jobs as progress)" or "JTBD (Ulwick, Outcome-Driven Innovation)"; this anchor's full name carries the Christensen qualifier for exactly that reason

### Kano Model

***Also known as***: Kano Analysis, Kano-Modell, Customer Satisfaction Model

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Two-dimensional Quality***: Customer satisfaction is not the simple inverse of dissatisfaction — they are two separate axes (presence/absence of a feature × resulting satisfaction)

***Five Feature Categories***: Every feature falls into one of five classes that map differently onto the satisfaction curve

***Must-be (Basic, Threshold)***: Expected baseline — absence causes strong dissatisfaction, presence is taken for granted and earns no credit (e.g., car has wheels, app does not lose data)

***One-dimensional (Performance, Linear)***: Satisfaction grows roughly linearly with how well the feature is delivered (e.g., fuel efficiency, response time, battery life)

***Attractive (Excitement, Delighter)***: Unexpected — absence causes no dissatisfaction, presence delights and differentiates (e.g., a thoughtful onboarding gesture, a surprising shortcut)

***Indifferent***: Customer does not care either way — flag for cost reduction

***Reverse***: Presence actually causes dissatisfaction for the target segment — flag for removal or segmentation

***Functional / Dysfunctional Questionnaire***: For each candidate feature, ask the user two paired questions: "How would you feel if this feature were present?" and "How would you feel if it were absent?". The cross-tab of answers maps the feature to one of the five categories

***Time Decay***: Categories migrate over time. Today's **Delighter** becomes tomorrow's **Performer** and eventually a **Must-be** as the market matures (mobile camera, HTTPS, dark mode)

***Key Proponent***: Noriaki Kano (Tokyo University of Science), originally published in 1984 in the Japanese journal **Hinshitsu** ("Quality")

***Historical Context***: Developed in the context of Japanese quality management, alongside Total Quality Management and the Kaizen movement; widely adopted in product management, UX research, and requirements engineering since the late 1990s.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Prioritising features in a product backlog beyond raw business value
* Distinguishing the "non-negotiables" (Must-be) from the "wow features" (Delighter) before estimation
* User research where you need to understand **why** a feature affects satisfaction, not just whether users like it
* MVP scoping: ensure all **Must-be** features are covered before investing in **Delighters**
* Product strategy reviews: spot **Delighters** that have decayed into **Performers** or **Must-be** and update positioning
* Combining with **MoSCoW Method** — Must-be → Must, Performance → Should, Delighter → Could

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* MoSCoW Method — complementary prioritisation lens (organisation-driven), often combined with Kano (customer-driven)
* Jobs To Be Done — discovery side: what job is the customer hiring the feature for, before classifying its impact
* EARS Requirements — once a feature is classified as Must-be, EARS gives it the unambiguous wording

***Counter-example***: Pure ROI-based ranking — useful but blind to the asymmetry between dissatisfaction (Must-be) and delight (Attractive). Kano corrects that.

### Kotter's 8-Step Change Model

***Also known as***: Kotter's 8 Steps for Leading Change, Kotter's Change Process

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Step 1 — Establish a Sense of Urgency***: Surface the threats and opportunities that make change necessary now; without urgency, the organisation defaults to the status quo

***Step 2 — Form a Guiding Coalition***: Assemble a powerful enough cross-functional group with the credibility, authority and energy to lead the effort; lone champions fail

***Step 3 — Develop a Vision and Strategy***: Create a clear, compelling vision of the future state and a strategy to reach it; the vision must be simple enough to communicate in five minutes

***Step 4 — Communicate the Change Vision***: Use every channel and repeat the vision constantly; walk the talk — leadership behaviour speaks louder than memos

***Step 5 — Empower Broad-based Action***: Remove the obstacles that block change — outdated structures, misaligned incentives, fearful middle management; enable people to act on the vision

***Step 6 — Generate Short-term Wins***: Plan, create and visibly celebrate quick, unambiguous improvements within 6–18 months; wins fund credibility and silence sceptics

***Step 7 — Consolidate Gains and Produce More Change***: Use the credibility from short-term wins to tackle bigger systems, structures and policies; do not declare victory too early

***Step 8 — Anchor the Changes in Corporate Culture***: Make the new approaches "the way we do things around here" by tying them to leadership succession, hiring, onboarding and storytelling

***The 8 Errors***: The model is the inversion of the **eight common errors** Kotter identified in failed transformations: complacency, no powerful coalition, underestimating vision, undercommunicating, ignoring obstacles, no short-term wins, premature victory, and not anchoring change in culture

***Linear but Iterative***: Kotter presents the steps as sequential because each step builds on the credibility and infrastructure of the previous ones, but in practice teams loop within and across steps as the change scales

***Key Proponent***: John P. Kotter (Harvard Business School), introduced in the 1995 **Harvard Business Review** article **"Leading Change: Why Transformation Efforts Fail"** and expanded in the 1996 book **Leading Change** (Harvard Business Press)

***Historical Context***: One of the most cited change management frameworks in business literature; widely used in M&A integrations, digital transformations, agile rollouts and culture change programmes; later complemented by Kotter's 2014 **Accelerate** (XLR8), which adds a "dual operating system" of hierarchy plus network for continuous change

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Planning a non-trivial organisational change (digital transformation, agile rollout, restructuring, M&A integration)
* Diagnosing why a stalled transformation is stalled — which of the 8 errors is biting?
* Sequencing communication and intervention activities so that quick wins land before the political resistance forms
* Stakeholder analysis and coalition building before kicking off a change initiative
* Reviewing whether a "completed" change is actually anchored in culture, or just a temporary policy

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* SWOT — strategic analysis to feed the urgency and vision steps
* Cynefin Framework — choose the right approach (Clear / Complicated / Complex / Chaotic) for the kind of change you face
* Wardley Mapping — visualise where change is needed in the value chain before defining the vision

***Counter-example***: Pure top-down mandate ("from Monday we will be agile") — Kotter's whole point is that without urgency, coalition, vision and short-term wins, the mandate produces compliance theatre, not change.

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* No empirical validation of the whole model: Appelbaum, Habashy, Malo & Shafiq, https://doi.org/10.1108/02621711211253231["Back to the future: revisiting Kotter's 1996 change model"] (Journal of Management Development 31(8), 2012) reviewed 15 years of literature — support for most individual steps, but no formal study validating the model as a whole; its popularity "appears to derive more from its direct and usable format than from any scientific consensus on the results"
* The evidence base of n-step change models in general is thin: Rune Todnem By, https://doi.org/10.1080/14697010500359250["Organisational change management: A critical review"] (Journal of Change Management 5(4), 2005) finds planned, step-based approaches — of which Kotter's is the best-known — "often contradictory, mostly lacking empirical evidence and supported by unchallenged hypotheses"
* Kotter's own revision concedes the linearity: his organization https://www.kotterinc.com/methodology/8-steps/[describes the original as "the linear 8 Step"] that he evolved into the 8 Accelerators of _Accelerate_ (2014; based on https://hbr.org/2012/11/accelerate["Accelerate!"], HBR 2012) with a "dual operating system" — an agile network running alongside the hierarchy

### Meaningful Human Control (MHC)

***Full Name***: Meaningful Human Control

***Also known as***: MHC, Meaningful Human Control over Individual Attacks

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Substantive human control***: Humans must retain genuine, substantive control over autonomous systems making high-stakes decisions — not merely formulaic "human-in-the-loop" oversight

***Situational awareness***: Human operators require adequate information about the target, context, weapon/system behavior, and foreseeable effects to make informed judgments

***Accountability chain***: Those responsible for assessing information and executing actions must be clearly identifiable and accountable for outcomes; accountability cannot be transferred to machines

***Sharkey's five levels***: Operational framework for human supervisory control: (L1) human deliberates before attack → (L2) program suggests targets, human chooses → (L3) program selects, human approves → (L4) program acts, human has restricted veto → (L5) fully autonomous without human involvement

***Positive human action***: Initiating critical actions (especially use of force) requires affirmative human authorization, not merely passive monitoring

***Predictable, reliable, transparent technology***: Autonomous systems must be designed for predictability, graceful degradation, and transparency to enable meaningful control

***Timely intervention***: Human operators must retain the capability for timely intervention, override, or abort — not just pre-programmed constraints

***Key Proponents***: Article 36 (coined the term, 2013), Noel Sharkey (five-level framework, 2014), ICRC (endorsed MHC as legal/ethical requirement, 2018), UN CCW GGE (Guiding Principles, 2019), IEEE Global Initiative (Ethically Aligned Design, 2019)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Designing or evaluating autonomous systems in high-stakes domains (weapons systems, medical AI, autonomous driving, critical infrastructure)
* Assessing whether human oversight of an AI system is genuinely effective or merely procedural
* Defining accountability chains for autonomous decision-making
* Requirements engineering for systems with autonomy in critical functions
* AI governance and ethics discussions in product management and policy
* Legal and compliance review of AI systems under emerging regulations (EU AI Act)

[discrete]
## **When NOT to Use**:

* Low-stakes automation decisions (content recommendations, spam filtering, routine data processing)
* As a substitute for domain-specific legal requirements (IHL, medical device regulation, data protection law)

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Regulated Environment
* Cynefin Framework
* Luhmann System Theory
* Simon Constructivism
* Systemic Consulting

[discrete]
## **Quality Criteria Checklist** (Tier-2 Justification)

This anchor is classified as **Tier 2 — Needs qualification**. It is not self-standing; it requires domain context and explicit verification criteria to be meaningfully applied. The following checklist documents the qualification requirements mapped to Issue #540.

1. ***Acceptance Criteria*** (measurable)
* High-stakes domain identified: yes/no — specify domain (weapons, medical, autonomous driving, critical infrastructure, algorithmic sentencing)
* Autonomy level classified: yes/no — specify Sharkey level (L1–L5) for each critical function
* Human operator identified: yes/no — specify role, training level, and decision authority
* Accountability chain documented: yes/no — specify who decides, who approves, who audits
* Legal/regulatory framework identified: yes/no — specify applicable law (IHL, EU AI Act, GDPR, etc.)

1. ***Evidence Types Required***
* System specification documenting autonomy boundaries and human-machine interaction points
* Operator training and qualification records
* Audit trail design demonstrating human accountability at each decision point
* Risk assessment showing residual risks after human oversight measures
* Legal review confirming compliance with applicable regulatory framework

1. ***Minimum Documentation / Artifacts***
* Human-Machine Interface (HMI) specification with override and abort mechanisms
* Decision authority matrix (who decides what, under what conditions)
* Operator situational awareness requirements (information feed, latency, decision time)
* Graceful degradation protocol for communication loss or system failure
* Test protocol validating human intervention capability under operational conditions

1. ***Validation Methods***
* Simulated scenario testing with time-pressure and information-degradation conditions
* Red-team evaluation of human-override effectiveness
* Independent audit of accountability chain completeness
* Legal review against applicable IHL or regulatory requirements
* Post-deployment monitoring plan for measuring MHC erosion over time

1. ***Tier-2 Justification Summary***
* **Why not Tier 3**: MHC cannot be evaluated without domain-specific context (weapons vs. medical vs. automotive). The same system may satisfy MHC in one domain and fail in another. Sharkey level L3 may be sufficient for cargo ships but not for lethal targeting.
* **Why not Tier 1**: MHC is a well-established, multi-source concept with clear definition, consistent usage across domains, attributable origin, and rich conceptual activation.
* **Qualification path**: To apply MHC, the user must answer: "Who controls what, with what information, under what constraints, and who is accountable?" The five criteria above operationalize this question.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The canonical reference is Santoni de Sio & van den Hoven, https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2018.00015["Meaningful Human Control over Autonomous Systems: A Philosophical Account"] (Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 2018), proposing the "tracking" and "tracing" conditions
* The prior is thin: an academic-only footprint anchored in one open-access philosophy paper (TU Delft ethics group) and a niche AI-ethics literature, with little practitioner coverage — supply the tracking/tracing definitions in the prompt when precision matters

### Muda, Mura, Muri

***Full Name***: Muda (無駄), Mura (斑), Muri (無理) — waste, unevenness, overburden; the "three Ms" of the Toyota Production System

***Also known as***: the 3Ms, the three evils, the seven wastes (muda only), TIMWOOD / TIMWOODS (muda only)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Anchor the Triple, Not Muda Alone***: This is the whole reason the anchor exists. Naming only waste hides what produces the waste. Muda is the symptom that is easy to see and easy to count; mura and muri are the conditions that regenerate it after every clean-up.

***The Three, Defined***: The Lean Enterprise Institute's lexicon:
* **Muda** — "Any activity that consumes resources without creating value for the customer."
* **Mura** — "Unevenness in an operation; for example, a gyrating schedule not caused by end-consumer demand but rather by the production system, or an uneven work pace in an operation causing operators to hurry and then wait."
* **Muri** — "Overburdening equipment or operators by requiring them to run at a higher or harder pace with more force and effort for a longer period of time than equipment designs and appropriate workforce management allow."

***The Causal Chain Runs Mura → Muri → Muda***: Jim Womack argues for reversing the conventional recital order: "I would tell them to have it read 'Mura, muri, muda.'" His reason is the mechanism itself — "The inevitable result is that mura creates muri that undercuts previous efforts to eliminate muda." Unevenness forces people and machines past their design point; overburden then manufactures the very waste that was eliminated last quarter.

***The Seven Wastes***: Ohno's categories are transporting, inventory, motion, waiting, over-production, over-processing and defects. Over-production is traditionally treated as the worst, because it generates most of the others.

***The Eighth Waste Is a Later Addition***: "Unused skills" was appended to the original seven, "as resolving this waste is a key enabler to resolving the others". The mnemonic "TIM WOOD" covers the seven; "TIM WOODS", with the S for skills, covers eight. The eighth is not Ohno's.

***Type One and Type Two Muda***: The lexicon distinguishes waste that cannot be removed quickly (rework a current process cannot avoid) from waste that kaizen can remove at once. The distinction stops "eliminate all waste" from being an instruction nobody can follow.

***In Software***: Mura is the release train that ships nothing for three weeks and everything on Thursday; muri is the sprint committed at 110% capacity; muda is the rework, the queue, the half-finished branch. Attacking the rework without touching the batching is the mistake the triple names.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Whenever a "waste elimination" or efficiency effort is being planned, to force the question of what regenerates the waste
* Capacity and scheduling discussions — mura and muri are the vocabulary that batching and overcommitment otherwise lack
* Retrospectives where the same waste keeps returning after being removed
* As the diagnostic layer under `kaizen`: kaizen is the habit, the three Ms are what it looks for

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "Lean is about eliminating waste" — that is muda only, and Womack's argument is that muda-first is the wrong order
* ❌ "There are eight wastes" — there are Ohno's seven plus a later, widely adopted eighth; the distinction matters when citing him
* ❌ "Muri means working hard" — it means being required to run past the design point of the person or machine, which is a property of the system, not of effort
* ❌ "Mura is just variation" — it is unevenness **manufactured by the system itself**, not demand variation from the customer
* ✓ "Fix mura first and much of the muda stops coming back" — this is Womack's point exactly

## **Criticism**:

* **The conventional ordering teaches the wrong reflex.** Womack's essay is itself a criticism of how the three Ms are usually taught and used — muda first, as a hunt for visible waste, with mura and muri as footnotes. He locates the failure in the sequence: "mura creates muri that undercuts previous efforts to eliminate muda", so a muda-first programme is structurally condemned to repeat itself. https://www.lean.org/the-lean-post/articles/mura-muri-muda/[Womack, "Mura, Muri, Muda?", Lean Enterprise Institute] (6 July 2006).
* **Muri, read from the shop floor, is the point of the system rather than a defect in it.** Jane Slaughter's account of "management by stress" describes a system tuned so that "The ideal state is achieved when the plant is running with all stations just on the line between green and yellow" — that is, deliberately at the edge of overburden, using the operator's inability to keep up as the signal for where to improve next. On this reading, muri is not an accident the method removes but a lever the method applies. https://www.multinationalmonitor.org/hyper/issues/1990/01/slaughter.html[Slaughter, "Management by Stress", _Multinational Monitor_, January/February 1990].
* **Waste-hunting without the people half is the common failure mode.** Bob Emiliani's Real Lean / Fake Lean distinction names it: Fake Lean is "the technical application of 'Continuous Improvement' tools and methods, invariably in a zero-sum fashion", while Real Lean is "the application of both 'Continuous Improvement' and 'Respect for People'". His summary of what actually happened: "Lean intends to correct two big problems in organizations: bad processes and bad management. But it usually corrected only one – bad processes." https://bobemiliani.substack.com/p/back-story-real-vs-fake-lean[Emiliani, "The Backstory: Real vs. Fake Lean"] (13 September 2013).

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Womack's reordering has not displaced the conventional recital.** "Muda, mura, muri" remains the common sequence in training material and in most model output, twenty years after the essay. Expect a model to produce the muda-first order and the seven wastes list unless the causal chain is named explicitly.
* **"The seven wastes" now usually means eight.** TIMWOODS, with unused skills or unused human potential added, is the version most current material teaches. Attributing all eight to Ohno is a common and avoidable error.
* **Type One / Type Two muda is fading from popular usage** even though it remains in the Lean Enterprise Institute lexicon. It is the distinction that makes waste lists actionable, and it is the first thing dropped in short-form summaries.

### Minimum Viable Product (MVP)

***Full Name***: Minimum Viable Product

***Also known as***: MVP, Lean Startup MVP

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Smallest thing that tests a hypothesis***: An MVP is the minimum product that allows a team to learn whether a specific hypothesis about user needs is valid — with the least amount of effort.

***Validated learning is the output***: The defining output is not a feature set, not revenue, not users — it is **learning**. "Did we learn whether our hypothesis is true?" is the only success criterion.

***One hypothesis at a time***: An MVP targets a single, falsifiable hypothesis ("users will pay for X", "users need feature Y more than feature Z"). Bundling hypotheses into one MVP makes the learning ambiguous.

***Minimum means minimum***: If a hand-drawn mockup, a landing page, or a concierge service can test the hypothesis, that **is** the MVP. Code is often not required. The "P" stands for product, but the product can be an illusion.

***Build-measure-learn loop***: The MVP is the first turn of a tight feedback cycle: build a minimal thing, measure how real users respond, learn from the data, then decide whether to pivot or persevere.

***Not a small v1***: A common misuse is calling the first release of a polished product "the MVP". A real MVP would be embarrassing to ship in production — its job is learning, not market entry.

***Pivot or persevere***: The MVP gives you the evidence to choose: continue in the same direction (persevere) or change course based on what you learned (pivot).

***Distinct from Walking Skeleton***: A Walking Skeleton validates **architecture**; an MVP validates **market demand**. You can have one without the other.

***Key Proponents***: Eric Ries ("The Lean Startup", 2011); Frank Robinson coined the term in 2001

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Validating whether a new product or feature solves a real user problem before investing in full development
* Testing pricing, positioning, or target-segment hypotheses with minimal risk
* Early-stage startups with limited runway who cannot afford to build the wrong thing
* Internal product experimentation where feature ideas need evidence before prioritization
* LLM prompting: "design an MVP for X" signals **test the hypothesis, don't ship a complete product**

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Jobs to be Done - Framework for articulating the user need an MVP is trying to validate
* Impact Mapping - Technique for aligning MVP scope with business outcomes
* User Story Mapping - Visual tool for identifying the minimum set of stories for an MVP
* Walking Skeleton - Architectural counterpart; validates structure rather than market demand

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* The term is diluted in practice: Nielsen Norman Group (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/mvp-definition/[Sara Paul, "Minimum Viable Product (MVP): Definition"]) notes that "'MVP' often means different things to different people" — from paper prototype to released product — and advises defining what you are testing and what you expect to learn before using the word
* Henrik Kniberg's widely cited corrective https://blog.crisp.se/2016/01/25/henrikkniberg/making-sense-of-mvp["Making sense of MVP — and why I prefer Earliest Testable/Usable/Lovable"] (Crisp, 2016 — the skateboard→car drawing) argues "Minimum" and "Product" mislead teams into shipping useless fragments; each increment should be a smaller complete solution to the user's need, not a piece of the final one
* Disambiguation advice: state which sense you mean — Ries's learning vehicle ("maximum validated learning for least effort") or Kniberg's Earliest Testable/Usable/Lovable staging — rather than relying on the bare acronym

### OKR (Objectives and Key Results)

***Full Name***: Objectives and Key Results

***Also known as***: OKRs; descended from Intel's iMBO (Intel Management by Objectives)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Objective***: A single qualitative, inspirational, time-bound statement of **what** you want to achieve; memorable and direction-setting, not a metric

***Key Results***: Typically 3-5 quantitative, measurable outcomes that prove the Objective is met; answer **how** you know you got there — outcomes, not a task list

***Objective + Key Results***: One Objective is paired with its Key Results; "if the Objective is the destination, the Key Results are the milestones that measure progress toward it"

***Quarterly cadence***: OKRs are usually set and reviewed on a quarterly rhythm, nested under annual or strategic OKRs

***Ambitious / stretch goals***: Aspirational "moonshot" OKRs are calibrated so that scoring ~0.7 of the way (70%) is considered success; consistently scoring 1.0 signals goals set too low

***Grading (0.0-1.0)***: At cycle end each Key Result is scored on a 0-1 scale; the score drives a conversation, not a verdict

***Transparency / alignment***: OKRs are public across the organization so teams can see and connect to each other's goals; alignment by visibility, not by mechanical cascade

***Decoupled from compensation***: OKRs are deliberately separated from bonuses and performance reviews, so people set honest stretch goals instead of sandbagging

***Key Proponents***: Andy Grove (originated the approach at Intel as "iMBO", documented in "High Output Management", 1983); John Doerr (learned it from Grove at Intel, introduced it to Google in 1999, popularized it in "Measure What Matters", 2018, https://www.whatmatters.com/[whatmatters.com])

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Translating strategy into focused, measurable quarterly goals for teams
* Creating organization-wide alignment and transparency around priorities
* Shifting a team's focus from output (tasks shipped) to outcomes (value delivered)
* Setting ambitious stretch goals where ~70% attainment counts as success
* Prompting an LLM to draft, critique, or grade an Objective with its Key Results

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* Definition of Done

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Goodhart's Law ("when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure") is the recurring failure mode: once a Key Result is the target, people optimise the number rather than the outcome. McKenna Agile Consultants, https://www.mckennaagileconsultants.com/applying-goodharts-law-in-okrs-avoiding-common-pitfalls-in-strategic-execution/["Applying Goodhart's Law in OKRs"] — the proposed mitigation is to pair quantity KRs with quality/guardrail KRs and to keep OKRs decoupled from rewards
* Ant Murphy, https://www.antmurphy.me/newsletter/escape-okr-theatre["Escape OKR Theatre"] — **cascading** OKRs assume strategy perfectly mirrors the org chart, which it rarely does; cascading is often a symptom of missing strategy and produces a "sea of OKRs". Murphy argues OKRs should **align, not cascade**, favouring fewer, strategy-derived OKRs
* "OKR theatre" / performance theatre: teams fluently discuss "driving key metrics" while struggling to name the problem they solve. Bjørn Broum, https://bbroum.substack.com/p/the-okr-performance-theater["The OKR Performance Theater"]

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* The framework remains widely adopted but reportedly hard to sustain: per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objectives_and_key_results[Wikipedia's OKR article], Google's Rick Klau later advised skipping **individual** OKRs to avoid a waterfall/cascade trap — a shift from the individual-level usage many training-data examples assume
* The canonical modern reference is Doerr's "Measure What Matters" (2018) and https://www.whatmatters.com/[whatmatters.com]; the original Grove formulation predates the term "OKR" and lives in "High Output Management" (1983)

### PERT

***Full Name***: Program Evaluation and Review Technique

***Also known as***: Three-Point Estimation, PERT Network Analysis

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Three-Time Estimation***: Each activity requires three duration estimates: Optimistic (O) — best case if everything goes well; Most Likely (M) — realistic expected duration; Pessimistic (P) — worst case if problems arise

***PERT Formula***: Weighted average: **E = (O + 4M + P) / 6** — weights the most likely estimate four times more than the extreme estimates

***Standard Deviation***: **σ = (P − O) / 6** — quantifies schedule uncertainty per activity; used to calculate confidence intervals for the project completion date

***Network Diagram***: Activities are represented as nodes or arrows in a directed acyclic graph; dependencies between activities are modelled explicitly

***Critical Path***: The longest path through the network determines the minimum project duration; any delay on the critical path delays the whole project

***Float / Slack***: Time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project end date; activities on the critical path have zero float

***Probabilistic Scheduling***: Unlike CPM (which uses single-point estimates), PERT treats duration as a random variable, enabling statistical confidence ranges for milestones

***Origin***: Developed in 1958 by D.G. Malcolm, J.H. Roseboom, C.E. Clark, and W. Fazar at Booz Allen Hamilton for the US Navy's Polaris submarine missile programme

***Key Proponents***: D.G. Malcolm, J.H. Roseboom, C.E. Clark, W. Fazar ("Application of a Technique for Research and Development Program Evaluation", 1959)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Estimating effort and schedule for projects with significant uncertainty
* Planning R&D, software development, or any novel work where duration is hard to predict
* Communicating schedule risk and confidence levels to stakeholders
* Identifying the critical path to focus risk management and resource allocation
* Complementing Story Points or T-shirt sizing with a probabilistic time dimension

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* MoSCoW
* User Story Mapping
* Impact Mapping

### Premortem

***Full Name***: Project Premortem

***Also known as***: Pre-mortem, prospective hindsight exercise

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **The failure is a premise, not a possibility.** The group is told the plan has already failed, comprehensively, and is asked why. This is the whole technique; everything else is staging.
* **Prospective hindsight.** Explaining an event stated as fact produces more concrete reasons than speculating about an event that might happen.
* **Before commitment, not after.** A postmortem examines a corpse; a premortem examines a plan that can still be changed.
* **Everyone writes first.** Each participant lists reasons independently before anything is shared, so the most senior voice does not set the frame.
* **Round-robin collection.** Reasons are read out one per person per turn, which surfaces the quiet objections that a free discussion buries.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Before committing to a plan that is hard to reverse -- a migration, a re-platforming, a fixed-date release
* When a team has converged suspiciously fast and nobody is arguing
* When the people who see the risks report to the people who made the plan
* As a complement to a risk register: the register lists known risks, the premortem generates the ones nobody wrote down

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Softening the question.** Asking "what could go wrong?" instead of "it failed -- why?" reverts the exercise to ordinary risk brainstorming and loses the effect the technique is named for.
* **Treating it as pessimism.** The purpose is to license dissent, not to kill the plan. It usually ends with a modified plan, not a cancelled one.
* **Running it after the decision.** Once commitment is public, the findings have nowhere to go.

## **Criticism**:

* **The evidence chain is weaker than the citation suggests.** Behavioural economist Jason Collins documents that the widely repeated "30 percent" figure does not say what it is used to say. https://corporate.jcx.au/premortem[Collins] traces it to Mitchell, Russo and Pennington (1989), whose result is that prospective hindsight increases the **number** of reasons generated -- and notes explicitly: "Mitchell, Russo, and Pennington (1989) did not assess the quality of the reasons." The common paraphrase, that the technique improves the ability to **correctly identify** reasons by 30 percent, originates in Klein's 2007 restatement rather than in the study.
* **The academic literature is thin.** Collins states it plainly: "The academic literature on the premortem is thin." The technique's standing rests largely on practitioner reports and on Klein's own 2010 study with Veinott and Wiggins, not on independent replication.
* **No independent methodological critique was found.** A search in English and German turned up no failed replication, no meta-analysis, and no peer-reviewed critique of the technique itself. Note the frame: the journals where such an evaluation would most plausibly sit -- work on structured analytic techniques in _Intelligence and National Security_ and the _International Journal of Intelligence and CounterIntelligence_ -- are paywalled and were not read. This is an absence in our search, not a demonstrated absence in the literature.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Established and unchanged.** Klein's own description in https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/seeing-what-others-dont/202101/the-pre-mortem-method[Psychology Today] (January 2021) matches the 2007 original; there is no revised edition or successor method to drift toward. He dates the technique's origin to roughly three decades before that writing, with the first formal description in "Performing a Project Premortem", _Harvard Business Review_ 85(9), 18–19, September 2007.
* **The failure modes Klein names are execution errors, not limits.** He lists three: softening the question, running it too slowly, and letting a senior participant dominate instead of going round-robin. These are the author's caveats about his own method, which is a different thing from independent criticism.

### Pugh-Matrix

***Full Name***: Pugh Decision Matrix (also Pugh Controlled Convergence)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Matrix layout***: Criteria as ROWS, alternatives as COLUMNS
***Reference (baseline)***: One alternative is designated as reference — scored entirely as 0/S
***Relative scoring***: Each alternative rated against the reference: Better (+), Same (S), Worse (−)
***Summary rows***: Σ(+), Σ(−), Σ(S), and Net Score per alternative at bottom of matrix
***Structured evaluation***: Systematic comparison across multiple dimensions
***Team decision-making***: Facilitates group consensus
***Hybrid solutions***: Combine strengths of different alternatives
***Iterative refinement***: Multiple rounds to converge on best solution

***Key Proponent***: Stuart Pugh ("Total Design", 1991)

[discrete]
## **Variants** (use as qualifier for consistent results):

***Unweighted 3-Point Pugh Matrix***: Original form. Default when no qualifier is given.
***Weighted 3-Point Pugh Matrix***: Criteria carry importance weights. Standard in Six Sigma / QFD contexts.
***Weighted 5-Point Pugh Matrix***: Finer granularity for closely ranked alternatives.
***Pugh Controlled Convergence***: Iterative multi-round process with elimination, hybrid creation, and reference rotation.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Multiple viable alternatives exist
* Decision criteria are known but trade-offs are unclear
* Team needs to reach consensus
* Architecture or technology selection decisions

### QFD

***Full Name***: Quality Function Deployment (品質機能展開, hinshitsu kinō tenkai)

***Also known as***: the House of Quality (its best-known matrix, not the method itself); voice-of-the-customer deployment

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Deployment, Not Translation***: QFD carries customer needs through a chain of matrices — customer needs into technical characteristics, those into part characteristics, those into process and production requirements. Each matrix inherits the priorities of the one before, so a need that mattered at the start still has weight at the machine. The word in the name is **deployment**: priority propagates.

***The House of Quality***: The first matrix, and the signature artifact. Customer needs (the WHATs) form the rows, measurable technical characteristics (the HOWs) the columns, and the body records how strongly each characteristic serves each need. Side rooms hold customer importance ratings and a competitive benchmark; the basement holds target values for each characteristic.

***The Correlation Roof Is the Part Nothing Else Has***: The triangular roof sits above the columns and records how the **technical characteristics relate to each other** — which ones reinforce, and, crucially, which ones conflict. Lighter and stiffer; faster and cheaper to run; more secure and simpler to operate. A `pugh-matrix` scores options against criteria and a `kano-model` classifies needs; neither asks what the engineering parameters do to each other. The roof forces those tradeoffs into the open before a design is chosen.

***Targets, Not Wishes***: The output is a ranked set of technical characteristics with numeric target values. "Responsive" becomes a millisecond figure. QFD is the machinery that gets from adjective to number.

***Customer Voice Stays Customer Voice***: Needs are recorded in the customer's words and only then mapped. The discipline exists because the usual failure is an engineer silently substituting a solution for a need.

***Key Proponents***: Yoji Akao and Shigeru Mizuno developed the method in Japan; Wikipedia dates the start to 1966 and records that "with the late Shigeru Mizuno, he developed Quality Function Deployment". The first large-scale application is the one everyone cites: the House of Quality "appeared in 1972 in the design of an oil tanker by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries". The yard is almost always named as Kobe; no primary source naming it could be confirmed, so this anchor stops at the company. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoji_Akao[Wikipedia, Yoji Akao] and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_function_deployment[Wikipedia, Quality function deployment].

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Turning a pile of vague stakeholder wishes into a ranked, measurable set of technical targets
* Early product or architecture definition, before options are generated — QFD frames the criteria a `pugh-matrix` will later score against
* Whenever quality attributes conflict and somebody has to name the tradeoff out loud
* As the requirements front end of a `dmaic` or DMADV project, where the customer's CTQs need to be derived rather than asserted
* Cross-functional work where marketing, design, and engineering keep talking past each other

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "QFD is the House of Quality" — the House is one matrix in a chain; the QFD Institute calls this "a most common myth"
* ❌ "QFD scores options" — it derives characteristics and targets; scoring competing designs is the `pugh-matrix` job
* ❌ "QFD replaces talking to customers" — it is a way to process the voice of the customer, not a substitute for collecting it
* ❌ "Bigger matrices are more thorough" — size is the dominant failure mode
* ✓ "The roof is where the conflicts live" — the most quoted reason to reach for QFD rather than a simpler tool

## **Criticism**:

* **The numbers it produces are not the kind of numbers engineers think they are.** Andrew Olewnik and Kemper Lewis, "Limitations of the House of Quality to provide quantitative design information", _International Journal of Quality & Reliability Management_ 25(2), 125–146 (2008), https://doi.org/10.1108/02656710810846916[DOI 10.1108/02656710810846916]. They argue that while the House supports conceptual design, "the quantitative information that results is largely invalid", because designers interpret the numerical outputs in ways the method's own assumptions do not license — and that relying on those outputs "can lead to potentially invalid and/or poor decisions". https://www.emerald.com/ijqrm/article-abstract/25/2/125/139984/Limitations-of-the-House-of-Quality-to-provide[Abstract at Emerald].
* **The matrix does not scale, and its authors' own institute says so.** The QFD Institute: "In some projects, the HoQ can have 1000 rows x 1000 columns = 1,000,000 relationships to examine and quantify. This could take years to complete!" It adds that "95% of the customer needs and functional/non-functional requirements identified in HoQ are too low priority to assign engineering resources or budget to improve." https://www.qfdi.org/classical-blitz-or-reverse[QFD Institute, "Classical, Blitz, or Reverse QFD"].
* **Western practice adopted the picture and dropped the method.** Glenn Mazur, via the QFD Institute: "Consider the HoQ as a highway interchange between the customer and the engineer. To limit QFD to only this tool is like building the interchange in an empty field without connecting roads." The Institute calls HoQ-only QFD "a most common myth" and notes the House "is neither the starting point nor the finish in most QFD studies." https://www.qfdi.org/house-of-quality[QFD Institute, "What is House of Quality (HoQ)?"].
* **The arithmetic was questionable from the start.** Mazur again, writing on the ISO standard: "Quality professionals have long decried the abacus math in Japanese models brought to the U.S. in the 1980s" — ordinal rating scales lacking "equality of intervals" were nevertheless multiplied and summed. https://www.qualitymag.com/articles/98216-iso-16355-the-new-standard-for-qfd-part-1[Mazur, "ISO 16355: The New Standard for QFD, Part 1", _Quality_ magazine, 26 August 2024].

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **QFD is standardised, and the standard demotes the House.** The nine-part ISO 16355 series covers QFD; Part 1 is https://www.sis.se/en/produkter/sociology-services-company-organization/quality/application-of-statistical-methods/iso-16355-12021/[ISO 16355-1:2021, "Application of statistical and related methods to new technology and product development process — Part 1: General principles and perspectives of quality function deployment (QFD)"], edition 2, approved 31 May 2021, superseding the 2015 first edition. Mazur summarises the shift: "The House of Quality and other time- and resource-intensive matrices are now optional and more efficient effect-to-cause diagrams are recommended for most projects."
* **Blitz QFD is the lean answer to the complexity complaint.** The QFD Institute created it "to address the trend towards Lean Thinking and Agile Development"; in Blitz QFD "the House of Quality may be completely unnecessary", replaced by a Maximum Value Table and an effect-to-cause wishbone that deploy only the top-priority needs.
* **Note the split between name and artifact.** The strong prior in most models is the House of Quality picture, not the full deployment chain or the ISO process. When you name QFD, say which you mean.

### Second-Order Thinking

***Full Name***: Second-Order Thinking

***Also known as***: Second-level thinking (Howard Marks); second- and third-order consequences (Ray Dalio)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

* **And then what?** The first-order effect is the one the decision was made for. The second-order effect is what happens once people adapt to the first.
* **First-order effects are visible and immediate; second-order effects are delayed and often dominant.** The delay is why they lose arguments they should win.
* **Chains, not lists.** The move is to follow one consequence into the next, rather than to enumerate more consequences at the same level.
* **The consequences that decide the outcome are usually behavioural.** Rules change incentives, incentives change behaviour, and behaviour produces the effect nobody planned.
* **Applies to the status quo too.** Not acting has second-order effects as well, and they are easy to omit because nothing appears to happen.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Evaluating a policy or process change that people will adapt to -- review rules, quality gates, on-call schedules, incentive structures
* Assessing a technical decision whose cost arrives later than its benefit
* Whenever a proposal's argument consists entirely of its immediate effect
* As a counterweight when a metric is about to become a target

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* **Adding more items instead of going deeper.** Twenty first-order effects are still first-order. One consequence followed three steps is the technique.
* **Treating it as an argument against acting.** It changes what you decide, not whether you decide. Inaction gets the same analysis.
* **Confusing it with risk analysis.** A risk is an event that may or may not occur. A second-order effect is a consequence a decision sets in motion once people adapt to it -- likely rather than certain, but systematic rather than accidental, and nobody has reacted to it yet.

## **Criticism**:

* **No named critique of the term itself was found.** A search in English and German produced no cited author arguing that second-order thinking is trivial, unfalsifiable or unusable. What search engines return as criticism -- analysis paralysis, time cost, context dependence -- appears in advice blogs without attribution and does not qualify.
* **The literature that popularised it is contested.** The criticism lands on the mental-models genre rather than on this term. Cedric Chin names Farnam Street directly in https://commoncog.com/the-mental-model-fallacy/["The Mental Model Fallacy"]: "The mental model fallacy is that it's worth it to read descriptions of mental models, written and aggregated by non-practitioners, in the pursuit of self-improvement and success", and adds that "the most valuable mental models do not survive codification". Richard Hughes-Jones argues in https://www.richardhughesjones.com/mental-models/["The Mental Models Paradox"] that such frameworks "make us smarter but only up to a point, after which they can actually constrain our thinking". Data scientist Boris Gorelik reviews Parrish's _The Great Mental Models_ at https://gorelik.net/2020/02/12/book-review-great-mental-models-by-shane-parrish[two out of five], calling it "ambitious but yet shallow".
* **None of those three critics discusses second-order thinking.** They criticise the packaging, not this entry. The distinction matters, and readers should not take the citations as a verdict on the technique.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The name that works is not the name in the sources.** Howard Marks contrasts "first-level" with "second-**level** thinking" in https://cup.columbia.edu/book/the-most-important-thing/9780231153683/[_The Most Important Thing_] (Columbia University Press, 2011). Ray Dalio's principle reads https://www.principles.com/principles/7658aec7-c3f6-4248-8cc6-57aa84b0a955/["Consider second- and third-order consequences, not just first-order ones"]. Neither writes "second-order thinking". That phrasing belongs to the popularisers, chiefly https://fs.blog/second-order-thinking/[Farnam Street], which adopts it as its own heading while stating plainly that Marks "calls it second-level thinking" and quoting Dalio on "second- and third-order consequences" -- the rename is deliberate and documented on the page that performs it. The entry is named for the string that reliably triggers the concept, not for the string with the better provenance -- and those diverge here. See the [prior-test register](#/prior-tests) for the measurement behind that choice.
* **The idea is much older than the label.** Frédéric Bastiat's "Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas" states the core move for economics: judge a measure by its unseen later effects, not only by its visible immediate one. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Ce_qu%E2%80%99on_voit_et_ce_qu%E2%80%99on_ne_voit_pas[French Wikisource] carries the text and dates the pamphlet to July 1850, Bastiat's last. Robert K. Merton formalised a close relative in "The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action", _American Sociological Review_ 1(6), December 1936, 894–904.

### SWOT

***Full Name***: SWOT Analysis

***Also known as***: SWOT Matrix, TOWS Analysis

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

SWOT = **S**trengths / **W**eaknesses / **O**pportunities / **T**hreats

***Strengths***: Internal positive attributes and resources that give the subject an advantage over others

***Weaknesses***: Internal negative attributes or limitations that place the subject at a disadvantage relative to others

***Opportunities***: External factors or trends that the subject could exploit to its advantage

***Threats***: External factors or conditions that could cause problems or jeopardise the subject's success

***Internal vs. External***: Strengths and Weaknesses are internal (within control); Opportunities and Threats are external (environmental)

***Present vs. Future orientation***: Strengths and Weaknesses reflect the current state; Opportunities and Threats look toward future conditions

***TOWS variant***: Systematic derivation of strategies by cross-referencing SWOT quadrants (SO, ST, WO, WT strategies)

***Key Proponent***: Albert Humphrey (Stanford Research Institute, 1960s–1970s)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Strategic planning for a product, project, organisation, or technology choice
* Competitive analysis to understand market positioning
* Evaluating an architectural or technology decision holistically
* Team retrospectives to assess current state before planning next steps
* Business case preparation and stakeholder communication

**Related Anchors**:

* Pugh Matrix
* Wardley Mapping
* MoSCoW

[discrete]
## **Criticism**:

* Hill & Westbrook, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0024-6301(96)00095-7["SWOT Analysis: It's Time for a Product Recall"] (Long Range Planning, 1997) — in a study of 20 companies, SWOT produced long, vague, unweighted bullet lists that were never verified and never used in the subsequent strategy process
* Criticized as a static snapshot: no prioritisation, no probability or impact weighting, and no built-in step from analysis to action — the TOWS variant exists precisely to patch this gap
* Alternatives named in the discourse: structured option evaluation (e.g. Pugh Matrix) and evolution-aware positioning (Wardley Mapping) where SWOT's four static quadrants fall short

### Toyota Kata

***Full Name***: Toyota Kata — Managing People for Improvement, Adaptiveness and Superior Results (Mike Rother, McGraw-Hill, 4 August 2009)

***Also known as***: Improvement Kata and Coaching Kata, IK/CK, Starter Kata, scientific thinking routine

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Two Routines, Not One Method***: Toyota Kata names a **pair**. The Improvement Kata is what the learner practises; the Coaching Kata is what the coach practises while the learner works. Naming only one of them loses the point, because the routine survives in an organisation through the coaching, not through the worksheet.

***The Improvement Kata, in Four Steps***: The learner cycles through:
* **Direction or challenge** — where the organisation is going, set long-range and rarely revisited
* **Grasp the current condition** — measured and observed at the process itself, not inferred from a report
* **Establish the next target condition** — a description of how the process should operate by a set date
* **Experiment toward the target condition** — one obstacle at a time, one experiment at a time, each with a prediction

***A Target Condition Is a Described Process Condition***: This is the load-bearing idea and the one most often dropped. A target condition says how the process **works** — the pattern, the sequence, the characteristics, plus the date — not merely which number should be higher by when. That is exactly what separates it from an `okr` Key Result or a KPI target. A number tells you whether you arrived; a target condition tells you what arriving looks like, so an experiment can be designed against it.

***The Coaching Kata Is Five Questions***: Christoph Roser renders the card as: 1. "What is the target condition?" 2. "What is the actual condition now?" 3. "What obstacles prevent you from reaching the target condition? Which ones are you addressing now?" 4. "What is your next step (your next PDCA cycle)?" 5. "Where can we go and see what we have learned from taking that step?" The coach asks; the coach does not answer.

***The Threshold of Knowledge***: Work happens at the edge of what is known. Where the path is clear, no kata is needed. The routine exists for the grey zone between current and target condition, where the honest answer is "we do not know yet" and the only way forward is a cheap, fast, predicted experiment.

***Starter Kata, Not Finishing Kata***: Rother calls the prescribed forms **starter** kata — scaffolding for practising scientific thinking, meant to be outgrown. Treating the worksheet as the deliverable inverts the intent.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Chronic problems that resisted a one-shot fix, where the cause is genuinely unknown
* Turning a vague "we should get faster" into something testable: a described condition plus a date
* Coaching — the Five Questions give a manager a way to develop a person without taking the problem away from them
* Any place where goals are set but no route is described; the kata forces the gap between target and current condition into the open
* As the daily-practice counterpart to a project-shaped method such as `dmaic`

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "A target condition is a target number" — it describes how the process should operate, with the number as one attribute among several
* ❌ "The Five Questions are the method" — they are the coach's half, worthless without a learner who has practised the Improvement Kata
* ❌ "Kata means rigid ritual" — Rother's **starter** kata are practice forms to be outgrown, like scales for a musician
* ❌ "Toyota teaches this under this name" — Rother derived and named the routines from observing Toyota; the framing is his
* ✓ "It is PDCA with a coach and a described destination" — a fair short summary

## **Criticism**:

* **The training industry has overtaken the practice.** Christoph Roser, professor at Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences: "the promotion and training of kata has overtaken the actual improvement process", and on the credential market, "I am not sure if a ~3-hour online Toyota Kata course really prepares someone to be a coach" — "true skill comes only from practice". He states plainly, "I am not overly fond of it" about kata-as-business, while holding that the underlying concept "is sound and valid". https://www.allaboutlean.com/toyota-kata/[Roser, "Toyota Kata"] (11 September 2018).
* **Managers grab the coaching card first.** Mark Rosenthal observes that managers "want to jump right into coaching" because "the '5 Questions' and some of them think that is all there is to it", and warns: "Until you have _struggled as a learner_ to apply the Improvement Kata…please don't just pick up the 5 Questions card." https://theleanthinker.com/2017/12/21/mike-rother-the-toyota-kata-practice-guide/[Rosenthal, "Mike Rother: The Toyota Kata Practice Guide"] (21 December 2017).
* **The 2009 book told you what, not how.** The same review describes the original as "a fairly high-level summary of research findings" that largely omitted "step-by-step guide of _how to practice and what to practice_" — which is why a separate practice guide had to follow eight years later.
* **Scientific thinking arrived without scientific scepticism.** Bob Emiliani credits Rother's 2009 book with putting "scientific thinking" into the Lean vocabulary, then argues the community never took the rest of the package: "The Lean community is anything but scientifically skeptical", with practitioners behaving as "true believers". https://bobemiliani.substack.com/p/scientific-thinking-without-skepticism[Emiliani, "Scientific Thinking Without Skepticism"] (30 June 2026).

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The how-to gap was closed by a second book.** Rother published _The Toyota Kata Practice Guide_ (McGraw-Hill, 2017) as the practice manual the 2009 book lacked — confirmed in Rosenthal's review above. When a model has read only the 2009 material, expect the concepts without the drills.
* **Absorbed into the Toyota Way rather than replacing it.** Jeffrey Liker restructured his Toyota Way model to put scientific thinking at its centre and positions the kata as the mechanism for developing it: "perhaps we can view the kata as a catalyst that juices scientific thinking, which, in turn, is the engine that drives the Toyota Way." He is explicit that this is not a substitution: "Does this mean that Toyota Kata now replaces the Toyota Way since scientific thinking is at the center? Certainly not." https://www.lean.org/the-lean-post/articles/the-toyota-way-and-toyota-kata-how-do-they-fit/[Liker, Lean Enterprise Institute] (18 March 2022).
* **The name is Rother's, not Toyota's.** Liker describes Rother as adopting "kata" from martial arts practice to label routines he observed. We found no source showing that Toyota itself teaches these routines under that name — treat "Toyota Kata" as the title of a book about Toyota, not as internal Toyota vocabulary.

### Wardley Mapping

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Value chain***: Map components from user needs down

***Evolution axis***: Genesis → Custom → Product → Commodity

***Movement***: Components naturally evolve over time

***Situational awareness***: Understanding the landscape before deciding

***Gameplay patterns***: Common strategic moves

***Climatic patterns***: Forces that affect all players

***Doctrine***: Universal principles of good strategy

***Inertia***: Resistance to change in organizations

***Strategic planning***: Visual approach to strategy

***Build-Buy-Partner decisions***: Based on evolution stage

***Key Proponent***: Simon Wardley

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Strategic technology planning
* Build vs. buy decisions
* Understanding competitive landscape
* Communicating strategy visually
* Identifying opportunities for disruption

---

## Testing & Quality Practices

### Andon

***Full Name***: Andon (行灯), Japanese for "paper lantern" — the signal system of the Toyota Production System

***Also known as***: andon cord, andon board, andon light, stop-the-line authority, the visible half of jidoka

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Two Halves, One Word***: Andon names both the **display** — a board or lamp above the line showing the status of every station — and the **trigger**, the cord or button an operator pulls when something is wrong. Wikipedia's definition covers the display side: "a system which notifies managerial, maintenance, and other workers of a quality or process problem."

***The Radical Part Is the Authority, Not the Hardware***: Any operator may signal, and the signal is binding on everyone above them. That is an inversion of ordinary factory hierarchy, and it is the part that does not ship in the box. Mark Graban puts it flatly: "It's not the cord or a button that matters… It's the process and the management system that matters."

***Three Colours, One Sentence Each***: Jane Slaughter's description of the board: "A green light indicates there are no problems; a yellow light shows that the operator is having trouble keeping up and needs help; and a red light means there is a problem which requires stopping the line."

***It Is a Call for Help Before It Is a Stop***: Graban corrects the popular version: a pull "sounds an alarm and turns on a yellow light", the line keeps moving to the next **fixed position**, and a team leader gets a window of "maybe 5 to 30 seconds" to respond. If they succeed, "the line never stops at all." Stopping at a fixed position — between work cycles, not mid-task — is deliberate, so an interrupted job does not compound the defect.

***A Rising Pull Count Is a Good Sign***: Early in an andon rollout, more pulls mean more problems **surfacing**, not more problems existing. Graban's comparison is the standard evidence: Toyota's Georgetown plant recorded roughly 2,000 pulls a week, a new Ford plant in Dearborn two — not because Ford had fewer problems, but because its workers did not trust the response. A count near zero is the alarming reading.

***The Visible Half of Jidoka***: Jidoka — automation with a human touch — means a process stops itself when it produces a defect. Andon is how a **human** exercises the same authority, and how the stop becomes visible to everyone at once.

***Software Analogues***: A red build that nobody may build on top of; blocking a deploy; halting a canary rollout on a failing metric; a pager that any engineer may fire without asking permission. In each case the mechanism is trivial and the authority is the whole design.

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Establishing who may halt work — the naming makes the authority explicit rather than implicit
* Red-build discipline and stop-the-line rules around CI, the direct descendant of the idea (`red-green-tdd`)
* Canary and progressive rollouts, where an automatic or manual abort is the andon
* Diagnosing a quiet team: if nobody ever stops anything, ask whether the authority exists or only the button does
* Designing escalation paths where the responder, not the reporter, owns the problem once the signal is raised

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "One worker pulling the cord stops the whole factory" — Graban calls this the myth; buffers between sections absorb a local stop, and the line halts only at the next fixed position
* ❌ "Andon is a line-stop device" — it is first a call for help; most pulls are resolved before any stop
* ❌ "Install the cord and you have andon" — without a responder within seconds and a no-blame reaction, the cord is decoration
* ❌ "Many pulls means the process is bad" — early on it means the process is finally visible
* ✓ "Andon is jidoka performed by a person" — accurate, and the reason it belongs next to `kaizen` rather than to tooling

## **Criticism**:

* **Read from the other side of the line, the board is a pacing device.** Jane Slaughter, in her account of what Labor Notes called "management by stress", treats andon as the emblem of the whole system: "Management by stress is the most sophisticated version of team concept, even though it contradicts many traditional notions of good management." The objection is precise, and it is about tuning: "The ideal state is achieved when the plant is running with all stations just on the line between green and yellow." A system deliberately balanced at the edge of "cannot keep up" uses the operator's distress signal as its control input. https://www.multinationalmonitor.org/hyper/issues/1990/01/slaughter.html[Slaughter, "Management by Stress", _Multinational Monitor_, January/February 1990]. Slaughter is co-author, with Mike Parker, of _Choosing Sides: Unions and the Team Concept_.
* **The transplanted version failed on arrival.** The Toyota/Ford pull-count gap is usually told as a culture story, but it is also a criticism of the mechanism: copied without the management system, the cord produced silence. Graban: Ford's rare pulls reflected worker distrust of how management would respond, not a better process. https://www.leanblog.org/2026/06/andon-cord-stop-the-line-myth/[Graban, "No, One Toyota Worker Can't Stop the Whole Factory"] (29 June 2026).
* **The popular story is wrong in its details, and the details carry the design.** Graban's whole piece is a correction of the andon legend circulating in management writing and software conference talks — the instant total stop, the lone heroic worker. The fixed-position stop, the 5-to-30-second response window and the required proximity of capable help are what make the practice work, and they are exactly what the legend omits.

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **Toyota replaced the cords with buttons.** Starting at the Toyota City plant in 2013, overhead cords gave way to wireless, waist-high yellow buttons, rolled out gradually worldwide while some plants kept cords. The stated reasons are mundane: "reduce overhead clutter, improve safety by removing tools…that could snag on the cord" and "simplify line reconfiguration". https://www.leanblog.org/2014/08/toyota-andon-cord-buttons/[Graban, "Why Toyota is Eliminating the Andon Cord from its Factories"] (2 August 2014, updated 17 May 2026). The word "cord" in "andon cord" is therefore already historical at the source.
* **The term survives in software mostly as metaphor.** "Pull the andon cord" is common shorthand in DevOps and SRE writing for stopping a release. The prior most training data carries is this metaphorical sense plus the myth version; the fixed-position stop and the responder-within-seconds requirement are usually absent, which is precisely why naming the anchor is worth doing.

### Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA)

***Full Name***: Arrange-Act-Assert — three named phases for the body of a single unit test, abbreviated "3A" by the author who named it

***Also known as***: 3A, the AAA pattern, Setup-Exercise-Verify (the first three phases of Gerard Meszaros' Four-Phase Test), Build-Operate-Check (the same split under different names in Robert C. Martin's _Clean Code_)

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Write the Name Out — the Acronym Points Somewhere Else***: "Arrange-Act-Assert" is the anchor. "AAA" is not: it is the standard abbreviation for Authentication, Authorization and Accounting in network access control, and that is what a model retrieves from the three letters alone (see **Current Status**). Spell it out in prompts, in test comments and in team vocabulary.

***Three Phases, One Action***: Bill Wake's own definitions. **Arrange**: "Set up the object to be tested. We may need to surround the object with collaborators." **Act**: "Act on the object (through some mutator). You may need to give it parameters." **Assert**: "Make claims about the object, its collaborators, its parameters, and possibly (rarely!!) global state." The decisive word is **one** action: a second Act in the same test means a second test.

***Origin, Dated by the Author Himself***: Wake's post https://xp123.com/3a-arrange-act-assert/["3A – Arrange, Act, Assert"] is dated 26 April 2011 and says: "I (Bill Wake) observed and named the pattern in 2001." The 2001 date is therefore the author's own recollection, written down ten years later, not a contemporaneous record.

***The Fourth Phase Is the One AAA Drops***: Meszaros' Four-Phase Test names "fixture setup, exercise SUT, result verification and fixture teardown". AAA renames the first three and leaves the fourth implicit — "In the fourth phase, we tear down the test fixture to put the world back into the state in which you found it." In a test that touches files, databases, clocks or global state, that omission is yours to fix; AAA will not remind you.

***Not the Same Altitude as Given-When-Then***: Given-When-Then shapes an **acceptance scenario** in the language of the domain, written to be read by people who do not read code (`gherkin`, `bdd-given-when-then`). Arrange-Act-Assert shapes the **body of one unit test** in code. The structures are parallel; the audience, the artifact and the level are not. Use Given-When-Then to agree on behaviour, Arrange-Act-Assert to lay out the test that checks it.

***A Swollen Arrange Is a Diagnosis***: When the Arrange block dwarfs Act and Assert, the test is telling you something about the design: too many collaborators, a constructor that demands irrelevant data, hidden dependencies. The two standard remedies are test doubles (`test-double-meszaros`) and builders that hide safe defaults (`test-data-builder`).

***Marking the Phases Is a Discipline, Not Decoration***: Meszaros' argument for writing the phases down: "Using comments to mark the phases of a Four-Phase Test is a good source of self-discipline in that it makes it very obvious when our tests are not Single Condition Tests."

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Asking for unit tests and wanting one behaviour per test instead of a single method that calls six things and asserts on all of them
* Reviewing tests: the three phases make it visible where a failure comes from — bad setup, wrong call, or wrong expectation
* Teaching test structure, where the named phases give beginners a shape to fill
* Refactoring a test suite whose Arrange sections have grown out of control, as the entry point to builders and test doubles
* Next to `bdd-given-when-then` when the team needs both levels and keeps confusing them

[discrete]
## **Common Misunderstandings**:

* ❌ "AAA" — the bare acronym retrieves Authentication, Authorization and Accounting, not testing; the written-out name is the anchor
* ❌ "Arrange-Act-Assert means exactly one assertion per test" — contested, and Wake himself writes of that guideline: "I don't follow that guideline too closely." See **Criticism**
* ❌ "It is just Given-When-Then for programmers" — same shape, different altitude and different audience
* ❌ "Three phases cover every test" — teardown is missing by construction, and shared setup and multi-step scenarios need adaptations
* ❌ "The comments are the pattern" — the single Act is the pattern; the comments only make a violation obvious
* ✓ "One action per test, with setup and expectation visibly separated from it" — accurate, and the part worth insisting on

## **Criticism**:

* **The strict reading — one assertion per test — is contested, and the pattern's own author is on the permissive side.** Dave Astels made the case for the rule in "One Assertion Per Test" (23 February 2004), arguing that tests are specifications of behaviour and that the rule keeps you working in "the smallest steps possible, both for the finest-grained long-term verification, and for the most flexible design evolution"; where a test wants several assertions, he decomposes it into separate fixtures instead. Wake answers eleven years later in "Multiple Asserts Are OK": "I first heard the 'one assert per test' idea years ago from Dave Astels, and others have picked it up since then", and "Multiple assertions can be a sign of trouble in tests. But as you'll see by the end, some situations make good use of groups of assertions." https://www.artima.com/weblogs/viewpost.jsp?thread=35578[Astels, "One Assertion Per Test", Artima, 23 February 2004] and https://www.industriallogic.com/blog/multiple-asserts-are-ok/[Wake, "Multiple Asserts Are OK", Industrial Logic, 29 September 2015]. Anyone who cites "AAA" as authority for a hard one-assert rule is citing a position its author declined to hold.
* **The three phases do not fit every test shape, and the teaching literature says so.** The Freie Universität Berlin's AG Software Engineering, in the course material for its Programmierpraktikum (Sommersemester 2026), names two cases where the plain structure breaks down: "Viele Tests teilen dasselbe aufwändige Setup — Kopieren kostet Zeit und erzeugt Fehlerquellen", and "Ein Testszenario besteht aus mehreren aufeinander aufbauenden Schritten, deren Zwischenzustände jeweils überprüft werden sollen." Their remedies are helper functions for the shared Arrange and an A-AA-AA shape with several Act/Assert cycles. The page presents these as adaptations rather than as grounds to abandon the pattern. https://www.inf.fu-berlin.de/inst/ag-se/teaching/K-ProPra-2026-04/pytest_aaa.html[AG Software Engineering, FU Berlin, "Das AAA-Muster: Strukturierte Unit-Tests"].
* **Asserting the precondition before acting is the other standing patch.** "Arrange-Assert-Act-Assert" adds a check that the setup really produced the state the test assumes, so a failure cannot be silently blamed on the action. Wake shows the shape himself in "Multiple Asserts Are OK": "// arrange / set up something hairy / // assert on setup / assert setup looks right / // act / probe a behavior / // assert / verify its consequences". The cost is that the test now has two kinds of assertion in it, and the reader has to tell them apart.
* **Teardown is a real gap, not a simplification.** Meszaros keeps the fourth phase for a reason — a test that does not put the world back breaks the next one — and AAA's three names give no place to put it. http://xunitpatterns.com/Four%20Phase%20Test.html[Meszaros, "Four-Phase Test", xunitpatterns.com] (the site serves plain HTTP only).

[discrete]
## **Current Status**:

* **The bare acronym anchors a different field entirely.** Asked "What is AAA?" in a clean room on `claude-haiku-4-5` (2026-10-03), the weak tier answered: "AAA stands for **Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting**, a security framework commonly used in networking and access control", went on through RADIUS and TACACS+, and mentioned the American Automobile Association before any testing sense. The written-out name is therefore the anchor; the acronym alone is not.
* **The prior behind the full name is dense enough to surface unprompted.** On a test-readability task measured the same day, the no-anchor baseline reached Arrange-Act-Assert by itself in two of four runs. Naming it makes the structure explicit and settles the one-assert question; it does not introduce an unfamiliar idea.

### BDD (Behavior-Driven Development)

***Also known as***: Specification by Example, Executable Specifications

[discrete]
## **Core Concepts**:

***Given-When-Then***: Structured scenario format — Given a precondition, When an action occurs, Then an expected outcome results

***Specification by Example***: Concrete examples as executable specifications that define system behavior

***Three Amigos***: Collaborative discovery sessions between developer, tester, and business representative

***Gherkin syntax***: Domain-specific language for writing human-readable, machine-executable scenarios

***Living documentation***: Tests that serve as always-current system documentation

***Outside-in specification***: Start from desired business behavior, work inward to implementation

***Ubiquitous language***: Shared vocabulary bridging technical and business stakeholders in scenarios

***Discovery workshops***: Structured conversations to uncover requirements through examples before implementation

***Key Proponent***: Dan North ("Introducing BDD", 2006), creator of JBehave which influenced Cucumber's design (Cucumber created by Aslak Hellesøy, 2008)

[discrete]
## **When to Use**:

* Cross-functional teams needing shared understanding of requirements
* Systems where business rules are complex and need clear documentation
* Projects requiring executable acceptance criteria
* Bridging communication gaps between technical and non-technical stakeholders

[discrete]
## **Related Anchors**:

* TDD, London School - Outside-in development approach that complements BDD
* TDD, Chicago School - Developer-focused TDD practice
* User Story Mapping - Requirements discovery that feeds BDD scenarios

### Defense in Depth
